topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Integers, factors and exact arithmetic

sections.heading: Structure before calculation
sections.body: An integer is a whole number, including zero and negative values. A prime has exactly two positive factors. Expressing a number as a product of primes exposes its structure: 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5. For a highest common factor, keep the smallest powers shared by both numbers. For a lowest common multiple, keep the largest powers appearing in either number.

sections.heading: Fractions and signs
sections.body: A fraction represents division. Use a common denominator to add or subtract; multiply numerators and denominators separately to multiply. Dividing by a fraction is multiplying by its reciprocal. Cancel common factors before multiplying to keep arithmetic manageable. A negative multiplied or divided by a negative gives a positive result; this sign rule does not replace the rules for addition.

sections.heading: Accuracy and sensible answers
sections.body: Use place value when rounding. Decimal places count digits after the decimal point; significant figures start at the first non-zero digit. Keep exact fractions during intermediate work and round at the end. Estimate before calculating so that a misplaced decimal point becomes obvious. Recurring decimals can be turned into fractions by multiplying to align the repeated blocks, then subtracting.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A prime-factor decomposition provides a useful check on both factor methods: HCF × LCM equals the product of the two positive starting integers. In a recurring-decimal conversion, choose powers of ten so the recurring blocks line up. If x = 0.272727…, then 100x − x = 27, giving x = 27/99 = 3/11. For a mixed recurring decimal, align the repeating section rather than subtracting digits that do not match. An exact answer keeps the fraction; a rounded decimal should carry the requested accuracy.

sections.heading: Use prime factors to find HCF and LCM
sections.body:
Write each number as a product of primes. For 18 and 24, use 18 = 2 × 3² and 24 = 2³ × 3.

The HCF uses the smallest power of each shared prime: 2 × 3 = 6. The LCM uses the largest power of every prime needed: 2³ × 3² = 72. The HCF divides both numbers. The LCM is a multiple of both. These checks catch a common mix-up.

sections.heading: Make fraction calculations easier
sections.body:
Look for factors you can cancel before multiplying fractions. In 15/28 × 14/25, cancel 15 with 25 to give 3 and 5, and 14 with 28 to give 1 and 2. The result is 3/10.

For addition, first use a common denominator: 2/3 + 1/4 = 8/12 + 3/12 = 11/12. Do not add the denominators. Keep a fraction exact until the question asks for a rounded decimal.

topics.tip: HCF cannot exceed either starting number. LCM must be divisible by both.

worked.question: Find the HCF and LCM of 72 and 90.
steps: The common factors with smallest powers give HCF = 2 × 3² = 18.
The largest powers give LCM = 2³ × 3² × 5 = 360.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Powers, roots, standard form and surds

sections.heading: Indices describe repeated multiplication
sections.body: For the same non-zero base, multiply powers by adding indices and divide by subtracting them. Raising a power to a power multiplies the indices. A zero power is 1; a negative power means a reciprocal. A fractional power combines a root with a power: x^(2/3) is the cube root of x, squared, where the real expression is defined.

sections.heading: Scale without a long string of zeros
sections.body: Standard form is a × 10ⁿ, where 1 ≤ a < 10 and n is an integer. Multiply the coefficients and the powers of ten separately, then renormalise. For addition, first express both values using the same power of ten. Your calculator display may use E to mean ×10 to a power, rather than the mathematical constant e.

sections.heading: Higher: keep irrational values exact
sections.body: Simplify a surd by extracting square factors: √72 = 6√2. Like surds combine as like algebraic terms; unlike surds usually do not. Rationalising a denominator changes the form without changing the value. For a two-term denominator, multiply by its conjugate so the denominator becomes a difference of squares. Keep an exact answer when the question requests one.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: Index laws apply to multiplication of equal bases, not addition: 2³ + 2² is 12, not 2⁵. To rationalise 1/(√5 + 2), multiply by √5 − 2 on the top and bottom. The denominator becomes 5 − 4 = 1. When using fractional indices, check real-number restrictions before taking an even root. Standard form is useful for estimating as well as computing: a result with coefficient 0.6 must be rewritten as 6 × 10⁻¹ times the remaining power of ten.

sections.heading: Handle negative and fractional powers
sections.body:
A negative power means a reciprocal: 5⁻² = 1/5² = 1/25. It does not make the answer negative. A fractional power combines a root and a power: 27^(2/3) means square the cube root of 27, giving 9.

Bracket a negative base. The expressions (−3)² and −3² have different meanings: the first is 9, while the second is −9 because the square is evaluated before the leading minus sign.

sections.heading: Separate powers of ten from ordinary numbers
sections.body:
To multiply numbers in standard form, multiply their coefficients and add the powers of ten. For (3 × 10⁴)(4 × 10⁻²), this gives 12 × 10² = 1.2 × 10³.

The final coefficient must be at least 1 and less than 10. When adding standard-form numbers, first give them the same power of ten. Index laws for multiplication cannot be used directly for a sum.

topics.tip: √(a + b) is not generally √a + √b.
topics.formula: aᵐ × aⁿ = a^(m+n); (aᵐ)ⁿ = a^(mn)

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Ratio, percentages, bounds and variation

sections.heading: Choose the correct whole
sections.body: Ratios compare quantities in matching units. Divide a total by the sum of the ratio parts, then multiply by each share. Percentage change compares the change with the original amount. Growth uses a multiplier above 1 and depreciation a multiplier below 1. Reverse percentage problems start from the final amount, so divide by the multiplier.

sections.heading: Repeated change and proportional models
sections.body: Compound growth applies the multiplier repeatedly: P(1 + r/100)ⁿ. Direct proportion has the form y = kx, or a stated power of x; inverse proportion has the form y = k/x. Find k using a known pair before predicting a new value. Do not assume proportionality just because both quantities increase.

sections.heading: Bounds express what rounding hides
sections.body: A length rounded to the nearest centimetre has a half-centimetre interval on each side. The lower endpoint is included; the upper is excluded under the usual school convention. For a maximum quotient of positive measurements, use the largest numerator and smallest denominator. A degree-of-accuracy answer must be justified by agreement between the calculated bounds.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: For a measurement recorded as 8.2 cm to the nearest 0.1 cm, the underlying interval is 8.15 ≤ length < 8.25. A compound calculation must use the most extreme combination that actually maximises or minimises the result. In an inverse-square relationship, doubling the input divides the output by four. Translate words such as proportional to the square into y = kx² before substituting. Ratios can also describe rates, but quantities with different dimensions should keep their units, for example kilometres per hour.

sections.heading: Share an amount using parts
sections.body:
To share £84 in the ratio 2:5, there are 2 + 5 = 7 parts altogether. One part is £84/7 = £12, so the shares are £24 and £60. Add them to check the total.

If you are told that the larger share is £60, that amount represents five parts, not all seven. Divide £60 by 5 to find one part. The wording tells you which quantity belongs to each part of the ratio.

sections.heading: Build a direct or inverse proportion rule
sections.body:
For direct proportion, y = kx. Use one known pair to find k, then use the same rule for other pairs. If y = 18 when x = 6, k = 3 and y = 3x.

For inverse proportion, y = k/x, so xy stays constant. If six identical workers take eight hours, the model gives 48 worker-hours. Twelve workers would take four hours only if the work can be shared equally without extra delays. State that assumption when judging a real situation.

topics.tip: Equal percentage increases and decreases do not cancel.
topics.formula: Percentage change = (change ÷ original) × 100

After the increase: 204 × 1.10 = £224.40.
The overall multiplier is 0.935, so the net change is a 6.5% decrease.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Bounds, percentage multipliers and compound measures

sections.heading: Write the rounding interval
sections.body:
A length of 4.8 cm to one decimal place could be as low as 4.75 cm, but it must be below 4.85 cm. Write 4.75 ≤ x < 4.85.

The limits sit halfway between neighbouring rounded values. The upper limit is excluded because 4.85 would round to 4.9 under the usual convention.

sections.heading: Choose bounds that make the answer largest or smallest
sections.body:
For positive speed, use distance divided by time. The largest speed comes from the largest possible distance and smallest possible time.

The smallest speed uses the smallest distance and largest time. Do not put upper bounds into every position. Think about how the whole expression changes.

sections.heading: Apply and reverse percentage changes
sections.body:
A 15% increase means multiply by 1.15. A 15% decrease means multiply by 0.85. For repeated changes, multiply the factors together.

To reverse a change, divide by its factor. A sale price of £72 after a 10% discount came from £72/0.9 = £80, not £72 plus 10%.

sections.heading: Convert units before using a formula
sections.body:
Use matching units for distance and time, or mass and volume. One square metre is 10 000 square centimetres because both dimensions are multiplied by 100.

One cubic metre is 1 000 000 cubic centimetres. Squaring or cubing a length conversion is essential for area and volume.

sections.heading: See why upper and lower bounds change a quotient
sections.body:
Imagine the same journey being a little longer but taking a little less time. Both changes increase speed. That is why an upper speed bound uses an upper distance and a lower time.

For 100 m to the nearest metre and 10.0 s to the nearest tenth, the upper bound is 100.5/9.95 ≈ 10.10 m/s. Keep extra digits until the end. An upper bound is a limit consistent with the measurements, not a claim that the actual speed reached it.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Algebraic manipulation and linear equations

sections.heading: An expression is not an equation
sections.body: Collect terms only when their variable parts match. Expand a bracket by multiplying every term inside it. Factorising reverses expansion: remove the highest common factor first. An identity is true for every allowed variable value; an equation normally restricts the possible values. Substitution into a formula must preserve brackets, especially around negative values.

sections.heading: Keep both sides balanced
sections.body: Solve linear equations by applying the same operation to each side. Clear fractions using a common multiple of the denominators, keeping every term. Rearranging a formula follows the same logic, although the result may remain symbolic. If the subject appears twice, collect its terms and factorise it before dividing.

sections.heading: Inequalities and simultaneous constraints
sections.body: Inequalities describe ranges, shown on a number line or coordinate region. Reverse the inequality sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative number. Simultaneous linear equations require both equations to hold: eliminate one variable using suitable multiples, or substitute one equation into the other. Check the resulting pair in both original equations.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: Rearranging a formula can involve a variable on both sides. From y = ax/(x + b), multiply to get yx + yb = ax, collect x terms and factorise: yb = x(a − y). Thus x = yb/(a − y), provided the original expression and the final denominator are defined. For inequality regions, draw each boundary and test a point not on it. A dashed boundary usually excludes the line, while a solid boundary includes equality. State integer solutions separately when the variable is restricted to integers.

sections.heading: Expand first, then collect like terms
sections.body:
A number outside brackets multiplies every term inside. For 3(2x − 5) − 2(x + 1), first write 6x − 15 − 2x − 2. Now collect the x terms and the constant terms to get 4x − 17.

A minus before brackets changes every sign inside: −(x − 4) = −x + 4. You can test an expansion by substituting a simple value, such as x = 2, into both versions.

sections.heading: Clear a fraction without losing a term
sections.body:
In x/3 + 2 = 7, subtract 2 first to get x/3 = 5, then multiply by 3 to get x = 15. Alternatively, multiply every term in the original equation by 3: x + 6 = 21.

Both methods keep the equation balanced. The common mistake is multiplying only the fraction and forgetting the other terms. Check the final value in the original equation, especially when brackets or negative signs are involved.

topics.tip: When clearing fractions, multiply every term, not just the fractional terms.

worked.question: Solve 2x + y = 11 and x − y = 1.
steps: Add the equations to eliminate y: 3x = 12.
Therefore x = 4.
Substitute into x − y = 1: 4 − y = 1, so y = 3.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Quadratics, algebraic fractions and proof

sections.heading: Three routes to a quadratic solution
sections.body: Write ax² + bx + c = 0 before factorising. The zero-product rule then sets each factor equal to zero. Completing the square exposes the turning point and is useful for graph interpretation. The quadratic formula works when a is non-zero; the discriminant b² − 4ac distinguishes two real roots, one repeated real root or no real roots.

sections.heading: Higher: fractions and non-linear systems
sections.body: Factorise numerator and denominator before cancelling common factors in algebraic fractions. You cannot cancel separate added terms. Record excluded denominator values from the original expression. For a linear-quadratic simultaneous system, substitute the linear expression into the quadratic, solve the resulting equation and calculate a corresponding coordinate for each valid root.

sections.heading: Reasoning with general forms
sections.body: A proof must establish a claim for all permitted values, not a few numerical examples. Write an even integer as 2n and an odd integer as 2n + 1. Use algebra to expose the required property. For inequalities involving products, use the roots as boundaries and check the sign in each interval instead of assuming the solution lies between the roots.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: Completing the square rewrites x² + 6x + 5 as (x + 3)² − 4, exposing a minimum at (−3, −4). For algebraic fractions, record excluded values before cancelling: (x² − 9)/(x − 3) simplifies to x + 3 only for x ≠ 3. A proof by contradiction starts from an assumption and reaches an impossibility; a counterexample disproves a universal claim with one valid failure. Numerical examples can suggest a pattern, but they cannot establish that it always holds.

sections.heading: Choose a quadratic method that suits the expression
sections.body:
For x² + 5x + 6 = 0, look for two numbers that multiply to 6 and add to 5. They are 2 and 3, so (x + 2)(x + 3) = 0. One factor must be zero: x = −2 or −3.

If the factors are not easy to find, use the quadratic formula. Write the equation in the form ax² + bx + c = 0 first. Keep the signs of b and c when substituting.

sections.heading: Use a general number to prove a statement
sections.body:
A few examples can suggest a pattern, but they do not prove it for every integer. Write an even integer as 2n and an odd integer as 2n + 1.

For example, the sum of two consecutive odd integers is (2n + 1) + (2n + 3) = 4n + 4 = 4(n + 1). This shows the sum is divisible by 4 for every integer n. Explain what the final factorised form tells you.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Quadratic inequalities and solution regions

sections.heading: Roots divide the number line
sections.body: For a quadratic inequality, first find the roots of the corresponding equality. They divide the real number line into intervals within which a continuous quadratic’s sign is fixed. A factorised expression helps determine the sign by considering each factor. Include a root when equality is permitted and exclude it for a strict inequality.

sections.heading: Use sign or graph evidence
sections.body: For an upward-opening quadratic with two distinct real roots, the graph is negative between the roots and positive outside. A downward-opening quadratic reverses that pattern. If the expression is multiplied or divided by a negative number during rearrangement, reverse the inequality sign. A test value from each interval provides a useful check and is safer than memorising between the roots as a universal rule.

sections.heading: Intersect simultaneous restrictions
sections.body: If a solution must satisfy several inequalities, take the intersection of their allowed regions. For integer solutions, identify which integers lie inside the final intervals and handle strict endpoints correctly. In coordinate problems, boundaries can be lines or curves and the feasible region consists of points satisfying every condition. State a union of separate intervals clearly when the permitted values are outside two roots.

sections.heading: Test the intervals between the roots
sections.body:
To solve x² − x − 6 < 0, factorise to (x − 3)(x + 2) < 0. The roots are −2 and 3. Test a value between them: at x = 0, the expression is −6, which is negative.

The upward-opening curve is below the x-axis between its roots, so −2 < x < 3. For ≤ instead of <, include both endpoints. A quick sketch helps you distinguish the middle interval from the two outer intervals.

sections.heading: Combine restrictions rather than choosing one
sections.body:
If a problem also requires x ≥ 1, keep only the values satisfying both conditions. Combining −2 < x < 3 with x ≥ 1 gives 1 ≤ x < 3.

For a shaded region on coordinate axes, draw each boundary and decide which side works by testing a point away from the line. Use a solid boundary when equality is allowed and a dashed boundary when it is not. The final region is where all the conditions overlap.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Simultaneous equations: lines, curves and intersections

sections.heading: Eliminate one unknown
sections.body:
For two linear equations, make the coefficients of one variable equal or opposite. Add or subtract the whole equations so that variable cancels.

Solve the remaining equation, then substitute back. If you multiply an equation first, multiply every term, including its constant.

sections.heading: Substitute into a curve
sections.body:
If one equation gives y in terms of x, substitute that expression for y in the other equation. A line meeting a quadratic usually leads to a quadratic equation in x.

Solve it and find y for each allowed x-value. Two different roots can give two intersection points.

sections.heading: Recognise no solution or repeated information
sections.body:
If elimination gives 0 = 5, no pair can satisfy both equations. The straight lines are parallel and different.

If one equation is simply a multiple of the other, they describe the same line. There are infinitely many pairs on that line, rather than one unique solution.

sections.heading: Check each coordinate pair
sections.body:
Put each answer into both original equations. Give coordinates as matched pairs, such as (2, 4) and (−1, 1).

In a real problem, also check restrictions. A negative side length is not allowed even if it solves the algebra.

sections.heading: Choose substitution when the subject is already clear
sections.body:
Suppose y = 5 − x and 2x + 3y = 12. Replace y in the second equation: 2x + 3(5 − x) = 12. Expand to get −x + 15 = 12, so x = 3 and y = 2.

The bracket matters because the whole expression 5 − x replaces y. Check: 2(3) + 3(2) = 12 and 2 = 5 − 3. This small check confirms that the values belong together.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Sequences and function notation

sections.heading: From a pattern to a rule
sections.body: For an arithmetic sequence, consecutive terms differ by a constant. Its nth term is a + (n − 1)d. For a geometric sequence, consecutive terms have a constant ratio, giving ar^(n−1). A quadratic sequence has constant second differences; half that second difference is the coefficient of n². Subtract that quadratic part to identify the remaining linear expression.

sections.heading: A function maps an input to an output
sections.body: The notation f(x) names the rule, not multiplication of f by x. Substituting an expression means replacing every x with that entire expression in brackets. Composite functions apply the inside function first. An inverse undoes a function on a suitable domain: exchange input and output and rearrange, checking whether a restriction is needed for a unique inverse.

sections.heading: Higher: iteration and transformations
sections.body: An iterative rule repeatedly uses the previous estimate to produce the next. State the starting value and show the sequence of estimates to the requested accuracy. On graphs, f(x) + a shifts vertically, f(x − a) shifts right, af(x) scales vertically and f(ax) scales horizontally by reciprocal factor. Track coordinates rather than memorising a vague movement.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: For a quadratic sequence with terms 3, 8, 15, 24, the first differences are 5, 7, 9 and the second differences are 2. Start with n², then subtract its values from the terms to obtain 2, 4, 6, 8; the nth term is n² + 2n. For an inverse, the permitted domain matters: squaring loses the sign of an input, so x² has no unique inverse on all real numbers. A restricted non-negative domain permits the inverse square-root function.

sections.heading: Find a rule from differences
sections.body:
The arithmetic sequence 7, 11, 15, 19 has common difference 4. Start with 4n, which gives 4, 8, 12, 16. Add 3 to match the sequence, so its nth term is 4n + 3.

A quadratic sequence has constant second differences. For 2, 6, 12, 20, the first differences are 4, 6, 8 and the second differences are 2, 2. This suggests a quadratic rule; here it is n² + n. Test it at several positions.

sections.heading: Keep the input separate from the output
sections.body:
For f(x) = 2x² − 1, f(3) means replace x with 3: 2(3²) − 1 = 17. By contrast, solving f(x) = 17 means find all inputs producing 17. This gives x² = 9, so x = 3 or −3 unless the domain excludes one.

When iterating a rule, use each output as the next input. Write down the starting value and keep enough digits between steps to avoid rounding errors.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Graphs, gradients and calculus

sections.heading: Read the relationship, not only the picture
sections.body: For y = mx + c, m is the gradient and c the y-intercept. Parallel straight lines have equal gradients; perpendicular non-vertical gradients have product −1. Use two points to calculate change in y divided by change in x. Plotting tables should include negative and zero inputs when appropriate, so the important shape is not missed.

sections.heading: Curves and real-life graphs
sections.body: Recognise quadratic, cubic, reciprocal and exponential shapes. Intersections represent simultaneous solutions. The gradient of a distance-time graph is speed; the gradient of a velocity-time graph is acceleration. Area under a velocity-time graph is displacement, so a region below the time axis contributes negatively. Use a tangent to estimate an instantaneous gradient.

sections.heading: Higher: differentiate polynomial terms
sections.body: Differentiation gives a gradient function. For y = axⁿ, dy/dx = anx^(n−1) for the polynomial terms studied here; constants differentiate to zero. Set the derivative equal to zero to find stationary points, then examine surrounding gradients or the curve. For a tangent at a point, calculate its gradient and substitute the point into y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A tangent calculation requires both a point and a gradient. For y = x³ at x = 2, the derivative 3x² gives gradient 12 and the point is (2, 8), so the tangent is y − 8 = 12(x − 2). For an optimisation problem, define a variable, build a formula for the quantity to maximise or minimise, then differentiate. Check that the stationary point lies in the physical domain and that its type matches the question. Endpoints can also matter when a domain is bounded.

sections.heading: Read straight-line rules from a graph
sections.body:
In y = mx + c, m is the gradient and c is the y-intercept. Find a gradient using change in y divided by change in x. Pick two clear points well apart and use the scale on each axis.

For a line through (1, 3) and (5, 11), m = (11 − 3)/(5 − 1) = 2. Substituting (1, 3) gives 3 = 2 + c, so c = 1 and the rule is y = 2x + 1.

sections.heading: Connect a derivative to a tangent
sections.body:
For y = x³ − 4x, the derivative is dy/dx = 3x² − 4. At x = 2, the gradient is 8. The point on the original curve is (2, 0), so the tangent satisfies y − 0 = 8(x − 2).

Use the derivative for the gradient and the original function for the point. Substituting into the derivative cannot give the curve’s y-coordinate. A sketch can check whether the tangent’s direction makes sense.

topics.tip: A zero gradient identifies a stationary point, not automatically a maximum.
topics.formula: Gradient = Δy/Δx; d(axⁿ)/dx = anx^(n−1)

steps: Differentiate: dy/dx = 2x − 4.
Set the gradient to zero: 2x − 4 = 0, so x = 2.
At x = 2, y = 4 − 8 + 1 = −3. The upward-opening curve has a minimum at (2, −3).

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Differentiation and optimisation models

sections.heading: Model the quantity before differentiating
sections.body: Define the variable and the physical or mathematical domain. Use the stated constraint to express the quantity being optimised in terms of one variable. Differentiation then identifies how that quantity changes. A stationary value is a candidate, not a complete answer until the domain and maximum-or-minimum condition have been considered.

sections.heading: Apply polynomial differentiation
sections.body: For polynomial terms, multiply by the power and reduce the power by one. Constants differentiate to zero. Set the derivative equal to zero to find stationary input values, then substitute into the original quantity to find the corresponding output. Check a change of derivative sign, the graph shape or another appropriate argument to establish whether the point is a maximum or minimum.

sections.heading: Interpret the result
sections.body: State the requested dimensions or quantity with units where relevant. A mathematically valid negative length is outside the domain and must be rejected. For a bounded domain, an endpoint may give an extreme value even if its derivative is not zero. An optimisation result is only as applicable as its model assumptions, such as fixed material length or negligible thickness.

sections.heading: Turn a perimeter condition into an area formula
sections.body:
A rectangle with perimeter 20 cm has 2x + 2y = 20, so y = 10 − x. Its area is A = xy = x(10 − x) = 10x − x².

Differentiate: dA/dx = 10 − 2x. Setting this to zero gives x = 5 and y = 5, with area 25 cm². The area graph is a downward-opening quadratic, so this stationary point is a maximum. The side lengths must also be positive.

sections.heading: Check what the stationary point means
sections.body:
A zero derivative gives a stationary point, not automatically a maximum. Look at the graph or check the gradient on either side. A gradient changing from positive to negative gives a local maximum; negative to positive gives a local minimum.

For a practical model, check the allowed interval and any endpoints that can be included. A mathematically correct stationary point outside the permitted dimensions cannot be used as the final design. Finish with units and the quantity requested, such as area rather than only x.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Composite and inverse functions: order, domain and notation

sections.heading: Substitute an input into a rule
sections.body:
If f(x) = 3x − 4, then f(5) = 11. Replace each x in the rule with the input.

The domain is the set of inputs you are allowed to use. A denominator cannot be zero, and a real square root cannot have a negative value inside it.

sections.heading: Read a composite from the inside out
sections.body:
fg(x) means f(g(x)). Apply g first, then put its whole output into f.

For f(x) = 2x + 1 and g(x) = x², fg(x) = 2x² + 1. In the other order, gf(x) = (2x + 1)². The order usually changes the answer.

sections.heading: Reverse a one-to-one rule
sections.body:
To find an inverse, write y = f(x), then rearrange to make x the subject. Use that rearranged rule with the inverse notation.

For y = 3x − 4, x = (y + 4)/3. Therefore f⁻¹(x) = (x + 4)/3. The inverse is not the reciprocal.

sections.heading: Check the allowed branch
sections.body:
Squaring can give the same output from two inputs: 3² and (−3)² both give 9. So x² needs a restricted domain to have one inverse rule.

If the original domain is x ≥ 0, the inverse is the positive square-root branch. Use that restriction when choosing an answer.

sections.heading: Check by going forwards and backwards
sections.body:
An inverse should undo the original rule. For f(x) = 3x − 4, start with 6: f(6) = 14. Apply the inverse to 14: (14 + 4)/3 = 6.

You can also check algebraically: f(f⁻¹(x)) = 3[(x + 4)/3] − 4 = x. This works on the allowed domain. If the result is not the starting input, look for an order mistake or a lost bracket.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Angles, constructions and circle reasoning

sections.heading: Build an angle argument
sections.body: Angles on a straight line sum to 180°, around a point to 360°, and in a triangle to 180°. Parallel lines create corresponding and alternate equal angles; co-interior angles sum to 180°. Name the reason for each step in a geometry proof. An n-sided polygon has interior-angle sum (n − 2) × 180°.

sections.heading: Circle theorems connect points
sections.body: The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference standing on the same arc. Angles in the same segment are equal; the angle in a semicircle is 90°. Opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°. A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at contact, and tangents from an external point have equal lengths. The alternate segment theorem links a tangent-chord angle to the opposite arc angle.

sections.heading: Loci and accurate constructions
sections.body: A perpendicular bisector is the locus of points equidistant from two fixed points. An angle bisector is equidistant from two intersecting lines. Keep compass arcs visible when a construction is required. Bearings are measured clockwise from north using three figures. Distinguish a diagram that supplies measurements from a sketch that is explicitly not drawn to scale.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A geometric proof should identify the exact points used by a theorem. If two angles stand on the same chord from the same segment, they are equal; angles on opposite segments can instead be supplementary. The sum of exterior angles of a convex polygon, taken one at each vertex in a consistent direction, is 360°. In a regular polygon each exterior angle is 360°/n. A locus diagram may require the intersection of several regions, so shade only points meeting every condition.

sections.heading: Name the reason for each angle step
sections.body:
Start with simple facts: angles on a straight line sum to 180°, around a point to 360°, and in a triangle to 180°. Equal sides in an isosceles triangle give equal opposite angles.

Parallel lines give equal corresponding or alternate angles. Do not use those rules unless the lines are stated or proved parallel. Write the angle and its reason together. This makes a long argument easier to follow and helps you see which fact is still missing.

sections.heading: Understand what common constructions locate
sections.body:
A perpendicular bisector marks points equally distant from the ends of a line segment. An angle bisector marks points equally distant from the two arms of an angle. These are different distance conditions.

For a point equally distant from A and B and also from two intersecting lines, draw the appropriate two loci and use their intersection. Leave the construction arcs visible. An accurate-looking line drawn by eye does not show the geometric construction required.

topics.tip: Circle theorems require points on the relevant circle and the correct arc.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Mensuration, similarity and trigonometry

sections.heading: Measure in the correct dimension
sections.body: Area is two-dimensional; volume is three-dimensional. Convert lengths before applying formulae. A prism has constant cross-section, so volume is cross-sectional area × length. A pyramid or cone has volume one third of base area × perpendicular height. Arc length and sector area are the corresponding fraction of a full circumference or circle.

sections.heading: Similarity scales different quantities differently
sections.body: Similar shapes have equal corresponding angles and proportional corresponding lengths. If the length scale factor is k, the area factor is k² and volume factor k³. Match corresponding sides before using the ratio. Congruent shapes are identical in size and shape, whereas similar shapes may be different sizes.

sections.heading: Choose a triangle method deliberately
sections.body: Pythagoras and SOHCAHTOA apply to right-angled triangles. For other triangles, the sine rule relates opposite angle-side pairs and the cosine rule relates three sides or two sides with the included angle. The formula ½ab sin C gives the area using two sides and their included angle. Draw a clear diagram for three-dimensional problems and identify the right-angled triangle you actually use.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: For a non-right-angled triangle, pair each side with its opposite angle before applying the sine rule. When two sides and an included angle are known, the cosine rule finds the third side. Surface area must account for which faces are actually exposed; a joined solid may hide surfaces. For a frustum, subtract the smaller similar solid from the larger and use the linear scale factor to find missing dimensions. Retain exact multiples of π until a decimal answer is requested.

sections.heading: Use the right scale factor for the measurement
sections.body:
If similar shapes have length scale factor k, corresponding areas have factor k² and volumes have factor k³. A model enlarged by a length factor of 3 therefore has nine times the area, not three times.

If two similar solids have volume ratio 8:27, their length ratio is 2:3 because 2³ = 8 and 3³ = 27. Find the length factor before using it to calculate an area ratio of 4:9.

sections.heading: Label a right triangle before choosing a ratio
sections.body:
The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle. Relative to the angle you are using, mark the opposite and adjacent sides. Then choose sin = opposite/hypotenuse, cos = adjacent/hypotenuse or tan = opposite/adjacent.

If a ladder of length 5 m makes a 60° angle with level ground, its vertical height is 5 sin 60° ≈ 4.33 m. The angle is measured from the ground, so the height is the opposite side, not the adjacent side.

topics.tip: Use perpendicular height for area and volume; a sloping edge is usually different.
topics.formula: a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A; area = ½ab sin C

worked.question: Two similar solids have corresponding lengths 4 cm and 10 cm. The smaller has volume 32 cm³. Find the larger volume.
steps: The length scale factor is 10/4 = 2.5.
The volume scale factor is 2.5³ = 15.625.
The larger volume is 32 × 15.625 = 500 cm³.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Non-right-angled trigonometry and choosing a triangle

sections.heading: Choose a rule from the information
sections.body:
The sine rule needs a known side and its opposite angle. It links other opposite side–angle pairs.

The cosine rule is useful for two sides and their included angle, or three sides and an unknown angle. Label side a opposite angle A, and use the same pattern for b and c.

sections.heading: Find a side or an angle carefully
sections.body:
For a side, use a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A, then take the positive square root.

For an angle, rearrange to isolate cos A before using inverse cosine. Check degree mode, keep intermediate digits and check that the answer could fit a triangle.

sections.heading: Use the included angle for area
sections.body:
Area = ½ab sin C uses the angle between sides a and b. Using an angle elsewhere in the triangle gives the wrong area.

When using inverse sine, consider whether an obtuse angle could also fit. The triangle’s angle sum or other given information may rule it out.

sections.heading: Split a 3D problem into triangles
sections.body:
First find a useful diagonal in a flat face. Then use the triangle containing the required line or angle.

The angle between a line and a plane is measured to the line’s projection on that plane. Draw this projection rather than choosing an edge simply because it is convenient.

sections.heading: See why the ambiguous sine answer needs a check
sections.body:
Both 30° and 150° have sine 0.5. So an inverse-sine calculation may give one candidate while the triangle could allow another.

If another angle is 70°, then 150° is impossible because 150° + 70° exceeds 180°. If the other information does not rule a candidate out, examine both. A picture marked “not to scale” cannot decide this for you. Use the stated lengths and angles, not how the drawing looks.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Circle theorems and building a geometric proof

sections.heading: Match angles to the same chord or arc
sections.body:
The centre angle is twice the circumference angle standing on the same arc. Circumference angles standing on the same chord in the same segment are equal.

An angle standing on a diameter is 90°. Check the chord or arc carefully before applying a theorem.

sections.heading: Use a tangent’s contact point
sections.body:
A radius is perpendicular to the tangent at its contact point. Two tangents from the same outside point have equal lengths.

The alternate-segment theorem matches the angle between a tangent and chord to the angle in the opposite segment. Identify that chord in your diagram.

sections.heading: Combine facts to find missing angles
sections.body:
Opposite interior angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add to 180°. You may also need triangle sums, isosceles-triangle facts or angles on a straight line.

A chord is only a diameter if it passes through the centre. Do not assume it is a diameter because it looks long.

sections.heading: Make each proof step easy to follow
sections.body:
Write the angle value or equality and its reason together. In angle ABC, B is the vertex. Name angles carefully so the reason matches the correct angle.

To prove lines parallel, establish the relevant equal alternate or corresponding angles, or the appropriate supplementary co-interior angles.

sections.heading: Follow a chain instead of listing theorem names
sections.body:
Suppose AB is a diameter, C lies on the circle and angle BAC is 28°. First, angle ACB is 90° because it stands on a diameter. Then angle ABC is 180° − 90° − 28° = 62° because triangle angles add to 180°.

Each statement follows from the last one. Writing only “semicircle theorem, triangle theorem” would not show which angle is which. A good proof can be read without guessing what you meant.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Vectors and transformation geometry

sections.heading: Describe the entire transformation
sections.body: A translation needs a column vector. A reflection needs a mirror line. A rotation needs a centre, angle and direction. An enlargement needs a centre and scale factor; a negative factor places the image on the opposite side of the centre. Trace corresponding points to check your description. A transformation description should identify a single operation unless a combination is requested.

sections.heading: Vectors carry direction and magnitude
sections.body: Treat a vector as a displacement. Reversing its direction changes its sign. Adding vectors follows a connected route; subtracting position vectors gives the displacement between the two positions. Multiplying by a scalar changes magnitude and may reverse direction. Equal vectors need not start at the same point.

sections.heading: Higher: prove a geometric relationship
sections.body: Two non-zero vectors are parallel if one is a scalar multiple of the other. To prove points are collinear, also show the relevant vectors share a point. Express a midpoint by averaging endpoint position vectors. For ratio division, use a consistent route from a known point and scale the entire displacement vector. Present each vector equality with its start and end points.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A vector proof can separate direction from position. Showing AB = 2CD establishes parallel directions with a 2:1 magnitude ratio, but says nothing about whether those segments lie on the same line. To divide AB internally in the ratio 2:3, start at A and travel 2/5 of the vector from A to B. For enlargements with a negative scale factor, image points lie on the opposite side of the centre. The magnitude of the factor sets their distance ratio.

sections.heading: Build a journey from known vectors
sections.body:
A vector from A to B is different from the position vector of B. If OA = a and OB = b, then AB = b − a: travel back from A to O, then from O to B.

If M is the midpoint of AB, OM = (a + b)/2. Two vectors being scalar multiples shows that they are parallel. To prove points are on the same straight line, also show that the relevant parallel vectors share the appropriate point.

sections.heading: Give every part of a transformation description
sections.body:
A rotation needs an angle, direction and centre. A reflection needs the mirror line. An enlargement needs a scale factor and centre. A translation needs a vector. Giving only “rotate 90°” leaves the result uncertain.

For a negative enlargement scale factor, the image lies on the opposite side of the centre. Corresponding vertices and the centre still lie on a straight line. Check more than one vertex so that a chance match does not hide the wrong centre.

topics.tip: Parallel vectors alone do not prove three points are collinear.

worked.question: Position vectors of A and B are a and b. Find the position vector of the midpoint M.
steps: The displacement from A to B is b − a.
Move halfway along it from A: a + ½(b − a).
Simplifying gives OM = ½(a + b).

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Data, distributions and statistical diagrams

sections.heading: A statistic answers a particular question
sections.body: The mean uses every value but is sensitive to extreme values. The median is the central ordered value. The mode is the most common value and may not be unique. The range describes total spread; the interquartile range describes the middle half. Compare both a measure of centre and a measure of spread when comparing distributions.

sections.heading: Grouped data and unequal intervals
sections.body: A mean estimated from grouped data uses class midpoints, multiplies each by its frequency, then divides by total frequency. It is an estimate because the individual values are unknown. For histograms, frequency is represented by area, not height: frequency density equals frequency divided by class width. Keep continuous class boundaries consistent.

sections.heading: Interpret relationships cautiously
sections.body: A scatter graph may suggest positive, negative or no correlation. A line of best fit supports interpolation within the observed range; extrapolation is less secure. Correlation alone does not establish cause. Cumulative frequency curves estimate medians and quartiles. A probability sample should reduce selection bias; explain how the sample represents the population rather than merely calling it random.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A grouped-data median is estimated from cumulative frequency at half the total frequency. The lower and upper quartiles correspond to one quarter and three quarters of the total. A box plot communicates these summaries but not the individual data values. In stratified sampling, allocate sample sizes in proportion to category sizes, then select appropriately within each category. A sample can be large yet biased if the selection excludes important parts of the population. Explain both the selection method and the population it represents.

sections.heading: Choose an average and understand its limits
sections.body:
The mean uses every value, so one unusually large or small value can move it strongly. The median is the middle value after ordering and is often more useful for skewed data. The mode is the most common value or category.

For 2, 3, 3, 4 and 28, the mean is 8 but the median is 3. Neither calculation is wrong: they describe the group differently. Use the context to decide which summary is more helpful.

sections.heading: Estimate a mean from grouped data
sections.body:
When exact values are unavailable, use the midpoint of each class as a representative value. Multiply each midpoint by its frequency, add these products, then divide by the total frequency.

For classes 0–10 and 10–20 with frequencies 4 and 6, the estimate is (5 × 4 + 15 × 6)/10 = 11. It is an estimate because the values need not be evenly spread around the midpoint in either class.

topics.tip: For a histogram, compare bar areas when you need frequencies.
topics.formula: Frequency density = frequency ÷ class width

steps: The first class width is 10 and its density is 30/10 = 3.
The second class width is 20 and its density is 40/20 = 2.
The first bar is taller even though its class has fewer observations.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Probability, sets and conditional events

sections.heading: List the sample space accurately
sections.body: Probabilities range from 0 to 1. Exhaustive mutually exclusive outcomes have probabilities summing to 1. The complement rule gives P(not A) = 1 − P(A). A sample-space diagram is useful only when its elementary outcomes are equally likely, or when each outcome is weighted correctly.

sections.heading: Trees and overlapping events
sections.body: Multiply probabilities along a complete tree path and add paths corresponding to the desired event. With no replacement, update both the category count and total before the second selection. For overlapping events, subtract the intersection when adding probabilities: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B). Venn diagrams help separate the regions.

sections.heading: Higher: conditions change the reference group
sections.body: Conditional probability restricts the denominator to outcomes satisfying the condition. P(A given B) = P(A and B)/P(B), when P(B) is non-zero. Independent events satisfy P(A and B) = P(A)P(B); mutually exclusive events have no shared outcomes. These descriptions are not interchangeable. A tree can still describe dependent events, provided each branch probability uses the appropriate condition.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A condition restricts the sample space. If 12 pupils study both art and music and 20 study music, the probability of art given music is 12/20, not 12 divided by the whole school. In a Venn diagram, place the intersection first, then fill exclusive regions and finally the outside. For at least one success, calculating one minus no successes can be simpler than listing every successful path. State independence only when the process or the data supports it.

sections.heading: Change probabilities after a draw without replacement
sections.body:
A bag contains three red and two blue counters. The probability of two red counters without replacement is 3/5 × 2/4 = 3/10. After the first red counter, only two red counters and four counters altogether remain.

With replacement, the second probability would stay 3/5. On a tree diagram, multiply along one complete path. Add separate paths for outcomes that cannot both happen, such as red then blue and blue then red.

sections.heading: Use the condition to choose the denominator
sections.body:
Conditional probability asks about a restricted group. If 12 of 20 students study French and 5 of those 12 also study German, the probability of German given French is 5/12. The condition tells you to look only at the French group.

Using 5/20 answers a different question: the probability that a randomly chosen student studies both. Writing “out of which group?” beside the denominator is a useful way to avoid this mistake.

topics.tip: Without replacement normally means the draws are dependent.
topics.formula: P(A given B) = P(A and B)/P(B)

worked.question: A bag has 3 red and 2 blue counters. Two are drawn without replacement. Find the probability both are red.
steps: The probability of red first is 3/5.
After a red draw, there are 2 red counters among 4 remaining, so the next probability is 2/4.

cards.answer: outcomes belonging to both sets

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Set notation and Venn-diagram reasoning

sections.heading: Describe membership precisely
sections.body: A set is a collection of specified objects or values. The universal set defines everything under consideration. A complement contains members of the universal set outside a named set. The intersection contains common members, while the union includes members of either set, counting the overlap once. A Venn diagram should represent the stated universal set, not an assumed unlimited collection.

sections.heading: Fill overlapping regions in a useful order
sections.body: Place the most specific overlap first, then subtract it from the given set totals to fill exclusive regions. Complete the outside region using the universal total. For three sets, distinguish a pairwise intersection that includes the central triple region from an exclusive two-set region. Check that the separate diagram regions add to the universal total.

sections.heading: Turn a region into a probability
sections.body: Probability from a count uses the number of relevant equally likely selections divided by the appropriate total. A conditional phrase such as given that the pupil studies music restricts that denominator. At least one set corresponds to a union; neither corresponds to the complement of the union. Translate the exact wording before substituting numbers.

sections.heading: Fill the overlap before the outer regions
sections.body:
Suppose 18 students play football, 12 swim and 5 do both. Put 5 in the overlap first. The football-only region is 18 − 5 = 13 and the swimming-only region is 12 − 5 = 7.

The number doing at least one activity is 13 + 5 + 7 = 25. If there are 30 students altogether, the neither region is 5. Adding 18 and 12 without subtracting the overlap counts the same five students twice.

sections.heading: Translate set symbols into ordinary words
sections.body:
A ∩ B means in both A and B. A ∪ B means in A or B or both. A′ means outside A but still within the universal set shown by the rectangle.

In a probability question, count the items in the shaded region and divide by the correct total. If a condition restricts the choice to B, the denominator becomes the number in B. Drawing a quick labelled sketch can be clearer than trying to manipulate symbols alone.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Histograms, cumulative frequency and distribution comparisons

sections.heading: Use density for a histogram
sections.body:
Frequency density = frequency divided by class width. The bar’s area then represents frequency.

A class of width 10 and frequency 30 has density 3. A class of width 20 and the same frequency has density 1.5. Equal frequencies do not require equal bar heights.

sections.heading: Find quartiles on a cumulative curve
sections.body:
Add frequencies as you move through the classes. Plot cumulative totals against the upper class boundaries.

For N observations, read the lower quartile at N/4, median at N/2 and upper quartile at 3N/4. The interquartile range, or IQR, is the upper quartile minus the lower quartile.

sections.heading: Compare typical value and spread
sections.body:
Use a median to compare typical values and an IQR to compare the middle half’s spread. A smaller IQR means those middle values are closer together.

Always link the comparison to the context. A higher median score means a higher typical score; it does not mean every score is higher.

sections.heading: Treat grouped readings as estimates
sections.body:
A cumulative curve does not reveal every original value. Readings from it are estimates, so do not claim more accuracy than the graph supports.

To estimate how many values exceed a threshold, subtract the cumulative reading at that threshold from the total frequency.

sections.heading: Recover a missing histogram scale
sections.body:
If a bar covers a class width of 8 and represents 40 observations, its density must be 40/8 = 5. Use that bar to work out the density scale on the vertical axis.

For another bar of width 12 and density 3, frequency is 12 × 3 = 36. Write the relation in both directions: divide by width to find density; multiply by width to find frequency. This helps with incomplete histogram questions.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: Life processes, groups and pathogens

sections.heading: What living systems do
sections.body: Living organisms carry out nutrition, respiration, excretion, response to surroundings, movement, growth and reproduction. A single organism need not reproduce during its lifetime to be alive. Cellular organisation connects molecules to cells, tissues, organs and organ systems. These levels describe increasing coordination, not simply increasing physical size.

sections.heading: Recognising the major groups
sections.body: Animals are multicellular, lack cell walls and obtain organic nutrients by feeding. Plants contain chloroplasts in photosynthetic cells and have cellulose cell walls. Fungi have chitin cell walls and feed by extracellular digestion followed by absorption. Protoctists are diverse eukaryotes, many of them single-celled. Bacteria are prokaryotes: their DNA is not enclosed within a nucleus.

sections.heading: Pathogens are not a separate kingdom
sections.body: A pathogen causes disease. Some bacteria produce toxins or damage cells, but many bacteria are harmless or useful. Viruses are much smaller than cells and reproduce only inside host cells. A virus consists of genetic material inside a protein coat; it has no independent cellular metabolism. Antibiotics act on suitable bacterial targets and do not treat viral infections.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: The distinction between eukaryotic and prokaryotic organisation concerns the nucleus and internal cell organisation, not simply cell size. A fungus can digest food outside its cells by secreting enzymes and then absorbing soluble products; this differs from ingesting solid food. A virus uses host-cell machinery to reproduce, so it is not described as a small bacterium. When comparing groups, choose corresponding features such as cell walls, genetic material, chloroplasts and nutritional method. A statement about a particular organism should not be applied automatically to every member of its group.

sections.heading: Tell the main groups apart
sections.body:
Plants have cells with chloroplasts where photosynthesis takes place. Fungi do not photosynthesise; many feed by releasing enzymes outside their bodies and absorbing the products. Their cell walls contain chitin rather than plant cellulose.

Bacteria are single cells without a nucleus. Viruses are much smaller particles that reproduce only inside host cells. These differences explain why a method affecting bacterial cell structures does not necessarily work against a virus.

sections.heading: Keep size and units in perspective
sections.body:
One millimetre contains 1000 micrometres. One micrometre contains 1000 nanometres. A cell measuring 20 micrometres is therefore 0.020 mm, not 20 mm.

For a microscope image, magnification = image size/actual size, using the same units. If a 0.020 mm cell appears 10 mm long, its magnification is 500 times. A scale bar lets you estimate the real size even after an image has been resized.

topics.tip: Do not describe every microorganism as harmful.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: Cells, enzymes and membrane transport

sections.heading: Cell structures explain cell functions
sections.body: The nucleus contains genetic material; ribosomes synthesise proteins; mitochondria support aerobic respiration. Plant cells additionally have a cellulose wall and a permanent vacuole, with chloroplasts in photosynthetic cells. Cell differentiation produces specialised structures. Stem cells can divide and differentiate; their use requires consideration of therapeutic benefits, tumour risk and ethical questions.

sections.heading: Enzymes work through a specific active site
sections.body: An enzyme is a biological catalyst. Substrates bind at an active site and products are released, leaving the enzyme available again. Heating initially increases collision frequency, but sufficiently high temperatures alter the active site and denature the enzyme. Extreme pH can do the same. Cooling normally slows activity rather than denaturing the protein.

sections.heading: Three different transport mechanisms
sections.body: Diffusion is net particle movement down a concentration gradient. Osmosis is net water movement through a partially permeable membrane from higher to lower water potential. Active transport moves substances against a concentration gradient using energy from respiration. Large surface area, a thin barrier and a maintained concentration difference favour rapid exchange; cells with high active-transport demand often contain many mitochondria.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A small cell has a large surface-area-to-volume ratio compared with a larger geometrically similar cell. As cell dimensions increase, surface area grows with the square of length while volume grows with the cube. This can make exchange too slow relative to demand, helping explain specialised exchange surfaces and transport systems. In an osmosis experiment, calculate percentage mass change to compare differently sized samples fairly. Keep solution concentration, temperature, sample preparation and duration controlled. A zero mass change indicates no net water movement under those conditions, not that water molecules have stopped crossing the membrane.

sections.heading: Understand net movement in diffusion
sections.body:
Particles move randomly in both directions. If more particles are on one side of a membrane, more usually cross from that side, so there is a net movement down the concentration gradient.

At equal concentrations, particles do not stop moving. Similar numbers move each way, so there is no net movement. Osmosis applies this idea to water moving through a partially permeable membrane. Active transport is different because it can move substances against their concentration gradient using energy.

sections.heading: See why small cells exchange materials more easily
sections.body:
For a cube with side length 1 unit, surface area is 6 and volume is 1, giving a 6:1 ratio. At side length 2, surface area is 24 and volume is 8, giving 3:1.

As size increases, there is less surface area available for each unit of volume. Large organisms therefore need specialised exchange surfaces and transport systems. Thin surfaces and a good supply of blood or air also help by reducing distance and maintaining gradients.

topics.tip: Osmosis concerns water; a definition about unspecified particles describes diffusion.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: Nutrition and photosynthesis

sections.heading: Plants build organic molecules
sections.body: Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and water to make glucose and oxygen, transferring light energy into chemical energy. Chlorophyll absorbs light. Glucose can fuel respiration, form cellulose, be stored as starch, or combine with mineral-derived nitrogen to make amino acids. Light intensity, carbon dioxide and temperature may limit the rate; a plateau means another factor has become limiting.

sections.heading: Digestion turns food into absorbable molecules
sections.body: A balanced diet supplies carbohydrate, protein, lipids, vitamins, minerals, fibre and water in appropriate proportions. Amylase breaks starch into sugars, proteases produce amino acids and lipases produce fatty acids and glycerol. Bile emulsifies fats and helps neutralise stomach acid. Villi provide a large thin exchange surface and a blood supply that maintains gradients; lacteals transport products of lipid absorption.

sections.heading: Practical evidence and controls
sections.body: For starch testing, decolourise a leaf using ethanol in a hot-water bath, rinse it, then add iodine. Blue-black indicates starch. Use a destarched plant and suitable light or carbon-dioxide controls to investigate requirements. For food tests, use iodine for starch, heated Benedict’s reagent for reducing sugar, Biuret reagent for protein and an ethanol emulsion test for lipids. Observe laboratory safety, particularly with flammable ethanol.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A leaf’s broad surface intercepts light, while its thin structure gives gases a short diffusion route. Palisade cells contain many chloroplasts and air spaces connect mesophyll surfaces to stomata. Magnesium is required for chlorophyll and nitrate supplies nitrogen for amino acids. In digestive questions, distinguish digestion, absorption and assimilation: digestion breaks large food molecules down, absorption moves soluble products into circulation, and assimilation incorporates or uses them in cells. Bile is not an enzyme; emulsification increases the area available for lipase without chemically hydrolysing lipid molecules.

sections.heading: Link a leaf’s layers to photosynthesis
sections.body:
A leaf is usually broad, giving a large area to absorb light. Its thin shape creates short distances for gas movement. Palisade cells contain many chloroplasts and lie near the illuminated upper surface.

Air spaces in the spongy mesophyll allow carbon dioxide to move through the leaf. Stomata connect those spaces to the outside air. A vascular bundle supplies water through xylem and carries sugars away through phloem. Each feature supports a different part of the process.

sections.heading: Explain mineral deficiencies clearly
sections.body:
Plants need nitrate ions to make amino acids and proteins. A shortage can reduce growth because new cells need proteins. Plants need magnesium ions to make chlorophyll; a shortage can cause leaves to become pale or yellow.

Minerals do not provide the carbon atoms in most of the plant’s organic material: those come mainly from carbon dioxide during photosynthesis. Fertiliser can correct a mineral shortage, but it cannot replace missing light, water or carbon dioxide.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: Respiration, gas exchange and transport

sections.heading: Respiration releases usable energy
sections.body: Aerobic respiration uses glucose and oxygen to produce carbon dioxide and water, releasing energy for cellular processes. Anaerobic respiration in human muscle produces lactate and releases less energy per glucose. In yeast, anaerobic respiration produces ethanol and carbon dioxide. Breathing moves air; respiration is a cellular chemical process. Do not use the terms interchangeably.

sections.heading: Exchange surfaces maintain diffusion
sections.body: Alveoli provide a large moist surface, very thin walls and a dense capillary supply. Ventilation and blood flow maintain oxygen and carbon-dioxide gradients. In leaves, stomata open into air spaces beside mesophyll surfaces. Guard cells regulate stomatal opening, balancing carbon-dioxide uptake with water loss. Smoking damages cilia and alveolar tissue and increases risks including cancer and cardiovascular disease.

sections.heading: Bulk transport connects exchange to demand
sections.body: The heart drives a double circulation through the lungs and body. Arteries carry blood away from the heart under pressure; veins return it with valves; capillaries support exchange. Red cells transport oxygen using haemoglobin, plasma carries dissolved substances and platelets contribute to clotting. Xylem carries water and mineral ions; phloem translocates dissolved organic nutrients between sources and sinks.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: The left ventricle has a thicker muscular wall than the right because it supplies the systemic circulation at higher pressure. Valves prevent backflow when pressure differences reverse. In plants, evaporation from mesophyll surfaces and diffusion through stomata drive a transpiration stream; water is pulled through xylem. A potometer measures water uptake, which estimates rather than directly measures transpiration because some water is used elsewhere. Temperature, air movement, humidity and light can alter the rate. Explain each effect through evaporation, diffusion gradients or stomatal behaviour rather than simply saying that the plant becomes more active.

sections.heading: Compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration
sections.body:
Aerobic respiration uses oxygen and releases more energy per glucose molecule than anaerobic respiration. In human muscle, anaerobic respiration forms lactic acid. It can support short periods when the energy demand exceeds the aerobic supply.

After vigorous activity, breathing and heart rate remain raised while the body recovers, including dealing with lactic acid. In yeast, anaerobic respiration produces ethanol and carbon dioxide. The products depend on the organism, so do not give the yeast equation for human muscle.

sections.heading: Explain how ventilation maintains gas exchange
sections.body:
When the diaphragm contracts and flattens, and the external intercostal muscles raise the ribs, chest volume increases. Pressure inside the lungs falls below outside pressure, so air moves in.

Air movement refreshes the air near the alveoli. Blood flow carries oxygen away and brings carbon dioxide to the lungs. Together, ventilation and circulation help maintain steep concentration gradients. Alveoli are effective because they also have a large surface area and a thin exchange barrier.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: Excretion, homeostasis and coordination

sections.heading: Keep internal conditions within limits
sections.body: Homeostasis maintains internal conditions despite external changes. Negative feedback detects a deviation and produces responses that oppose it. Temperature control balances heat loss and production: sweating cools through evaporation, and changes to skin blood flow alter heat transfer. Blood glucose control involves insulin and glucagon acting on processes such as glucose uptake and glycogen conversion.

sections.heading: The kidney removes wastes while conserving useful substances
sections.body: Excretion removes metabolic waste, including urea produced from excess amino acids in the liver. In a nephron, ultrafiltration moves small molecules from blood into the tubule under pressure while retaining blood cells and large proteins. Selective reabsorption recovers useful substances. ADH alters collecting-duct water permeability, helping regulate blood water concentration.

sections.heading: Responses can be electrical or chemical
sections.body: A receptor detects a stimulus. Sensory neurones carry impulses to the central nervous system, relay neurones connect pathways and motor neurones activate effectors. Synapses transmit signals chemically in one direction. Reflex pathways produce rapid protective responses. Hormones travel in blood and act on target cells. Plants respond through growth regulators such as auxin, with differing effects in roots and shoots.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: Ultrafiltration and selective reabsorption have different roles. Pressure filters small molecules, including both glucose and urea, into the nephron, while large proteins and blood cells remain in circulation. Glucose is normally reabsorbed rather than deliberately excreted. Negative feedback should be written as a causal sequence: a change is detected, a coordinating response is produced, an effector acts and the variable moves back towards its regulated range. In a reflex arc, the rapid response does not require a conscious decision, although information may also reach the brain.

sections.heading: Follow a negative-feedback response
sections.body:
If body temperature rises, sweating increases. Evaporation of sweat transfers energy away from the skin. Skin blood vessels can widen, increasing blood flow near the surface and heat transfer to the surroundings.

As temperature returns towards its usual range, these cooling responses decrease. That is negative feedback: the response opposes the original change. A cold response uses different effectors, such as shivering and reduced skin blood flow. Sweat cooling depends on evaporation, not simply on liquid being present.

sections.heading: Separate blood-glucose control from eating sugar
sections.body:
After a carbohydrate-rich meal, absorbed glucose can raise blood glucose concentration. The pancreas releases insulin, which helps lower it by promoting glucose uptake and storage, including glycogen formation in the liver and muscles.

Blood glucose is a concentration in the blood, not the total amount of sugar eaten. Between meals, stored material can help supply glucose. In an explanation, name the stimulus, the hormone and its effect rather than saying only that the body “balances sugar”.

topics.tip: Urea is made in the liver and excreted by the kidneys; urine is not the same as urea.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: Immunity, antibodies and vaccination

sections.heading: Three complementary defences
sections.body: Physical barriers reduce entry of pathogens. Skin forms a protective barrier, mucus can trap particles, and cilia help move contaminated mucus away from parts of the respiratory tract. If a pathogen enters tissues, white blood cells contribute to defence. Phagocytes can engulf and digest microorganisms. Lymphocytes participate in more specific responses, including antibody production and the formation of immune memory. These roles should be distinguished rather than attributing every process to every white blood cell.

sections.heading: Specific recognition and memory
sections.body: Antigens are molecular features recognised by the immune system. An antibody has a binding region complementary to a particular antigenic feature. Following recognition, suitable lymphocyte populations multiply, producing a targeted response. Some cells persist as memory cells. On a later exposure to the same relevant antigen, a faster and larger response may control the pathogen before serious disease develops. Specificity explains why immunity to one infection does not imply equal protection against every other infection.

sections.heading: Interpreting vaccination evidence
sections.body: Vaccination introduces a preparation that safely stimulates a response to relevant antigens without the same risk as the disease itself. The form of the preparation varies. A primary response develops over time; later doses can strengthen immune memory. In a graph, compare delay, peak response and duration, and link those observations to memory rather than simply labelling the second curve better. Population-level protection depends on the pathogen, vaccine effectiveness and participation; it is not an absolute guarantee for every individual.

sections.heading: Read the primary and secondary response curves
sections.body:
A first exposure usually has a delay before antibody concentration rises strongly. Suitable lymphocytes become active and multiply. Some cells remain as memory cells after the immediate response falls.

On a later exposure to the same relevant antigen, the response can begin sooner and reach a higher level. On a graph, compare the delay and concentration, then explain these differences using memory cells. Do not claim the second curve is faster simply because it is drawn higher.

sections.heading: Understand protection without claiming certainty
sections.body:
Vaccination aims to prepare immune memory without the same risks as the disease itself. If enough people have suitable protection, some infections spread less easily through a population, helping protect others too.

The effect depends on the pathogen, how well protection works and how it changes with time. It is not a guarantee that every vaccinated person will never become infected. For course questions, explain the immune process and use the evidence supplied rather than inventing a universal percentage threshold.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: The eye, reflexes and accommodation

sections.heading: Light detection and protection
sections.body: Light enters through the cornea and pupil, passes through the lens and reaches the retina. The iris changes pupil diameter, controlling how much light enters. The retina contains light-sensitive cells; the optic nerve carries resulting information towards the brain. The sclera provides a tough outer layer and the choroid supports the retina and reduces internal reflection. Name the structure first, then connect its property to its function.

sections.heading: Focusing at different distances
sections.body: Accommodation changes lens shape. For a near object, ciliary muscles contract, suspensory ligaments become less taut, and the lens becomes thicker and more strongly converging. For a distant object, ciliary muscles relax, ligaments become taut, and the lens becomes thinner. The cornea provides substantial refraction, but normal accommodation primarily changes the lens. The objective is to focus the image at the retina rather than move the retina towards the focus.

sections.heading: Two responses with different purposes
sections.body: The pupil reflex responds to light level, whereas accommodation responds to focusing demand. In bright light, the pupil becomes smaller, reducing incoming light. A reflex pathway can protect tissues without a conscious decision. Distinguish stimulus, receptor, coordinator and effector in the response. Do not claim that increasing the pupil size automatically brings a blurred near image into focus; that confuses light regulation with changing the optical power of the lens.

sections.heading: Distinguish rods, cones and the blind spot
sections.body:
The retina contains light-sensitive cells. Rods are useful in dim light, while cones support colour vision and fine detail in suitable light. The fovea has a high concentration of cones.

At the blind spot, the optic nerve leaves the eye and there are no light receptors. The blind spot is not the pupil: the pupil is the opening at the front through which light enters. Naming both the location and function helps keep these structures apart.

sections.heading: Explain the muscles controlling the pupil
sections.body:
In bright light, circular muscles in the iris contract and radial muscles relax. The pupil becomes smaller, reducing the light entering the eye. In dim light, radial muscles contract and circular muscles relax, making the pupil larger.

This is a response of the iris muscles, not the pupil contracting as a tissue. Accommodation instead changes lens shape through ciliary muscles and suspensory ligaments. Pupil size mainly regulates light quantity; lens shape adjusts focus.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: Food tests and enzyme investigations

sections.heading: Separate the tests and observations
sections.body: Iodine changes from orange-brown to blue-black when starch is present. Benedict’s reagent is used with a suitable heated-water-bath method to test for reducing sugars, producing a coloured precipitate when positive. The Biuret test gives a purple or lilac colour with protein. An ethanol emulsion method gives a cloudy white emulsion with lipid. Use the reagents and safety instructions supplied by the school; ethanol is flammable and should not be heated over a flame.

sections.heading: Control the enzyme reaction
sections.body: An enzyme experiment changes one independent variable while measuring a defined response. For amylase and starch, repeated sampling into iodine can identify when starch is no longer detected. Keep reagent quantities, mixing, sampling interval and other conditions consistent. A pH investigation needs suitable buffers; a temperature investigation needs time for reagents to reach the intended temperature. Use repeat trials to check consistency.

sections.heading: Interpret a time endpoint
sections.body: For a fixed amount of substrate, shorter completion time usually indicates a faster rate under comparable conditions. Reciprocal time can provide a comparative rate measure. It does not mean every enzyme reaction has exactly that rate law. An endpoint has uncertainty because the change may occur between samples. Denaturation explains loss of function at sufficiently high temperature, whereas lower temperature normally reduces rate without permanently changing the active site.

sections.heading: Distinguish observation from conclusion
sections.body:
With iodine, a blue-black colour is the observation; starch being present is the conclusion. With heated Benedict’s reagent, a coloured precipitate supports the presence of reducing sugar. With the Biuret test, a purple or lilac colour indicates protein.

Record what you actually see before naming the substance. A control sample helps show that the reagent and method worked. Follow the school procedure for reagent amounts, heating and safe handling rather than inventing a new test from the colour alone.

sections.heading: Keep the endpoint consistent in an enzyme test

Bring solutions to the selected temperature before mixing, keep reagent amounts the same and use a suitable buffer for pH control. Rate comparisons based on 1/time only make sense when each run reaches the same endpoint with comparable starting amounts.
