topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: Nephrons, water balance and ADH

sections.heading: Filtration is selective by size
sections.body: Blood pressure drives small molecules from the glomerular blood into the kidney capsule. Water, ions, glucose and urea can enter the filtrate, while blood cells and large proteins are normally retained. This initial filtering does not identify which substances the body should discard. The composition must be modified further as the filtrate passes through the nephron.

sections.heading: Useful substances are recovered
sections.body: Selective reabsorption transfers useful substances back into the blood. Glucose is normally recovered, along with needed water and ions. Different nephron regions contribute to concentration and regulation. Final urine therefore differs from the initial filtrate. Urea derives from amino-acid metabolism in the liver and is removed through the kidneys; naming the place of excretion is not the same as naming where the waste was formed.

sections.heading: ADH coordinates a water-saving response
sections.body: When blood water potential falls, the coordinating system increases ADH release. ADH increases water permeability of the collecting ducts, allowing more water to be reabsorbed under the appropriate gradients. The resulting urine volume is lower and more concentrated. When more water is available, lower ADH reduces this water-saving effect. Explain the response as negative feedback with a detected change, hormone action and an outcome that opposes the original deviation.

sections.heading: Separate filtration from selective reabsorption
sections.body:
Pressure in the glomerulus drives small substances, including water, urea, ions and glucose, into the nephron. Blood cells and large proteins normally remain in the blood. Filtration does not remove only wastes.

Useful substances are then taken back into the blood. In the healthy school model, all filtered glucose is reabsorbed, along with needed water and ions. Urea and excess material remain in the fluid that becomes urine. This two-stage process explains why glucose can enter the filtrate without normally appearing in urine.

sections.heading: Follow the effect of more ADH
sections.body:
When the blood has a lower water potential, more ADH can be released. ADH increases the collecting duct’s water permeability, so more water returns to the blood by osmosis. Urine volume falls and urine becomes more concentrated.

When less ADH acts, less water is reabsorbed there and urine can be more dilute. The hormone changes permeability; it does not create water or push it against the water-potential gradient. Use urine volume and concentration together when describing the response.

a hormone regulating collecting-duct water permeability

topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: Digestion, bile and absorption at the villus

sections.heading: Break large molecules into small products
sections.body:
Chewing breaks food into smaller pieces and mixes it. Enzymes carry out chemical digestion. Amylase acts on starch, proteases on proteins and lipases on lipids.

The products are small enough to be absorbed. Not every food becomes glucose: proteins supply amino acids and lipids supply fatty acids and glycerol.

sections.heading: Match enzymes to their conditions
sections.body:
The stomach is acidic, which suits its protease and helps kill many microorganisms. The small intestine receives digestive enzymes from the pancreas and has different conditions.

Enzyme activity depends on pH and temperature. Unsuitable conditions can change the active site, so the substrate no longer fits properly.

sections.heading: Explain bile’s two main jobs
sections.body:
The liver makes bile and the gall bladder stores it. Bile helps neutralise acidic material entering the small intestine.

It also breaks fat into small droplets. This is emulsification: more surface is available for lipase to act on. Bile is not itself an enzyme and does not chemically digest the lipid.

sections.heading: Link villus features to absorption
sections.body:
Villi and microvilli give a large surface area. The thin epithelial layer gives a short distance for transport. Capillaries carry absorbed glucose and amino acids away.

A lacteal carries absorbed lipid material. Explain how each feature helps, rather than listing structures without their functions.

sections.heading: Follow one food molecule through the process
sections.body:
Starch in a piece of bread is too large to be absorbed intact. Digestive enzymes break it into smaller sugars, and further digestion produces glucose. Glucose crosses the small-intestinal lining and enters the blood.

Blood carries it to tissues, where cells can use it in respiration or store material made from it. Digestion, absorption and respiration are three different stages: breaking food down, moving products into the body’s transport system, and releasing energy inside cells.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: The heart, double circulation and coronary disease

sections.heading: Trace blood through both sides
sections.body:
Blood from the body enters the right atrium, then the right ventricle. It travels through the pulmonary artery to the lungs.

Oxygenated blood returns through the pulmonary vein to the left atrium and left ventricle. The aorta carries it to the body. Arteries go away from the heart; veins return towards it.

sections.heading: Explain muscle thickness and valves
sections.body:
The left ventricle needs a thicker muscular wall because it pumps around the whole body at higher pressure. The right ventricle supplies the nearby lungs at lower pressure.

Valves prevent blood flowing backwards when pressure changes. They respond to those pressure differences rather than pumping blood themselves.

sections.heading: Compare the blood vessels
sections.body:
Arteries have muscular, elastic walls suited to high pressure. Veins return blood at lower pressure and many contain valves.

Capillaries form networks close to cells. Their very thin walls allow substances to exchange over a short distance. Link vessel structure to its particular job.

sections.heading: Explain a coronary blockage
sections.body:
Coronary arteries supply the heart muscle. If they narrow, less oxygen can reach that muscle, especially when demand rises.

This can limit aerobic respiration and the energy available for contraction. A severe blockage can damage heart tissue. Risk factors affect the chance of disease, not a guaranteed outcome for every person.

sections.heading: Understand why two circuits are useful
sections.body:
After blood passes through lung capillaries, it returns to the heart before being pumped around the body. This allows the body circuit to receive a fresh pressure boost while the lung circuit operates at a lower pressure.

The two sides also keep oxygenated and deoxygenated blood largely separate. Remember the pulmonary vessels as exceptions to a misleading rule: the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood and the pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood. Vessel names describe direction, not oxygen content.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: Xylem, phloem and investigating transpiration

sections.heading: Give each tissue its own job
sections.body:
Xylem carries water and dissolved mineral ions from roots towards the leaves. Its conducting elements form hollow, strengthened pathways.

Phloem transports dissolved sugars from sources to sinks. A source releases sugar; a sink uses or stores it. A growing root can be a sink, so phloem transport is not simply always downwards.

sections.heading: Follow water through a plant
sections.body:
Water enters root hair cells by osmosis. It moves into xylem and up towards the leaves.

Water evaporates from moist leaf-cell surfaces and diffuses out through stomata as vapour. The transpiration stream replaces this loss. Root hairs increase the area in contact with soil water.

sections.heading: Use the gradient to predict changes
sections.body:
Wind removes humid air near a leaf, often increasing water loss. High humidity reduces the water-vapour gradient and usually slows it.

Temperature and light also affect the process. Under severe water stress, stomata may close, so one factor does not always control the rate on its own.

sections.heading: Read a potometer result correctly
sections.body:
A bubble potometer measures water uptake, which is an indirect estimate of transpiration. Track bubble distance per time in the same capillary.

Keep other conditions steady, allow the shoot to adjust and check for leaks. Some absorbed water is used or retained, so uptake and water-vapour loss are not exactly the same.

sections.heading: Compare rates using equal time or a calculated rate
sections.body:
A bubble moving 24 mm in two minutes has a distance-based uptake rate of 12 mm/min. Another moving 30 mm in five minutes has a rate of 6 mm/min, despite travelling farther in total.

Compare rates, not distances measured over different times. If capillary areas differ, distance alone is also insufficient: volume moved equals cross-sectional area × distance. State which measure your apparatus actually provides.

a region using or storing substances delivered by translocation

topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: Photosynthesis: limiting factors and practical evidence

sections.heading: Explain what the plant makes
sections.body:
Chlorophyll in chloroplasts absorbs light. Photosynthesis produces glucose and releases oxygen.

The plant can use glucose in respiration, store it as starch or turn it into materials such as cellulose. Mineral ions help make other substances, but they do not replace carbon dioxide as the main carbon source.

sections.heading: Identify the factor limiting the rate
sections.body:
At low light levels, increasing light can increase the rate. A plateau means more light no longer increases the measured rate in that range.

Another factor, such as carbon dioxide or temperature, may now limit it. A plateau does not mean photosynthesis has stopped.

sections.heading: Measure oxygen with a fair method
sections.body:
An aquatic plant can produce oxygen that is collected over a fixed time. Gas volume is often a better measure than bubble count because bubble sizes vary.

Keep temperature, plant size and carbon dioxide supply comparable. Moving a lamp can also heat the water, so control that extra change.

sections.heading: Understand what a starch test shows
sections.body:
Destarch a plant before testing for newly produced starch. Compare properly controlled conditions, such as covered and uncovered leaf regions.

Follow the teacher’s heating and ethanol procedure. Plants respire as well as photosynthesise, so a gas measurement may show the net effect of both processes.

sections.heading: Read a limiting-factor graph in stages
sections.body:
First describe what changes on the graph. For example, oxygen production rises as light intensity increases, then levels off. Next explain the rising part: more light supports faster photosynthesis.

Finally explain the plateau: light is no longer limiting, so changing a different factor may raise the rate. To test whether carbon dioxide is the new limit, increase its availability while keeping the other conditions controlled. The graph suggests a next investigation; it does not identify the new limiting factor by itself.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: Reproduction, development and cell division

sections.heading: Two routes to a new organism
sections.body: Asexual reproduction uses one parent and produces genetically similar offspring, apart from mutation. Sexual reproduction combines genetic material from gametes and creates variation. Mitosis produces genetically identical daughter cells for growth, repair and some asexual reproduction. Meiosis reduces chromosome number to produce haploid gametes and contributes to variation.

sections.heading: Flowering plant reproduction
sections.body: Anthers produce pollen and the stigma receives it during pollination. A pollen tube grows toward an ovule; fertilisation fuses male and female nuclei. The ovule develops into a seed and the ovary into a fruit. Seed germination requires water, oxygen and a suitable temperature. Pollination and fertilisation are different stages and may be separated in time.

sections.heading: Human reproduction and development
sections.body: The testes produce sperm and the ovaries produce ova. Fertilisation usually occurs in an oviduct, forming a zygote that divides and implants in the uterus. The placenta supports exchange between maternal and fetal circulations without normal direct mixing of their blood. Hormones coordinate the menstrual cycle; contraception can prevent gamete production, transport, fertilisation or implantation by different mechanisms.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: An insect-pollinated flower often has features that promote contact between the insect and pollen-bearing or pollen-receiving surfaces. Wind-pollinated plants instead commonly expose anthers and have structures that catch airborne pollen. These are functional adaptations, not rules based on flower colour alone. After fertilisation, a seed contains an embryo and food reserves; water activates processes, oxygen supports respiration and temperature affects enzyme action. The placenta provides a large exchange surface, but it is not an absolute barrier to all harmful substances. Maternal and fetal blood normally remain in separate circulations.

sections.heading: Compare mitosis and meiosis
sections.body:
In mitosis, the genetic material is copied before division and two daughter cells are formed with the same chromosome number as the parent. This supports growth, repair and some forms of asexual reproduction.

Meiosis produces haploid cells for sexual reproduction and creates genetic variation. In humans, a typical body cell has 46 chromosomes while a normal gamete has 23. Fertilisation joins two gamete nuclei and restores the diploid number. Do not say that fertilisation halves chromosome number.

sections.heading: Explain how the placenta supports development
sections.body:
The placenta provides an exchange surface between maternal and fetal circulations. Oxygen and nutrients pass towards the fetus, while carbon dioxide and other wastes pass towards the mother for removal. The blood normally remains in separate circulations.

A thin exchange barrier and a good blood supply help transfer substances. The placenta is not an absolute barrier to every harmful substance or pathogen. A good answer names what moves, its direction and why the fetus needs it.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: DNA, genetic crosses and evolution

sections.heading: Information is stored in base sequence
sections.body: DNA contains nucleotide bases arranged along two complementary strands. A gene is a DNA sequence that influences a product, commonly a protein. The order of bases determines the order of amino acids through the genetic code. Alleles are alternative versions of a gene. Genotype describes alleles; phenotype describes expressed characteristics shaped by genotype and environment.

sections.heading: Predict inheritance carefully
sections.body: For a simple dominant-recessive cross, specify allele symbols and parental genotypes, list gametes and combine them in a Punnett square. Probability predicts expected proportions across many offspring, not a guaranteed pattern in a small family. A recessive phenotype requires two recessive alleles in this model. Sex determination in the standard XX/XY model depends on whether the fertilising sperm carries X or Y.

sections.heading: Variation fuels natural selection
sections.body: Mutation can generate new alleles. Environmental conditions favour some heritable variants, whose carriers survive and reproduce more successfully. The advantageous alleles become more frequent over generations. Antibiotic resistance can spread when antibiotics select resistant bacteria; individual bacteria do not develop a needed mutation because they try to adapt. Selective breeding instead chooses parents for desired inherited traits.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: In protein synthesis, transcription produces an RNA copy from a DNA template, and translation uses the RNA base sequence to assemble amino acids at ribosomes. A mutation may alter an amino-acid sequence, change the amount of product made or have no detectable effect. Codominance differs from simple dominance because both alleles influence the heterozygous phenotype. Polygenic characteristics are influenced by several genes and often show continuous variation, with environmental effects as well. In a pedigree, a phenotype alone may not identify a unique genotype, so state uncertainty where several allele combinations remain possible.

sections.heading: Read a genetic cross as a probability
sections.body:
For a simple dominant–recessive cross Tt × Tt, each parent can supply T or t. The four equally likely combinations are TT, Tt, Tt and tt. The recessive phenotype has probability 1/4.

This does not mean exactly one of every four children must show it. Each fertilisation is a new chance event. Large numbers tend to show proportions nearer the predicted ratio, but small families may differ greatly.

sections.heading: Keep sex chromosomes separate from all other genes
sections.body:
In the usual simplified human model, an egg carries X and a sperm carries X or Y. An X-carrying sperm gives XX and a Y-carrying sperm gives XY. A basic cross therefore predicts about equal probabilities for these combinations.

The model describes the inheritance pattern used in this course; it should not be stretched into claims about every aspect of a person’s biology. In any cross, label the alleles or chromosomes clearly so the symbols do not become mixed up.

topics.tip: Dominant does not mean common, stronger or automatically beneficial.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: Hormonal control of the menstrual cycle

sections.heading: Coordinate the ovary and uterus
sections.body: The menstrual cycle involves related changes in the ovary and uterine lining. FSH supports follicle development and stimulates oestrogen secretion. Rising oestrogen supports rebuilding of the uterine lining and participates in feedback on pituitary hormone release. A suitable hormonal pattern leads to a surge of LH, which triggers ovulation. These are coordinated processes, so a complete explanation links a hormone to its target and effect.

sections.heading: After ovulation
sections.body: The remains of the follicle form the corpus luteum, which secretes progesterone. Progesterone helps maintain the uterine lining and inhibits further FSH and LH release. If pregnancy is not established, hormone levels fall as the corpus luteum declines, and the lining is shed. If pregnancy is established, other hormonal signals maintain support. A simplified school cycle diagram illustrates relationships, but actual cycle lengths and timings vary.

sections.heading: Read a graph rather than memorising one date
sections.body: Use the plotted hormone pattern and the question’s time scale to identify events. A sharp LH peak is associated with ovulation; a later progesterone rise relates to the corpus luteum. Different graphs may use different scales for different hormones, so apparent line heights cannot always be compared as absolute concentrations. State the hormone, its source where required, its effect and the relevant feedback link.

sections.heading: Build the sequence around the main events
sections.body:
FSH supports follicle development and oestrogen production. Oestrogen helps rebuild the uterine lining. A surge in LH triggers ovulation. After ovulation, the corpus luteum releases progesterone, which helps maintain the lining.

If pregnancy is not established, the corpus luteum declines, hormone concentrations fall and the lining is shed. The cycle diagram is a simplified model. Use its actual time axis; real cycles do not all have the same length or ovulation day.

sections.heading: Connect feedback to the next stage
sections.body:
Hormones do not act as four separate switches. They affect the release of other hormones. Progesterone inhibits FSH and LH, helping prevent another follicle cycle beginning immediately. Falling progesterone removes part of that inhibition.

When a graph asks you to explain an event, state the hormone change and its effect on a target. Avoid comparing line heights if different hormones use different vertical scales. A tall line on one scale does not automatically represent the highest concentration.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: DNA to protein: transcription and translation

sections.heading: The code is a sequence
sections.body: DNA consists of two strands with complementary base pairing. The sequence along a strand carries information; the fact that a molecule contains four kinds of base is not sufficient to specify a protein. A gene contains information related to a functional product. In protein-coding contexts, the order of bases determines a sequence of amino acids through an RNA intermediate. An amino-acid chain must fold appropriately to perform its biological role.

sections.heading: Transcription and translation are different stages
sections.body: During transcription, an RNA copy is made from a DNA template. RNA contains uracil rather than thymine in the usual school comparison. During translation, a ribosome reads the messenger-RNA sequence in codons, and transfer RNA helps deliver corresponding amino acids. The growing chain follows the codon sequence. Do not describe the DNA molecule as leaving the nucleus and travelling to every ribosome as part of this normal eukaryotic process.

sections.heading: Relate mutation to function carefully
sections.body: A base change can alter a codon, which may alter an amino acid and protein structure. This can affect an active site or another functional region. However, some changes produce no amino-acid change, and some amino-acid changes have little detectable effect. A causal explanation should avoid claiming every mutation is harmful or every mutation must change a protein. Use the exact sequence or evidence supplied in the problem.

sections.heading: Follow the information in the correct order
sections.body:
In transcription, RNA is made using a DNA template. In translation, a ribosome reads the messenger RNA in groups of three bases called codons. Transfer RNA brings amino acids that match the coding instructions.

The chain of amino acids then folds into a protein. Its shape helps determine its function. DNA does not normally leave the nucleus and become the protein itself. Keep the information pathway separate from the molecules being built.

sections.heading: Explain how a mutation may affect a protein
sections.body:
A mutation changes a DNA base sequence. This may change a codon, which may change an amino acid. A different amino-acid sequence can alter folding and therefore the protein’s shape and function.

Not every mutation changes the final protein or causes a visible effect. Some codon changes still specify the same amino acid, and some changes occur outside the protein-coding sequence. Use “may” where the outcome depends on the mutation rather than claiming every change has the same effect.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: Natural selection, antibiotic resistance and interpreting change

sections.heading: Start with variation already present
sections.body:
Individuals differ. Mutations can create new alleles, and sexual reproduction produces new combinations. Some differences can be inherited.

An organism does not produce a useful mutation because it knows it needs one. Identify the existing difference before explaining which individuals survive better.

sections.heading: Link survival to reproduction
sections.body:
A selection pressure makes some inherited traits more useful. Individuals with those traits may be more likely to survive and reproduce.

They pass alleles to offspring. Over generations, the traits can become more common. Survival alone is not the whole explanation: contribution to later generations matters.

sections.heading: Apply this to antibiotic resistance
sections.body:
Some bacteria may already have resistance. An antibiotic affects susceptible bacteria more strongly. Resistant survivors reproduce, increasing their share of the population.

Antibiotics do not treat viruses in the same way. Explain selection in bacteria rather than saying the drug teaches them how to resist it.

sections.heading: Distinguish a fraction from a number
sections.body:
The percentage of resistant bacteria can rise just because susceptible bacteria die. The number of resistant bacteria need not have increased yet.

To compare actual resistant numbers, you need the total population sizes as well as percentages. Use the measure shown on the graph.

sections.heading: Explain adaptation without saying a population is trying
sections.body:
Imagine beetles with inherited colour differences on a dark surface. Birds may more easily see pale beetles. Darker beetles are therefore more likely to survive and breed, passing their alleles to more offspring.

After many generations, dark colour may be more common. The beetles did not decide to change colour. If the background changes, the same trait may no longer be as useful. An adaptation’s advantage depends on the environment.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: Populations, feeding and environmental change

sections.heading: Energy flows; nutrients cycle
sections.body: Producers transfer light energy into biomass, and consumers obtain energy by feeding. Arrows in food chains show the direction of energy transfer. At each trophic level, energy is lost through respiration, movement, waste and uneaten material; not all biomass becomes growth in the next level. Decomposers break down organic matter and return nutrients to the environment.

sections.heading: Measure a habitat without selecting a convenient result
sections.body: Quadrats estimate abundance of stationary organisms. Use random coordinates for an unbiased area sample; use a transect to investigate a gradient. Repeat sampling and calculate a mean before scaling to a larger area. Measure relevant abiotic variables such as light, temperature, water availability and pH. Correlation between abundance and a variable does not by itself establish cause.

sections.heading: Human activity changes ecological systems
sections.body: Burning fuels and deforestation affect the carbon cycle and atmospheric greenhouse gases. Fertiliser runoff may cause eutrophication: algal growth shades submerged plants, dead biomass is decomposed and decomposer respiration reduces dissolved oxygen. Sulfur dioxide contributes to acid deposition. Conservation can protect habitats, maintain biodiversity and support sustainable resource use, but decisions may involve competing social and economic priorities.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: The carbon cycle follows carbon atoms through photosynthesis, feeding, respiration, decomposition and combustion. The nitrogen cycle involves a different set of transformations: fixation introduces usable nitrogen from atmospheric nitrogen, decomposers release ammonium compounds, nitrifying organisms oxidise them, and denitrification returns nitrogen to the atmosphere. Energy flows through an ecosystem and is dissipated, while elements are recycled. A pyramid of biomass records living material at each level; it need not have the same shape as a pyramid counting organisms. Sampling conclusions should acknowledge spatial variation and the limitations of the chosen method.

sections.heading: Explain energy loss between feeding levels
sections.body:
Plants capture some incoming light energy in organic material. Only part reaches the next feeding level. Some material is not eaten, some eaten material is not digested, and organisms use energy in respiration.

Energy is transferred to the surroundings, including as thermal energy, so less remains available in new biomass. This helps explain why long food chains are limited. Decomposers recycle nutrients, but energy is not recycled around the food chain in the same way.

sections.heading: Follow the steps of eutrophication
sections.body:
Nitrate-rich runoff can increase algae growth in water. Dense algae can block light, so submerged plants may die. Microorganisms decompose dead material and respire, using dissolved oxygen.

If oxygen falls greatly, fish and other aerobic organisms may die. The fertiliser has not simply “poisoned the fish” in this explanation: the important chain is nutrient increase, growth, death, decomposition and oxygen loss. Conditions such as water movement and the amount of material affect how severe the outcome is.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: Carbon and nitrogen cycles

sections.heading: Follow atoms through transformations
sections.body: Photosynthesis takes carbon from carbon dioxide into organic molecules. Feeding transfers these molecules between organisms, while respiration releases carbon dioxide. Decomposers use organic material from dead organisms and waste, releasing carbon through respiration. Combustion releases carbon from fuels or biomass. Carbon is transferred and chemically rearranged; energy entering the ecosystem is not recycled by exactly the same processes.

sections.heading: Nitrogen becomes usable through microorganisms
sections.body: Atmospheric nitrogen is not directly usable by most plants. Nitrogen fixation converts it into compounds that can enter biological systems. Decomposition releases ammonium compounds from organic nitrogen. Nitrifying microorganisms oxidise ammonium through nitrite to nitrate under suitable aerobic conditions. Plants absorb mineral nitrogen and use it in molecules such as amino acids. Denitrifying microorganisms can return nitrogen to the atmosphere, particularly where oxygen is limited.

sections.heading: Connect the cycle to farming and pollution
sections.body: Harvest removes nitrogen-containing material from an area, so nutrient replacement may be needed to sustain production. Excess fertiliser can enter waterways and contribute to eutrophication. Waterlogged soils can favour nitrogen losses through denitrification. When asked about bacteria, identify the process and chemical direction rather than saying all bacteria make nitrates. Biological cycles describe interacting populations and environmental conditions, not one universal linear chain.

sections.heading: Track carbon through named processes
sections.body:
Photosynthesis takes carbon dioxide from the air and puts carbon into organic molecules. Feeding passes some of that carbon to animals. Respiration by plants, animals and microorganisms releases carbon dioxide.

Decomposition breaks down dead material, and decomposers also respire. Combustion of fuels or biomass releases carbon dioxide too. When describing a cycle arrow, name both the process and the carbon store it connects. “Carbon goes back” does not explain whether this happens by respiration, decomposition or burning.

sections.heading: Keep the nitrogen bacteria’s jobs separate
sections.body:
Nitrogen-fixing bacteria convert atmospheric nitrogen into forms that enter biological pathways. Decomposers break down nitrogen-containing material and can release ammonium compounds. Nitrifying bacteria convert these towards nitrates under suitable aerobic conditions.

Plants take up nitrate ions to make amino acids and proteins. Denitrifying bacteria can return nitrogen to the atmosphere, especially under low-oxygen conditions. Fixation and nitrification are not the same step. Soil oxygen conditions help explain why waterlogging can reduce nitrate availability.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: Sampling, biodiversity and ecological data

sections.heading: Match sampling to the question
sections.body: Use quadrats for organisms that can be sampled in a fixed area and a transect to investigate change along a gradient. Random coordinates reduce selection of unusually convenient or impressive locations. Repeated quadrats provide a mean and some information about variability. Systematic positions along a transect can reveal a relationship with distance, but they answer a different question from a random area survey.

sections.heading: Calculate with the sampled area
sections.body: Density is number counted divided by total area sampled. Multiply a representative density by habitat area to estimate abundance. Percentage cover can be more useful than counting individual plants when boundaries between individuals are unclear. Compare results using equal effort or an appropriate adjustment. Species richness is a count of species; biodiversity can also involve how evenly individuals are distributed among those species.

sections.heading: Evaluate the conclusion
sections.body: A correlation between light intensity and a species’ abundance does not isolate light as the cause: soil moisture or disturbance may vary too. Explain how variables are measured, consider replication and identify realistic limitations. Sampling may miss seasonal or mobile organisms. Give an estimate with a justified degree of confidence rather than claiming a quadrat survey measures every organism in the entire ecosystem directly.

sections.heading: Turn quadrat counts into an estimate
sections.body:
Suppose ten 0.25 m² quadrats contain 40 plants altogether. The sampled area is 2.5 m², so the estimated density is 40/2.5 = 16 plants per m². A similar 100 m² habitat would contain about 1600 plants.

That estimate depends on the samples representing the habitat. Use random coordinates for a general abundance estimate and enough samples to reduce the effect of clumped patches. Report an estimate rather than claiming an exact count of every plant.

sections.heading: Choose a transect when conditions change
sections.body:
A transect follows a line across a habitat, such as from shade into open ground. Sample at stated intervals to investigate how distribution changes along that environmental gradient.

This systematic approach answers a different question from randomly scattered quadrats. Record the relevant environmental variable as well as the organism count where possible. Repeat parallel transects to see whether one unusual patch dominates the result. Correlation along the line suggests a relationship, but other changing conditions may also matter.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: Food production, biotechnology and genetic methods

sections.heading: Increase yield while considering consequences
sections.body: Greenhouses control light, temperature and carbon dioxide, but added energy and infrastructure have financial and environmental costs. Fertilisers supply mineral nutrients; biological control uses living organisms to reduce pests. Intensive livestock systems can limit movement and heat loss to improve growth efficiency, while raising welfare, disease and pollution questions that should be evaluated explicitly.

sections.heading: Use microorganisms as biological factories
sections.body: Yeast fermentation supports bread and alcoholic-drink production. Industrial fermenters maintain suitable temperature, pH, nutrients and, when needed, oxygen. Aseptic conditions reduce contamination; stirring distributes resources and heat. Pectinase can increase fruit-juice extraction and lactase can produce lactose-reduced milk. Conditions depend on the organism and desired product rather than one universal optimum.

sections.heading: Modify or copy genetic material
sections.body: Genetic engineering transfers selected genetic information between organisms, using tools such as restriction enzymes, ligase and vectors. Bacteria can be engineered to produce human insulin. Cloning generates genetically similar organisms through methods such as tissue culture or nuclear transfer. Benefits must be weighed against reduced diversity, animal welfare and unintended ecological effects. Describing a method is different from evaluating its use.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A fermenter is designed around its organism and product. Aeration is important for an aerobic process, while ethanol fermentation uses anaerobic conditions. A temperature jacket removes excess heat, and sensors allow conditions to be monitored rather than assumed. In genetic modification, a selected gene can be inserted into a vector and introduced into host cells; identifying successful transformants and controlling expression are essential steps. Clones share much genetic information, but environmental conditions and some biological details can still produce differences. Evaluation should separate evidence of a benefit from a claim that every use is equally safe or useful.

sections.heading: Explain the controls inside a fermenter
sections.body:
A fermenter needs a suitable nutrient supply, temperature and pH for the chosen microorganism. For an aerobic process, oxygen must also be supplied. Mixing helps distribute oxygen, nutrients and heat.

Microbial respiration can release heat, so cooling may be needed to prevent conditions becoming too hot. Sterilising the equipment and incoming materials reduces contamination by other organisms. Each control should be linked to its purpose; “keep conditions ideal” is too vague to explain the method.

sections.heading: Follow a simple genetic-engineering pathway
sections.body:
A desired gene can be placed in a vector, such as a bacterial plasmid. Suitable enzymes cut DNA and join the gene into the vector. The vector enters a host cell, and cells containing the intended genetic change are identified and grown.

If the gene is expressed successfully, the host can make the required product, which may then need collection and purification. Moving a gene is only one stage: correct expression and product quality also matter. Use this sequence to explain the process, not merely list enzyme names.

topics.tip: Genetic engineering transfers selected genetic material; selective breeding chooses parents over generations.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: Cloning, micropropagation and evaluating biotechnology

sections.heading: Distinguish a clone from sexual offspring
sections.body:
Asexual reproduction can produce genetically identical copies, apart from changes such as new mutations. A cutting can grow into a clone of a plant.

Sexual reproduction combines gametes and usually creates more genetic variation. Clones can still differ in growth because they experience different light, water or disease conditions.

sections.heading: Follow micropropagation step by step
sections.body:
Small plant-tissue samples are grown on a suitable nutrient medium under controlled, sterile conditions. Hormones help direct growth and development.

The plantlets are transferred and gradually established in growing conditions. Sterility reduces contamination by microorganisms that might compete with or damage the plant tissue.

sections.heading: Weigh uniformity against shared risk
sections.body:
Cloning can produce plants with consistent useful features, such as crop quality. But low genetic diversity can make many plants vulnerable to the same disease.

The outcome depends on the variety and growing conditions. Clones are not automatically unhealthy, and high yield in one environment does not guarantee high yield elsewhere.

sections.heading: Keep cloning and genetic modification separate
sections.body:
Cloning copies genetic information. Genetic modification deliberately changes it. Either a modified or an unmodified plant can be cloned.

In a simple animal nuclear-transfer model, a donor nucleus is placed into an egg whose nucleus has been removed. Evaluate the method using evidence about success, welfare and its purpose.

sections.heading: Judge success beyond the first stage
sections.body:
Producing many plantlets is not enough to prove that a crop-production method works well. Plantlets must survive transfer to soil, grow and produce a useful crop.

A fair comparison considers survival percentage, time, cost, disease status and final performance. For example, 1000 plantlets with 40% survival give fewer established plants than 700 with 90% survival. Follow the process to the stage that matters for the stated goal, instead of judging it from the largest early number.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Particles, separation and atomic structure

sections.heading: A particle model explains state changes
sections.body: Solids have particles vibrating around fixed positions, liquids have nearby particles that can move past one another, and gases have widely spaced particles moving freely. Melting and boiling overcome attractions between particles; they do not usually split the particles into atoms. Diffusion arises from random particle movement and produces net spreading down a concentration gradient.

sections.heading: Separate physical mixtures appropriately
sections.body: Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid. Crystallisation recovers a dissolved solid; distillation recovers a solvent or separates liquids with different boiling behaviours. Fractional distillation uses repeated vaporisation and condensation. Paper chromatography separates substances through differing movement between stationary and mobile phases. Rf compares spot travel with solvent-front travel from the same baseline.

sections.heading: Atoms and isotopes
sections.body: Atoms contain protons, neutrons and electrons. Atomic number counts protons; mass number counts protons plus neutrons. Isotopes share proton number but differ in neutron number. A neutral atom has equal proton and electron numbers. Relative atomic mass is an abundance-weighted mean. Electron arrangement explains many chemical patterns; ion formation changes electrons, leaving the nucleus unchanged.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: The movement of a chromatographic spot depends on its interactions with both the stationary and mobile phases. A substance more strongly retained by the stationary phase travels less far under otherwise identical conditions. Rf values are useful for comparison only when relevant conditions match. Isotopic abundance calculations use an average of isotope masses weighted by their proportions; the result does not imply that an individual atom has a fractional number of neutrons. In a heating curve for a pure substance, a plateau marks a phase change under the idealised constant-pressure conditions, while supplied energy continues to overcome attractions.

sections.heading: Calculate relative atomic mass from isotopes
sections.body:
Isotopes of one element have the same proton number but different neutron numbers. They therefore have different masses but belong to the same element.

For an element with 75% atoms of mass 35 and 25% of mass 37, the weighted mean is (75 × 35 + 25 × 37)/100 = 35.5. This is not the mass number of one atom. It is an average that accounts for how common each isotope is.

sections.heading: Separate dissolved and undissolved substances
sections.body:
Filtration works when a solid is insoluble in the liquid. Dissolved particles pass through with the solvent, so filtering salt water does not remove the salt.

To recover the solvent, use suitable distillation. To recover the dissolved solid, concentrate the solution and allow crystals to form using the approved method. Choose the process from the physical-property difference and the substance you want to collect. A separation does not usually change a substance’s chemical identity.

topics.tip: A chromatography baseline is drawn in pencil and kept above the initial solvent level.
topics.formula: Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent front

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Bonding, structure and chemical formulae

sections.heading: Ionic and covalent bonds are different attractions
sections.body: Ionic bonding is electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions in a lattice. Covalent bonding is attraction involving nuclei and a shared pair of electrons. Metallic bonding is attraction between positive ions and delocalised electrons. Balance ionic charges to write formulae; a neutral compound has no net charge, even though it contains charged ions.

sections.heading: Structure determines observable behaviour
sections.body: Giant ionic substances have high melting points and conduct when molten or dissolved because ions can move. Simple molecular substances often have low melting points because intermolecular attractions are weaker than their internal covalent bonds. Giant covalent structures such as diamond require many strong bonds to be broken; graphite has layers and mobile electrons. Metals conduct because delocalised electrons move through the structure.

sections.heading: Represent atoms without losing them
sections.body: A balanced equation conserves atoms of each element. Change coefficients, not chemical formulae, to balance it. State symbols distinguish solids, liquids, gases and aqueous solutions. Dot-and-cross diagrams show outer-shell electron contributions; bracket and charge ionic species correctly. For electron transfer, oxidation is loss of electrons and reduction is gain; these occur together.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: For a dot-and-cross diagram, show only the required outer electrons and identify which atom contributed each shared electron. For ions, bracket the resulting ion and show its charge rather than drawing the transferred electron as a covalent bond. A small molecule can contain strong covalent bonds yet form a substance with a low boiling point because the attractions between molecules are relatively weak. Graphite conducts because some electrons are delocalised within its structure, whereas the electrons of diamond are held in its covalent bonding framework. Explain observed properties using both structure and the relevant moving or interacting particles.

sections.heading: Build an ionic formula from charge balance
sections.body:
An ionic compound must have no overall charge. Magnesium forms Mg²⁺ and chloride is Cl⁻, so two chloride ions are needed for each magnesium ion: MgCl₂. Aluminium oxide is Al₂O₃ because two Al³⁺ ions balance three O²⁻ ions.

The small numbers in the formula show the simplest ratio of ions. They do not mean that a giant ionic lattice consists of separate molecules with only that many ions.

sections.heading: Explain a property using the actual structure
sections.body:
A simple molecular substance has covalent bonds within molecules and forces between molecules. Melting usually overcomes the forces between molecules, not all of the covalent bonds inside them.

A giant covalent structure, such as diamond, has a network of strong covalent bonds, so much more energy is needed to disrupt it. Metallic conduction instead depends on electrons able to move through the metal. Name the moving particles when explaining conductivity; “it has bonds” is not enough.

topics.tip: Melting a molecular substance overcomes intermolecular attractions, not the covalent bonds inside each molecule.

The neutral formula is Al₂O₃.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Moles, concentrations and electrolysis

sections.heading: Count chemical amounts with moles
sections.body: Relative formula mass adds the relative atomic masses in a formula. Amount in moles equals mass divided by molar mass. Use balanced-equation coefficients as mole ratios, then convert to the required mass, volume or concentration. The limiting reactant is used up first. Percentage yield compares actual with theoretical yield; atom economy concerns the fraction of reactant mass incorporated into the desired product.

sections.heading: Concentration connects amount to volume
sections.body: For molar concentration, use concentration = moles/volume in dm³. Divide cm³ by 1000 before substitution. In gas calculations, use the molar gas volume specified by the question; the common school value at room conditions is 24 dm³ mol⁻¹. Empirical formulae follow the simplest whole-number mole ratio, not the simplest mass ratio.

sections.heading: Electricity drives a chemical change
sections.body: Electrolysis requires mobile ions. Cations move to the negative cathode, where reduction occurs; anions move to the positive anode, where oxidation occurs. A molten binary ionic compound produces its elements. In aqueous solutions, water-derived species compete, so identify the ions and the electrode rules before predicting products. In electroplating, the object to be coated is the cathode.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A limiting-reactant calculation first converts both starting amounts to moles. Divide each by its balanced-equation coefficient to compare available reaction units; the smaller value limits product formation. In electrolysis, electrons move through the external circuit and ions carry charge through the electrolyte. At an electrode, a half-equation must balance both atoms and net charge. For copper deposition, Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu describes reduction. An aqueous electrolyte may generate a product from water-derived ions, so predictions must consider all relevant species and the stated electrode materials.

sections.heading: Keep mass concentration and molar concentration separate
sections.body:
Mass concentration is mass of solute divided by solution volume. If 5.0 g is dissolved to make 0.250 dm³ of solution, the mass concentration is 20 g/dm³.

Molar concentration uses moles instead of grams. For a solute with molar mass 40 g/mol, those 5.0 g are 0.125 mol, so the molar concentration is 0.500 mol/dm³. The two answers describe the same solution but use different quantities and units.

sections.heading: Use coefficients after converting to moles
sections.body:
In 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, two moles of hydrogen react with one mole of oxygen. The ratio is not two grams to one gram.

If 0.30 mol hydrogen reacts completely with enough oxygen, it forms 0.30 mol water and uses 0.15 mol oxygen. Convert a required amount back to mass by multiplying by molar mass. Write the unit at each stage so grams, moles and cubic decimetres do not become mixed up.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Empirical formulae and molecular formulae

sections.heading: Mass ratios are not atom ratios
sections.body: A formula records relative numbers of atoms. Start from masses or percentage composition and divide each element’s mass by its relative atomic mass. The resulting mole values are proportional to atom numbers. Dividing by the smallest value gives a ratio that may need multiplying to remove simple fractions. Do not round a ratio near 1.5 directly to 2; check whether multiplying all parts by two gives a sensible whole-number ratio.

sections.heading: From empirical to molecular information
sections.body: An empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio. A molecular formula gives the actual atom numbers in a molecule. Divide the molecular relative mass by the empirical-formula mass to obtain an integer multiplier, then multiply every subscript. Ionic giant structures are described by their formula ratio rather than a molecular formula for an isolated molecule in the same way.

sections.heading: Interpret an experiment critically
sections.body: A metal-oxide experiment can use the change in mass as oxygen gained, under the stated assumptions. Loss of product, incomplete oxidation or reaction with another gas can affect the inferred composition. State which mass is measured directly and which is found by subtraction. Repeating a heating-and-weighing cycle to constant mass can support completion, but does not prove every other experimental assumption is correct.

sections.heading: Convert a percentage composition into a ratio
sections.body:
For a compound containing 40% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen and 53.3% oxygen, imagine a 100 g sample. Divide each mass by the relative atomic mass: about 3.33, 6.7 and 3.33 mol respectively.

Divide by the smallest value to get approximately 1:2:1, so the empirical formula is CH₂O. Do not use the percentages directly as subscripts: the same mass of different elements contains different numbers of atoms.

sections.heading: Do not round away a meaningful half ratio
sections.body:
After dividing by the smallest mole value, a ratio such as 1:1.5 is not ready to become a formula. Multiply both parts by 2 to get 2:3. Likewise, a ratio involving thirds may need multiplication by 3.

Once you have the empirical formula, calculate its formula mass. If the molecular mass is three times larger, multiply every empirical subscript by 3. The molecular formula must preserve the same simplest ratio.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Electrolysis: ions, electrodes and balanced half-equations

sections.heading: Identify what carries charge
sections.body:
Ions carry charge through a molten ionic substance or a suitable solution because they can move. In a solid ionic lattice, they cannot move freely.

Electrons carry charge through the wires. Do not describe liquid conduction as free electrons travelling between the ions.

sections.heading: Identify the electrolyte before predicting products
sections.body:
A molten compound contains its own ions. An aqueous solution also has species from water, so product choices can differ.

Positive ions move towards the negative cathode. Negative ions move towards the positive anode. Product prediction also depends on concentration and whether the electrodes take part in the reaction.

sections.heading: Balance a half-equation
sections.body:
At the cathode, particles gain electrons: this is reduction. Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu has equal charge on both sides.

At the anode, particles lose electrons: this is oxidation. For chloride, write 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻. Check both atom counts and total charge.

sections.heading: Explain a changing electrode
sections.body:
With copper electrodes in copper sulfate solution, copper can dissolve from the anode and deposit at the cathode. The electrodes are taking part.

With inert electrodes, anode reactions are different. Name the electrode material and electrolyte before explaining a deposit, gas or mass change.

sections.heading: Follow a copper ion from solution to the electrode
sections.body:
A Cu²⁺ ion has two fewer electrons than a neutral copper atom. At the cathode it gains two electrons supplied through the external circuit. It becomes a copper atom and joins the solid deposit.

The ion does not turn into an electron, and its positive charge is not carried away by a copper nucleus moving through the wire. Separating ion movement in the liquid from electron movement in the wire makes the whole circuit easier to understand.

loss of electrons

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Limiting reactants, gas volumes, yield and atom economy

sections.heading: Find the reactant that runs out first
sections.body:
Convert each reactant amount to moles, then compare with the equation coefficients. The limiting reactant is used up first and sets the maximum product amount.

The smaller mass is not necessarily limiting. Different substances have different molar masses and may react in a ratio other than 1:1.

sections.heading: Calculate a gas volume
sections.body:
At the same temperature and pressure, gas volumes follow mole ratios. Use the molar gas volume given in the question, often 24 dm³/mol at room conditions.

Convert cm³ and dm³ consistently. A calculated volume assumes the stated conditions and complete reaction of the relevant amount.

sections.heading: Compare actual and theoretical yield
sections.body:
Theoretical yield is the maximum calculated from the available reactants. Actual yield is what is collected.

Percentage yield = actual/theoretical × 100. Loss during transfer, incomplete reaction or side reactions can lower it. A result above 100% can indicate wet product, contamination or a calculation error.

sections.heading: Distinguish yield from atom economy
sections.body:
Atom economy measures how much of the reactant mass ends up in the desired product in the balanced reaction. It does not measure how much product was collected.

A process can have high yield but still make much unwanted by-product. Costs and energy use also matter when comparing routes.

sections.heading: Use a recipe analogy without forgetting the mole ratio
sections.body:
Suppose a reaction needs two units of A for every one of B. Having six units of A and five of B allows only three complete reaction sets: A runs out, leaving two units of B.

Chemical coefficients work in moles, not arbitrary grams. For a real calculation, convert masses to moles first. Then use the limiting amount and equation ratio to find product moles, before converting the result to the requested mass or volume.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Chromatography, solubility and choosing a separation method

sections.heading: Choose the property that separates the mixture
sections.body:
Filtration removes an insoluble solid from a liquid. Crystallisation can recover a dissolved solid. Distillation can collect a solvent or separate suitable liquids.

Ask what you want to collect and which property differs, such as solubility or boiling point. Filtering cannot remove a substance that is fully dissolved.

sections.heading: Set up chromatography correctly
sections.body:
Place a small sample spot on a pencil baseline above the solvent. The solvent rises through the stationary phase and carries the sample components.

Different interactions with the two phases make components move differently. Ink can interfere, and submerging the spot can wash the sample into the solvent reservoir.

sections.heading: Calculate an Rf ratio
sections.body:
Rf = component distance divided by solvent-front distance. Measure both from the same baseline. Measure to the centre of a clear spot.

Rf has no unit. Compare values only under matching conditions, including solvent and stationary phase. A matching value supports an identification but does not uniquely prove it.

sections.heading: Be careful about a single spot
sections.body:
Several separated spots show several detectable components. One spot does not guarantee purity: substances may overlap or be missed by the method.

Use additional evidence when needed. Small starting spots, a suitable solvent and clear marking of the solvent front help make the result useful.

sections.heading: Explain why the same substance can move differently
sections.body:
A component’s movement depends on its attraction to the stationary phase and how readily it travels with the solvent. Changing the solvent changes that balance, so the same substance can have a different Rf.

That is why a reference sample should be run under the same conditions as an unknown. If two substances overlap in one solvent, another suitable solvent may separate them. A chromatogram is evidence from a particular method, not a permanent label independent of conditions.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Periodic trends, air and water

sections.heading: The table organises electron patterns
sections.body: Elements in a group have related outer-electron arrangements and similar chemistry. Across a period the proton number increases. Group 1 metals react with water to produce hydroxides and hydrogen; reactivity generally increases down the group as the outer electron is more easily lost. Group 7 halogens form negative ions; a more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halide from solution.

sections.heading: Atmospheric gases have distinctive uses and tests
sections.body: Air is mostly nitrogen and oxygen, with argon, carbon dioxide and variable water vapour. Oxygen supports combustion and relights a glowing splint. Hydrogen burns with a squeaky pop in a suitable test. Carbon dioxide turns limewater cloudy. Combustion in insufficient oxygen can produce poisonous carbon monoxide and particulates. Complete hydrocarbon combustion produces carbon dioxide and water.

sections.heading: Water treatment is a sequence of processes
sections.body: Sedimentation and filtration remove suspended material; disinfection reduces harmful microorganisms. Dissolved salts may require desalination, for example through distillation or membrane methods, with energy and infrastructure costs. Pure water is a single substance; potable water is safe to drink but may contain dissolved substances. Chemical tests must distinguish an observed result from the conclusion drawn from it.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: In Group 1, increasing distance and shielding make the outer electron easier to remove down the group, despite increasing nuclear charge. For halogens, the attraction for an incoming electron generally weakens down the group, so their displacement trend is opposite. When identifying gases, specify the test material and observation: a glowing splint relights in oxygen, while carbon dioxide makes limewater cloudy. Water treatment may disinfect without removing dissolved ions. Desalination and sterilisation solve different problems, and potable water does not need to be chemically pure.

sections.heading: Explain the Group 1 trend using electron loss
sections.body:
Group 1 atoms have one electron in their outer shell. They form positive ions by losing it. Down the group, the outer electron is farther from the nucleus and more shielded by inner electrons.

It is therefore lost more easily, so reactivity increases in the usual comparison. The larger proton number alone does not decide the trend: distance and shielding also matter. This is different from Group 7, where reactivity involves gaining an electron.

sections.heading: Connect an air-volume change to oxygen content
sections.body:
A suitable school experiment can remove oxygen from a trapped air sample using a reaction. If its volume falls from 100 cm³ to 79 cm³ after cooling to the original temperature, 21 cm³ was removed. That suggests about 21% oxygen.

The comparison needs a complete reaction, no leaks and matched temperature and pressure. A smaller volume loss could mean oxygen was not fully removed. A volume measured while still hot would not be directly comparable with the starting measurement.

topics.tip: Reactivity trends down Group 1 and Group 7 go in opposite directions.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Metals, extraction and corrosion

sections.heading: Reactivity predicts competing reactions
sections.body: A more reactive metal can displace a less reactive metal from a compound. The reactivity series also helps predict reaction with water, steam and dilute acids. Metal oxides can often be reduced by carbon if the metal is less reactive than carbon; more reactive metals generally require electrolysis of a suitable molten compound. Extraction method therefore depends on chemical reactivity and economic conditions.

sections.heading: Extraction involves chemical and practical decisions
sections.body: In iron extraction, carbon monoxide reduces iron oxide while limestone-derived material removes acidic impurities into slag. Aluminium extraction uses electrolysis of aluminium oxide dissolved in molten cryolite, reducing operating temperature. The carbon anodes are consumed because oxygen formed there reacts with them. Recycling metals often needs less energy than extraction from ore, but collection and sorting also have costs.

sections.heading: Rusting needs water and oxygen
sections.body: Iron corrosion can be reduced by barriers such as paint, grease or plastic. Galvanising adds a zinc coating that acts both as a barrier and as sacrificial protection. A more reactive attached metal preferentially oxidises. Alloys contain more than one element; differently sized atoms can disrupt the layers and make sliding more difficult, often increasing hardness.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: An alloy is not simply a mixture that must always be harder; its composition and processing determine the useful properties. For many common alloys, different atomic sizes hinder layer movement compared with a pure metal. In extraction questions, separate reduction of the metal compound from removal of impurities. In aluminium production, cryolite lowers the operating temperature of the electrolyte mixture, reducing energy demand compared with melting pure aluminium oxide. Sacrificial protection needs an electrical connection and a suitable environment for the corrosion cell; a disconnected zinc object nearby does not automatically protect iron.

sections.heading: Choose extraction from reactivity
sections.body:
A metal less reactive than carbon may be extracted from a suitable oxide by reduction with carbon or carbon monoxide. The oxygen is removed from the metal compound. More reactive metals, such as aluminium, need other methods, commonly electrolysis of a suitable molten mixture.

Electrolysis needs electrical energy, which affects cost. The extraction method must suit the compound, not just the metal’s name. An ore also contains unwanted material, so extraction can involve several separation and chemical stages.

sections.heading: Explain rusting and protection as a chain
sections.body:
Iron rusts when both water and oxygen are available. A barrier coating can keep them away from the surface, but a scratch may expose iron.

A zinc coating can also provide sacrificial protection because zinc is more reactive and can oxidise in preference to the iron under suitable conditions. This explains why galvanising and painting are not exactly the same protection method. Rust is not a useful permanent protective layer in the way some other metal oxides can be.

topics.tip: A barrier coating and sacrificial protection are different mechanisms.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Acids, salts and chemical analysis

sections.heading: Neutralisation is a reaction of ions
sections.body: Acids produce H⁺ in aqueous solution and alkalis produce OH⁻. Neutralisation forms water from these ions. Acid + metal forms a salt and hydrogen; acid + carbonate forms a salt, water and carbon dioxide. Hydrochloric acid forms chlorides, sulfuric acid sulfates and nitric acid nitrates. Strong versus weak describes ionisation, whereas concentrated versus dilute describes amount per volume.

sections.heading: Choose the correct salt-preparation route
sections.body: For a soluble salt from an insoluble base, add excess base to warm acid, filter off unreacted solid and crystallise the filtrate. For an acid and soluble alkali, a titration identifies the reacting volumes without leaving excess reagent. An insoluble salt can be made by precipitation from two suitable soluble solutions, followed by filtration, washing and drying.

sections.heading: Observations identify substances
sections.body: Flame tests give characteristic colours for selected metal ions. Sodium hydroxide can form characteristic hydroxide precipitates with metal ions. Acidified silver nitrate tests for halides; acidified barium solution tests for sulfates. Carbonates release carbon dioxide with acid. Ammonium ions release ammonia when warmed with alkali; ammonia turns damp red litmus blue. State the reagent, conditions and actual observation.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A titration measures the volume needed for reactants to reach the required stoichiometric relation. Rinse a burette with the solution it will contain, record readings consistently, and add dropwise near the endpoint while mixing. Repeat to obtain concordant titres rather than averaging a rough result indiscriminately. For a pure salt from an acid and alkali, the measured quantities can be reacted again without indicator. Analytical observations should distinguish precipitate colour from gas evolution. Acidification in some ion tests removes interfering ions; the choice of acid must not introduce the ion being tested.

sections.heading: Do not confuse strong with concentrated
sections.body:
A strong acid ionises almost completely in water in the school model. A weak acid ionises only partly. Concentration tells you how much acid is present per unit volume.

So a dilute strong acid and a concentrated weak acid are both possible. Strength and concentration are different properties. When comparing pH or reaction rate, check both the acid identity and concentration rather than assuming the word “weak” means there is only a small amount of acid.

sections.heading: Explain each stage of an insoluble-base salt method
sections.body:
To make a soluble salt from an acid and a suitable insoluble base, add enough base to use up the acid. Excess solid is evidence that no more is reacting under the conditions.

Filter away the extra solid. The salt remains dissolved in the filtrate, which can be concentrated and crystallised by the approved method. Filtering does not collect the dissolved salt at that stage. This method is unsuitable for every reactant: a soluble alkali cannot be removed simply by filtering.

topics.tip: Do not heat a crystallising solution to complete dryness if the aim is well-formed crystals.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Titration calculations and soluble salts

sections.heading: Use the reacting ratio
sections.body: A titration combines measured volumes with a balanced chemical equation. Convert volumes to dm³ when using mol dm⁻³. Calculate the moles in the known solution, use the equation’s coefficient ratio, then find the concentration of the unknown. An acid-base reaction is not always a 1:1 mole relationship; sulfuric acid reacting fully with sodium hydroxide is a useful counterexample.

sections.heading: Make the measured volume reliable
sections.body: An initial rough titration locates the approximate endpoint. Later trials approach it carefully with mixing and dropwise addition near the change. Use suitable concordant titres according to the question or laboratory guidance. Read the burette consistently and calculate delivered volume from the difference between readings. Rinse apparatus appropriately so unwanted water or residues do not alter the effective concentrations.

sections.heading: Prepare a salt without indicator contamination
sections.body: When both acid and base are soluble, adding an excess leaves contamination that cannot simply be filtered away. A titration establishes the required amounts. A preparation can then use measured quantities without indicator before concentration and crystallisation. The actual method and indicator depend on the chemicals and school instructions. In evaluation, identify a specific source of error and explain the direction of its effect where possible.

sections.heading: Use the mean titre that matches the method
sections.body:
The titre is the burette volume delivered: final reading minus initial reading. Record the readings with suitable precision and repeat to obtain consistent results. A rough trial helps locate the endpoint but is not usually included in the final mean.

Use the concordant results specified by the method or question. Averaging every value, including an obvious poor trial, can make the answer worse. A burette reading is not automatically the volume of solution originally placed in the flask.

sections.heading: Include the acid–alkali mole ratio
sections.body:
For H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O, one mole of acid reacts with two moles of sodium hydroxide. If the alkali amount is 0.0040 mol, the acid amount is 0.0020 mol.

Only then divide by the acid volume in dm³ to find its concentration. Equal measured volumes do not imply equal concentrations or equal moles. The balanced coefficients decide the chemical ratio.

sections.heading: Test a clear hypothesis
sections.body: Analytical tests identify evidence for particular ions under stated conditions. Flame tests can identify selected metal ions, such as sodium’s yellow or copper’s characteristic blue-green flame. Avoid transferring contamination between samples. Sodium hydroxide can form coloured metal hydroxide precipitates, while some white precipitates dissolve in excess reagent. State the observation before inferring the ion.

sections.heading: Use suitable reagents for negative ions
sections.body: A halide test commonly uses nitric acid followed by silver nitrate: chloride gives a white precipitate, bromide cream and iodide yellow. A sulfate test uses an appropriate acidified barium reagent to form white barium sulfate. Carbonates release carbon dioxide with a suitable acid; identify that gas using limewater. The exact acid matters because it must not introduce the ion being tested or create a misleading precipitate.

sections.heading: A test result has conditions and limits
sections.body: The presence of one ion may interfere with a test for another, so sequence and acidification are part of the method. A negative result could reflect low concentration or an unsuitable procedure as well as genuine absence. Use the specification’s required ions and the method supplied in an exam. Handle reagents under school supervision; these notes explain observations rather than authorise unsupervised chemical testing.

sections.heading: Keep common hydroxide precipitates separate
sections.body:
In the relevant sodium-hydroxide tests, copper(II) ions form a blue precipitate, iron(II) a green precipitate and iron(III) a brown precipitate. Aluminium ions form a white precipitate that dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide under the standard test conditions.

Describe a precipitate as a solid forming from solution, not simply “the liquid changes colour”. Distinguish the colour before adding reagent from the colour of the new solid. Use the particular test scheme required by the course.

sections.heading: Use a flame test for suitable metal ions
sections.body:
In the usual school flame tests, sodium gives yellow, potassium lilac, lithium red, calcium orange-red and copper blue-green. Contamination can hide a result, especially the strong sodium colour.

Follow the teacher’s cleaning and handling method and compare with suitable references. A flame colour is an observation supporting an identification; a mixture can be harder to interpret than a pure sample. Do not confuse a flame test with a precipitate test just because both involve colours.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Halogens, displacement reactions and redox evidence

sections.heading: Explain the reactivity trend
sections.body:
Halogens form negative ions by gaining an electron. Down Group 7, atoms are larger and inner electrons provide more shielding.

The incoming electron is attracted less strongly, so reactivity decreases in the usual comparison. Distinguish a halogen molecule such as Cl₂ from its halide ion, Cl⁻.

sections.heading: Predict whether displacement happens
sections.body:
Chlorine is more reactive than bromine, so it can form bromine from bromide ions. Bromine does not normally displace chlorine from chloride.

Check the reactivity order before writing products. If no displacement is predicted, do not invent an equation just because the reactants have similar names.

sections.heading: Identify electron loss and gain
sections.body:
In Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂, bromide loses electrons and is oxidised. Chlorine gains electrons and is reduced.

Sodium or potassium ions can be spectators and are left out of the ionic equation. The oxidising agent is the species accepting electrons.

sections.heading: Describe the observation before the conclusion
sections.body:
A colour change can support the formation of a halogen. Its appearance depends on the starting sample, concentration and solvent.

Compare the samples under the specified conditions. Do not identify gases by smelling them. One reaction establishes a comparison between two halogens, not a complete reactivity table by itself.

sections.heading: Check that electrons cancel between the two half-equations
sections.body:
For chlorine reacting with bromide, write Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻ and 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻. Add them and cancel the two electrons appearing on both sides.

The remaining equation is Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂. There are two chlorine atoms and two bromine atoms on each side, and total charge is −2 on each side. These checks help distinguish a valid ionic equation from one with missing coefficients.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Energy changes and reaction rates

sections.heading: Follow the energy balance
sections.body: Exothermic reactions transfer energy to the surroundings; endothermic reactions absorb it. Bond breaking requires energy and bond formation releases energy. Estimate enthalpy change as total energy needed to break reactant bonds minus energy released forming product bonds. A catalyst changes activation energy but does not change the energy difference between reactants and products.

sections.heading: Use collision theory to explain a change in rate
sections.body: Reacting particles must collide with sufficient energy and suitable orientation. Higher concentration or gas pressure increases collision frequency. Higher temperature increases particle speed and the fraction of collisions exceeding activation energy. Greater exposed surface area makes more particles available. A catalyst offers an alternative pathway with lower activation energy and is regenerated overall.

sections.heading: Make a fair rate measurement
sections.body: Measure gas volume, mass loss or another appropriate change over time. Control other conditions and repeat trials. The slope of a quantity-time curve gives rate; a tangent gives instantaneous rate. A curve flattening means the measurable change has stopped, not that particles have stopped moving. Distinguish faster completion from a greater final quantity, which depends on reacting amounts.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: In simple calorimetry, q = mcΔT estimates energy transferred to the measured liquid. To calculate a molar energy change, divide by the moles corresponding to the stated reaction basis and assign the sign from the system’s energy transfer. Heat loss to surroundings and heating the apparatus commonly reduce the measured liquid temperature change, affecting the result. A rate experiment may instead measure time for a fixed visible change; 1/time is then a comparative rate measure under the stated conditions, rather than a universal rate with units of amount per second.

sections.heading: Use bond energies in the correct direction
sections.body:
Breaking bonds needs energy. Forming bonds releases energy. An exothermic reaction releases more energy while forming new bonds than it takes in while breaking old ones.

The estimated energy change is energy needed to break bonds minus energy released when bonds form. A negative result is exothermic. Do not say energy is released by breaking a fuel’s bonds alone: both sides of the bond-energy balance must be considered.

sections.heading: Explain why temperature affects rate
sections.body:
At a higher temperature, particles have more kinetic energy. They collide more frequently, and a larger fraction of collisions have at least the activation energy. More collisions therefore lead to reaction each second.

A catalyst provides a pathway with lower activation energy. It does not supply energy to every particle or change the reaction’s overall energy change. A concentration increase mainly changes how frequently particles meet; it is not the same explanation as a temperature increase.

topics.tip: A higher temperature is not explained only by more collisions; mention the larger fraction with enough energy.
topics.formula: ΔH ≈ energy to break bonds − energy released making bonds
