topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Reversible reactions and equilibrium

sections.heading: An equilibrium is still active
sections.body: A reversible reaction can proceed in both directions. In a closed system, a dynamic equilibrium is reached when forward and reverse reaction rates become equal. Reactant and product concentrations remain constant, but are not necessarily equal. Material must not continuously escape if the equilibrium model is to remain appropriate.

sections.heading: A changed condition favours a response
sections.body: Increasing a reactant concentration tends to favour the direction consuming it. Increasing pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules, where the gaseous mole totals differ. Raising temperature favours the endothermic direction. Use the balanced equation and the thermal direction together; a memorised slogan without the relevant details is incomplete.

sections.heading: Industry balances several objectives
sections.body: Conditions that maximise equilibrium yield may produce an impractically slow rate. Industrial choices also consider energy, equipment, separation and recycling. A catalyst speeds both forward and reverse processes and allows equilibrium to be reached sooner, but does not alter equilibrium composition at the same temperature. When evaluating operating conditions, separate yield effects from rate effects.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A change in pressure only shifts a gaseous equilibrium through this argument when the balanced sides have different gas-mole totals. Compressing an equilibrium with equal gaseous mole totals does not favour one direction by that rule. Temperature must be related to the exothermic or endothermic direction; treating temperature as just another concentration can produce a wrong conclusion. The concentration-time graph after a disturbance should settle to new constant values once equal forward and reverse rates are re-established. Those final values need not match each other or the original values.

sections.heading: Distinguish a reversible change from a finished reaction
sections.body:
In a one-way model, a reaction can stop because a reactant has been used up. At dynamic equilibrium, the forward and reverse reactions are still happening. The amounts present stay constant because the two rates match.

Imagine equal numbers of people entering and leaving a room each minute. The number inside can stay the same even though people keep moving. The analogy explains equal rates, but it does not mean the numbers on the two sides must be equal.

sections.heading: Keep rate changes separate from equilibrium yield
sections.body:
A catalyst lets a suitable reversible reaction reach equilibrium faster. At the same temperature, it speeds both directions and does not move the equilibrium position.

Changing temperature can do two jobs at once: it changes reaction speeds and changes the equilibrium mixture. For an exothermic forward reaction, cooling can increase product yield but slow production. This is why an industrial choice must consider both how much product is possible and how quickly it is made.

topics.tip: A catalyst changes how quickly equilibrium is reached, not the equilibrium yield.

worked.question: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), explain the effect of higher pressure on equilibrium ammonia yield.
steps: There are four gaseous moles on the reactant side and two on the product side.
Higher pressure favours the side with fewer gaseous molecules.
The equilibrium shifts towards ammonia, increasing its equilibrium yield.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Calorimetry and uncertainty in energy measurements

sections.heading: Define the system and the measured change
sections.body: A simple reaction calorimeter commonly measures the temperature change of a solution. Approximate heat transferred using q = mcΔT, stating assumptions about density, heat capacity and heat losses. The solution gaining heat corresponds to the reaction transferring energy out. A positive solution temperature rise therefore does not mean the reaction’s enthalpy change is positive.

sections.heading: Scale to a stated amount of reaction
sections.body: Use moles of the appropriate limiting reactant and the equation’s reaction basis when calculating a molar energy change. Convert joules to kilojoules consistently. An approximate water heat capacity must not be mixed with an incompatible mass unit. For combustion, heat absorbed by water is only a portion of the fuel’s total transferred energy in a simple open experiment.

sections.heading: Explain realistic limitations
sections.body: Heat escaping to the surroundings, energy absorbed by the container, incomplete combustion and evaporation can each influence the result. Name the mechanism and explain its likely effect rather than saying human error. Insulation and a lid can reduce some losses but introduce their own practical considerations. Repeat measurements estimate consistency; they do not automatically correct a systematic error present in every trial.

sections.heading: Choose the mass that matches the calculation
sections.body:
In q = mcΔT for a solution, m is the mass of the solution being warmed or cooled. It is not automatically the mass of the solid reactant added. A question may allow you to use a density close to 1 g/cm³ to estimate solution mass from volume.

Use the stated heat capacity and consistent units. ΔT is final temperature minus initial temperature, not the final temperature alone. The unit J/(g °C) goes with mass in grams.

sections.heading: Explain the direction of a heat-loss error
sections.body:
For an exothermic reaction in an uninsulated container, some released energy warms the surroundings instead of the measured solution. The observed temperature rise is then smaller than it would be in the ideal calculation.

The calculated energy released has a smaller magnitude. If expressed as a negative reaction enthalpy, it is usually less negative. State the direction of the effect rather than writing only “heat loss causes error”. A lid and insulation reduce some losses but do not make every assumption exact.

a consistent bias arising from the measurement method or apparatus
agreement among measurements made under comparable conditions

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Designing rate experiments and reading curves

sections.heading: Choose a measurable change
sections.body: A reaction rate can be investigated by gas volume, loss of mass or time to a specified visual change. Each method measures a particular consequence of reaction and has different limitations. A gas syringe can measure accumulated gas, but leaks and delayed connection reduce the measured amount. A balance measures mass lost when gas escapes, so its interpretation depends on which species leave and whether evaporation also occurs.

sections.heading: Control the comparison
sections.body: For a concentration investigation, keep relevant quantities such as reactant form, temperature and total liquid volume appropriately controlled. For surface area, use the same reactant mass while changing particle size. Record sufficient points to show the early steep region and later plateau. Compare initial gradients to investigate rate, while final gas volumes reflect reacting amounts and limiting reagents rather than rate alone.

sections.heading: Use gradients with units
sections.body: Mean rate is change in measured quantity divided by time interval. Instantaneous rate uses a tangent to a curve at the stated time. Draw a sufficiently large gradient triangle and read both axes carefully. For time-to-endpoint methods, reciprocal time can compare runs with the same endpoint. A catalyst can make completion earlier without changing the theoretical final product amount from fixed starting quantities.

sections.heading: Read a slope as rate, not total product
sections.body:
On a gas-volume–time graph, a steeper slope means faster gas production. A flat section means the measured volume is no longer increasing. The final height shows total gas collected, not the speed at the start.

Two reactions can finish at the same height but reach it at different times. They may produce the same total amount at different rates. To compare initial rates, use the early gradient or a tangent at the start as required.

sections.heading: Choose measurements that fit the reaction
sections.body:
A gas-producing reaction can be followed using collected gas volume or, in a suitable setup, loss of mass as gas leaves. Both methods need the same timing convention and suitable repeated measurements.

If you compare particle sizes, keep the reactant mass and other conditions the same. Smaller pieces provide a larger exposed surface area without changing the starting amount. Leaks, delayed timing and gas that dissolves in the liquid affect what the equipment records.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Dynamic equilibrium and balancing yield against rate

sections.heading: Explain why the system must be closed
sections.body:
If a reactant or product can escape, the mixture may not reach or keep the stated equilibrium. In a closed system, both reaction directions can continue.

Equal rates do not mean equal amounts of reactants and products. They mean neither side changes in amount overall at that point.

sections.heading: Predict concentration and pressure effects
sections.body:
Adding a reactant can favour its use and increase product formation. For gases, increasing pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules in the balanced equation.

Count gaseous coefficients. If both sides have the same number of gas molecules, this simple pressure rule favours neither side.

sections.heading: Use temperature and catalyst rules separately
sections.body:
Increasing temperature favours the endothermic direction. Decreasing it favours the exothermic direction. Identify which direction is which before deciding the change in yield.

A catalyst speeds both directions and reaches equilibrium sooner. It does not change the equilibrium mixture at the same temperature.

sections.heading: Explain an industrial compromise
sections.body:
Ammonia formation is exothermic and goes from four gas molecules to two in the equation ratio. Higher pressure and lower temperature favour its equilibrium yield.

But low temperature can make production slow, while high pressure costs more. A suitable temperature, pressure and catalyst balance these practical needs.

sections.heading: Distinguish one-pass yield from overall production
sections.body:
Not all nitrogen and hydrogen become ammonia in one pass through the reactor. After ammonia is separated, unreacted gases can be returned for another pass.

Recycling can make overall material use high even when one-pass conversion is limited. It does not mean the catalyst has changed the equilibrium yield. Separate three ideas: how fast the reaction runs, the mixture at equilibrium under the chosen conditions, and how the whole process recovers product and reuses reactants.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Crude oil, alkanes and alkenes

sections.heading: Separate a mixture before using it
sections.body: Crude oil is a mixture, mainly of hydrocarbons. Fractional distillation separates fractions by different boiling ranges. Smaller molecules generally have lower boiling points and greater volatility; longer chains are generally more viscous. Fractions are mixtures with similar properties rather than single pure compounds. Complete combustion needs sufficient oxygen; incomplete combustion can create carbon monoxide and soot.

sections.heading: Homologous series organise chemical behaviour
sections.body: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons with only carbon-carbon single bonds; open-chain alkanes have general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. Alkenes have a carbon-carbon double bond and, for one double bond in an open chain, formula CₙH₂ₙ. Alkenes undergo addition reactions. Bromine water is decolourised by a suitable unsaturated compound, providing a test for the double bond in this context.

sections.heading: Cracking changes the product balance
sections.body: Cracking breaks larger hydrocarbons into smaller molecules, often including an alkane and an alkene, using heat and an appropriate catalyst or other specified conditions. It supplies useful fuels and chemical feedstocks. Balance atoms in any proposed equation. Structural formulae show bonding and can distinguish structural isomers, which share a molecular formula but have different connectivity.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A homologous series shares a functional pattern and general formula while successive members differ by a CH₂ unit. Chain length changes physical properties gradually, while the functional group strongly influences reaction type. Alkanes can react with halogens by substitution under suitable light conditions; alkenes undergo addition at a carbon-carbon double bond. A displayed or structural formula must show a chemically valid bonding arrangement, with carbon making four bonds in the usual neutral structures. Two compounds with the same molecular formula can have different connectivity and therefore be structural isomers.

sections.heading: Explain fractional distillation without breaking molecules
sections.body:
A fraction is a mixture of molecules with a similar boiling range. Shorter hydrocarbon molecules generally boil at lower temperatures than longer ones, so they condense in cooler parts of a fractionating system.

Fractional distillation separates molecules that are already present. It does not turn long chains into short chains. Cracking is the chemical process that breaks some larger molecules into smaller ones, often making alkenes as well as alkanes.

sections.heading: Check a cracking equation using atom counts
sections.body:
One possible balanced cracking equation is C₁₀H₂₂ → C₈H₁₈ + C₂H₄. Both sides contain ten carbon atoms and twenty-two hydrogen atoms. The products include an alkane and an alkene.

An alkene has a carbon–carbon double bond and can take part in addition reactions. In the standard bromine-water test, an alkene removes the orange colour under the test conditions. An alkane does not give the same rapid result under those conditions. State the observation as well as the conclusion.

topics.tip: A cracking equation must balance both carbon and hydrogen atoms.

worked.question: Complete the cracking equation C₁₀H₂₂ → C₈H₁₈ + ___.
steps: Subtract eight carbon atoms from ten, leaving two.
Subtract eighteen hydrogen atoms from twenty-two, leaving four.
The second product is C₂H₄, ethene.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Alcohols, acids, esters and polymers

sections.heading: Functional groups change behaviour
sections.body: Alcohols contain the −OH functional group; carboxylic acids contain −COOH. Ethanol can be made by fermentation of sugars using yeast under suitable anaerobic conditions, or by adding steam to ethene using an appropriate catalyst and industrial conditions. Oxidising ethanol can form ethanoic acid. Describing an alcohol as simply a hydrocarbon is incorrect because it also contains oxygen.

sections.heading: Esterification links an acid to an alcohol
sections.body: An alcohol and a carboxylic acid can react to form an ester and water, usually with acid catalysis and warming. Ester names combine the alcohol-derived alkyl group with the acid-derived carboxylate group. Many esters have useful aromas or solvent properties. Conditions, separation and equilibrium affect practical yield; the reaction equation alone does not describe a complete manufacturing process.

sections.heading: Small molecules become macromolecules
sections.body: Addition polymerisation joins alkene monomers by opening their carbon-carbon double bonds. The repeating unit must preserve every atom of the monomer, with continuation bonds through brackets. Condensation polymerisation links monomers with suitable functional groups and eliminates a small molecule. Disposal choices include reuse, recycling and energy recovery, each with limitations including sorting, contamination, emissions and persistence.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: To draw an addition-polymer repeat unit, retain the monomer’s side groups, change the double bond to a single bond and show continuation bonds through both sides of the brackets. A condensation polymer has linking groups related to its monomers’ functional groups and forms a small molecule in the linking reaction. A polymer can be chemically resistant yet difficult to recycle because of mixed grades, additives or contamination. In ethanol production, compare fermentation and hydration using feedstock, purity, conditions, rate and separation rather than assuming one method is best under every industrial constraint.

sections.heading: Follow ethanol to ethanoic acid
sections.body:
Ethanol contains an alcohol group and can be oxidised to ethanoic acid under suitable conditions. Ethanoic acid contains the carboxylic-acid group. The substance has changed chemically, not just lost water.

Complete combustion is a different oxidation process: with enough oxygen, ethanol forms carbon dioxide and water. When a question says “oxidation”, use the stated conditions and purpose to decide which change is meant rather than giving one product for every situation.

sections.heading: Build an ester name from two reactants
sections.body:
An ester can form from an alcohol and a carboxylic acid, with water also produced in the simple school reaction. Ethanol and ethanoic acid form ethyl ethanoate.

The first part of the ester name comes from the alcohol; the second comes from the acid. Identify the –COO– linkage in the structure. The name alone is not enough when you are asked to draw the product: check which carbon group is attached on each side of the linkage.

topics.tip: In addition polymerisation the monomer’s atoms remain in the polymer repeat unit.

steps: The double bond opens to form single-bond connections.
Many ethene molecules link into a long chain.
The repeating unit is −CH₂−CH₂− and no small molecule is eliminated.

sections.heading: A formula must show the intended connectivity
sections.body: A molecular formula gives atom counts but not a unique arrangement. Structural and displayed formulae communicate how atoms connect. Check carbon’s usual valency of four, oxygen’s of two and hydrogen’s of one in the neutral compounds studied. A branch can change the name and physical behaviour without changing the molecular formula. Different drawings can also represent the same connectivity after rotation, so compare bonds rather than the page orientation.

sections.heading: Use the functional group in the name
sections.body: An alcohol and a carboxylic acid can form an ester and water under suitable catalysed conditions. The alcohol gives the ester’s alkyl part; the acid gives its carboxylate part. Methanol and ethanoic acid therefore produce methyl ethanoate. The functional group determines much of the chemistry, while carbon-chain length also influences physical properties. The OH within a carboxyl group is not a separate free hydroxide ion.

sections.heading: Link representation to polymerisation
sections.body: In addition polymerisation, open the alkene double bond to show connections to neighbouring repeat units and retain side groups. Include continuation bonds through brackets. In condensation polymerisation, show the relevant linking groups and identify the small molecule eliminated in the stated reaction. A formula exercise assesses atom conservation as well as recognition of a reaction name.

sections.heading: Count carbons before naming the functional group
sections.body:
For a straight-chain alcohol, find the carbon chain and the position of the –OH group where needed. Propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol have the same molecular formula but different connections.

In a carboxylic acid, the carboxyl carbon counts as part of the carbon chain. CH₃COOH has two carbon atoms, so it is ethanoic acid. Leaving out the carbon in –COOH leads to a wrong name and formula.

sections.heading: Distinguish an isomer from a rotated drawing
sections.body:
Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different atom connections. Butane and methylpropane both have C₄H₁₀, but one is straight-chain and the other branched.

Turning a drawing upside down does not create a new isomer if every atom remains connected to the same neighbours. Check carbon valency and count all atoms before accepting a proposed structure. Different molecular formulae cannot represent structural isomers of each other.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Addition and condensation polymers from their structures

sections.heading: Recognise an addition monomer
sections.body:
An alkene’s carbon–carbon double bond can open so monomers link together. In simple addition polymerisation, all monomer atoms remain in the repeat units.

The backbone bonds become single bonds. Keep the original side groups attached to the correct carbon atoms.

sections.heading: Draw a repeat unit correctly
sections.body:
Replace the monomer double bond with a single backbone bond, add continuation bonds and put brackets around the repeat pattern with n outside.

To go backwards, identify the two-carbon pattern and restore its double bond. A repeat unit is part of a chain, not an isolated fully capped molecule.

sections.heading: Explain condensation using functional groups
sections.body:
Suitable monomers have reactive groups at both ends so a chain can keep growing. A diol and a dicarboxylic acid can form ester links.

Water is also produced in the simple polyester model. Unlike addition polymerisation, not every atom of the reactants stays in the main polymer product.

sections.heading: Link structure to use and disposal
sections.body:
Polymer properties depend on chain arrangement, side groups and links between chains. Different polymers therefore behave differently when heated, bent or stretched.

Reuse, recycling and disposal depend on the material and available facilities. Calling something recyclable does not prove a suitable local process exists.

sections.heading: Count atoms when converting a monomer to a repeat unit
sections.body:
For propene, CH₂=CHCH₃, the two carbons of the double bond become the backbone. The CH₃ group stays as a side group, giving –CH₂–CH(CH₃)–.

The repeat pattern still has three carbons and six hydrogens, matching the monomer. A drawing that loses the CH₃ group cannot be correct. Atom counting is especially helpful when two structures look similar or when a question asks you to recover a monomer from a polymer chain.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Motion graphs and acceleration

sections.heading: Describe change with quantities and directions
sections.body: Distance measures total path length, while displacement is change in position with direction. Speed is distance divided by time; velocity includes direction. Average speed uses total distance divided by total time. Acceleration is change in velocity per unit time and can describe a change of direction even if speed is constant.

sections.heading: Gradients and areas have physical meanings
sections.body: The gradient of a displacement-time graph is velocity. On a velocity-time graph, gradient is acceleration and signed area is displacement. A flat velocity-time section represents constant velocity, whereas a flat displacement-time section represents rest. Use a tangent to estimate a gradient at a particular instant on a curve, showing the triangle used.

sections.heading: Uniform acceleration is a restricted model
sections.body: For constant acceleration, v = u + at and v² = u² + 2as. Choose the equation that contains your known quantities and the desired unknown. State a positive direction before substituting signed values. Convert km/h to m/s by dividing by 3.6. Stopping distance combines thinking and braking distances; fatigue, speed and road conditions affect different stages.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A curved displacement-time graph has a changing gradient and therefore changing velocity. A straight sloping velocity-time segment represents uniform acceleration, even if the velocity itself is negative. For a journey with several stages, add the distances and times before calculating average speed. In experimental motion work, light gates or video measurements reduce some timing limitations, but the physical quantity still depends on gate spacing, flag length or scale calibration. State the model assumptions when applying constant-acceleration equations, because a single average acceleration does not prove the acceleration was uniform throughout.

sections.heading: Distinguish distance, displacement, speed and velocity
sections.body:
Distance is the total path travelled. Displacement is the change from starting position to finishing position, including direction. A runner completing a 400 m lap travels 400 m but has zero displacement.

Speed uses distance divided by time. Velocity uses displacement and includes direction. An object can have a constant speed while its velocity changes if it turns. A negative velocity means movement opposite to your chosen positive direction; it does not mean a negative amount of travel.

sections.heading: Read a velocity graph in two ways
sections.body:
On a velocity–time graph, gradient gives acceleration. A rise from 2 m/s to 10 m/s in 4 s gives (10 − 2)/4 = 2 m/s². The area between the graph and time axis gives displacement.

A section below the axis contributes negative displacement. To find total distance, add the magnitudes of the areas instead of allowing them to cancel. A distance–time graph is different: its gradient gives speed, and its area does not give distance.

topics.tip: A descending velocity-time line can indicate slowing down or speeding up in the negative direction; examine the sign.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Forces, moments, momentum and springs

sections.heading: Resultant force changes motion
sections.body: Force is a vector. A zero resultant force means zero acceleration, not necessarily zero velocity. For a constant mass, F = ma. Weight is the gravitational force mg, whereas mass measures the amount of matter and resistance to acceleration. Free-body diagrams show forces on one object; action-reaction pairs act on different objects.

sections.heading: Turning and balancing
sections.body: A moment is force multiplied by perpendicular distance to the pivot. For rotational equilibrium, clockwise and anticlockwise moments balance. A body’s centre of gravity is where its weight can be treated as acting. Stability depends on the centre of gravity and the support base. A spring follows F = kx only within its linear range; extension is the increase from original length.

sections.heading: Momentum accounts for interactions
sections.body: Momentum is mass × velocity. In an isolated interaction, total momentum is conserved. A resultant force equals rate of change of momentum; increasing collision time can reduce mean force for the same momentum change. During terminal fall, resistive force grows until it balances weight and acceleration becomes zero. Energy transfers may still continue while terminal speed is maintained.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: For an object in equilibrium, both the resultant force and resultant moment must be zero. Balancing moments about a convenient pivot removes the moment of any force acting through that pivot, but the force still matters in the overall force balance. A spring constant is the gradient of a force-extension graph in the linear range. The area under that graph is elastic energy transferred; for a linear spring this is ½Fx = ½kx². In a collision, use one positive direction consistently before applying conservation of momentum.

sections.heading: Find the resultant before using F = ma
sections.body:
Forces in opposite directions must be combined with signs. If a 5 kg trolley has 18 N forwards and 8 N backwards, its resultant is 10 N forwards. Acceleration is then 10/5 = 2 m/s² forwards.

Balanced forces give zero acceleration, not necessarily zero velocity. A moving object can continue at constant velocity with zero resultant force. Newton’s third-law partner forces act on different objects, so they are not simply cancelled on one object’s force diagram.

sections.heading: Separate extension from total spring length
sections.body:
Extension is stretched length minus original length. A spring growing from 12 cm to 17 cm has extended by 5 cm, or 0.050 m. In the proportional range, F = kx uses that extension.

If k = 80 N/m, the force is 4 N. Elastic energy stored is ½kx², giving 0.10 J here. Beyond the limit of proportionality, the straight-line force–extension rule no longer describes the spring. Unloading behaviour determines whether it has returned to its original shape.

topics.tip: Use a signed velocity change when an object reverses direction.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Measuring motion and evaluating timing

sections.heading: Define the measured interval
sections.body: Average speed uses distance travelled during a measured interval. In a light-gate experiment, a known interrupting flag length and blockage time can estimate the object’s speed at the gate. Between two gates, use their separation and the travel time for average speed over that region. These are different intervals and must not be confused. A video method needs a distance scale and known frame interval.

sections.heading: Calculate and compare acceleration
sections.body: Estimate acceleration from a change in measured velocity divided by elapsed time. For motion on a slope, identify forces and the intended control variables. A constant average acceleration over one interval does not prove the acceleration is unchanged at every instant. Repeated trials can reveal variability, while calibration of length and timing affects systematic accuracy.

sections.heading: Judge improvements specifically
sections.body: Reducing human reaction-time effects can be useful for short intervals, but an automatic instrument still needs correct setup. An incorrectly measured flag length biases every speed calculated from it. Increasing travel distance can make manual timing relatively less sensitive to a fixed timing uncertainty, provided the motion remains appropriate for the model. Record units and keep enough significant figures during intermediate calculations.

sections.heading: Use a light gate for a short time interval
sections.body:
If a card of known length passes through a light gate, speed near the gate can be estimated as card length divided by interruption time. This measures a short section of motion rather than the whole journey.

Two separated gates can provide speeds at two positions. To calculate acceleration, use the change in velocity divided by the time between those measurements. Keep the direction the same in the comparison and use a method that measures the relevant interval.

sections.heading: Explain how repeats help and what they cannot fix
sections.body:
Repeated timings reveal spread and allow a mean to reduce the effect of random variation. They do not automatically remove a systematic error, such as a consistently wrong distance or a timer starting late by the same amount.

Human reaction time is especially important for short intervals. A longer measured journey can reduce its percentage effect, provided the speed being measured is still the intended one. State a particular improvement and the error it reduces, rather than writing only “repeat for accuracy”.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Momentum, collisions and safety through stopping time

sections.heading: Include the direction of motion
sections.body:
Momentum p = mv. Choose a positive direction and keep the signs of velocities. An object moving the other way has negative momentum in that convention.

Add signed momenta for the whole system. Adding every speed as a positive number can give the wrong collision result.

sections.heading: State when total momentum is conserved
sections.body:
Total momentum stays the same when the resultant external force is zero or negligible during the interaction. Forces between two carts are internal to the two-cart system.

If the carts stick together, use their combined mass and one final velocity. Each cart’s own momentum can change.

sections.heading: Use stopping time to explain a safety feature
sections.body:
Average resultant force = change in momentum divided by time. For the same person and initial speed, coming to rest gives the same momentum change.

An airbag or suitable crumple zone increases stopping time. That reduces the average force; it does not erase the initial momentum.

sections.heading: Check energy separately
sections.body:
Momentum conservation does not guarantee that kinetic energy stays the same. A collision can transfer energy into deformation, heating and sound.

A negative final velocity simply means motion opposite to the chosen positive direction. Check total momentum before and after, and interpret the sign in words.

sections.heading: Understand why bouncing changes momentum more than stopping
sections.body:
A 0.20 kg ball travelling at +5 m/s has momentum +1.0 kg m/s. If it stops, the change is −1.0 kg m/s. If it rebounds at −5 m/s, its final momentum is −1.0 kg m/s and the change is −2.0 kg m/s.

The rebound reverses direction, so the velocity change is 10 m/s in magnitude, not zero. Write final minus initial with signs before calculating a force from the change.

a system with no resultant external force for the conservation argument

v = 2 m/s in the original moving cart’s direction.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Moments, centre of gravity and stable equilibrium

sections.heading: Use perpendicular distance
sections.body:
Moment = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot to the force’s line of action. A force acting through the pivot has zero moment.

The handle length is not always the correct distance. Draw the line of action and its perpendicular distance before substituting.

sections.heading: Balance clockwise and anticlockwise effects
sections.body:
For rotational equilibrium, total clockwise moment equals total anticlockwise moment about the same pivot.

An object at rest also needs zero resultant force. Include its weight when relevant. A uniform horizontal beam’s weight acts at its midpoint in the standard model.

sections.heading: Explain toppling from the weight line
sections.body:
The weight acts through the centre of gravity. An object can topple when this line falls outside its supporting base.

A wider base or lower centre of gravity usually allows more tilt before that happens. Greater weight alone does not guarantee stability.

sections.heading: Measure a turning-effect investigation carefully
sections.body:
Use the distance to each force’s line of action, include hanger and beam weights where needed and check for pivot friction.

Repeat suitable arrangements and compare predicted with measured balance. A labelled force diagram is more useful than an unexplained statement that the beam balanced.

sections.heading: Choose a pivot that removes an unknown force
sections.body:
Suppose a beam rests on two supports. Taking moments about one support makes that support’s upward force have zero moment, because its line of action passes through the pivot.

You can then find the other support’s force from the known weights and distances. Finally, use vertical force balance to find the first support’s force. Changing the chosen pivot does not change the physical answer; it changes which terms are easiest to work with.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Charge, current, voltage and circuit rules

sections.heading: Current is moving charge
sections.body: Charge flow is Q = It. Current has the same value through components in series; currents entering a junction sum to those leaving. Potential difference is energy transferred per unit charge, V = E/Q. In parallel branches the potential difference is equal. An ammeter is placed in series and a voltmeter in parallel with the component being measured.

sections.heading: Components respond differently
sections.body: An ohmic resistor has constant resistance at constant temperature. A filament lamp’s resistance increases as its temperature rises. A diode conducts much more readily in one direction. The resistance of a thermistor commonly decreases as temperature rises; an LDR’s resistance decreases as light level rises. Interpret each component using its current-voltage behaviour, not by assuming every graph is a straight line.

sections.heading: Resistance and power in networks
sections.body: For series resistors, add resistances. Parallel paths reduce the total resistance compared with any individual branch. V = IR relates a component’s potential difference, current and resistance. Electrical power is P = VI and, for a resistive component, P = I²R. Energy transferred is E = Pt. Match units: watts and seconds give joules.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: In parallel branches, equal potential difference does not imply equal current unless the branch resistances are equal. For two resistors, the reciprocal relation 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ gives a combined resistance below either individual resistance. In a potential divider, the fraction of supply voltage across a series component depends on its share of the total resistance. Measurements must distinguish a component’s current-voltage behaviour from changes caused by heating. Connect equipment correctly and keep current low enough to avoid unwanted temperature changes when investigating an ohmic resistor.

sections.heading: Connect charge, current and energy
sections.body:
A current of 2 A means 2 coulombs of charge pass a point each second. In 30 s, charge Q = It = 60 C. It does not mean each electron carries two coulombs.

A potential difference of 6 V means 6 joules are transferred per coulomb. If 60 C passes through that component, the energy transfer is 360 J. Charge is not used up in the component; energy is transferred from the electrical supply to other stores.

sections.heading: Explain series and parallel using the junctions
sections.body:
In a series circuit there is one path, so current is the same through each component. The supply potential difference is shared between them.

In parallel, each branch connects across the same two supply points and has the same potential difference. Current splits between branches and recombines; the total entering a junction equals the total leaving it. Adding a parallel branch reduces the total resistance, so a fixed-voltage supply can provide a larger total current.

topics.tip: Current is not used up as it travels around a circuit.
topics.formula: Q = It; V = IR; P = VI; E = Pt

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Mains safety and static electricity

sections.heading: Protect the user when something goes wrong
sections.body: A live conductor is at an alternating potential relative to earth; neutral provides the return path. An earth conductor connects exposed conducting parts to earth so a fault can create a large current and operate protective devices. A fuse melts when excessive current heats it. Double-insulated equipment has appropriate insulating barriers and does not rely on an earth wire for exposed metal protection.

sections.heading: Choose protective ratings sensibly
sections.body: Calculate normal current from P/V before choosing the next suitable fuse rating above it, allowing for the specified equipment characteristics. Overloading sockets can overheat wiring. Electrical energy billing commonly uses kilowatt-hours: multiply power in kilowatts by time in hours. A kilowatt-hour is an energy unit, not power per hour.

sections.heading: Charge transfer creates static effects
sections.body: Rubbing insulating materials can transfer electrons. Losing electrons leaves a positive charge; gaining them leaves a negative charge. Like charges repel and unlike charges attract. A charged object can attract a neutral object by redistributing its charges. Static build-up may cause sparks, so fuel handling and other sensitive processes use earthing and suitable precautions.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: An alternating supply reverses direction repeatedly; a direct supply has a fixed direction. A fuse is chosen to tolerate normal operation while protecting against excessive current in a suitable circuit. The live path must be interrupted by the protective or switching device where specified, because leaving internal parts connected to live can remain dangerous. Static induction redistributes charges within a nearby object without requiring net charge transfer to it. When a conductor is earthed, electrons may flow to or from Earth according to the surrounding charge arrangement.

sections.heading: Give the earth wire and fuse their separate roles
sections.body:
The earth wire connects an exposed conducting case to earth in equipment that requires it. If a live wire contacts the case, a large fault current can flow through a low-resistance path, causing an appropriate fuse to melt or a protective device to disconnect the supply.

The fuse belongs in the live path so disconnection removes that connection. It does not absorb excess current. Double-insulated equipment uses a different protection arrangement and does not rely on an earthed outer metal case.

sections.heading: Explain charging without moving protons
sections.body:
When two suitable materials rub, electrons can transfer from one to the other. The material gaining electrons becomes negatively charged; the one losing them becomes positively charged. Protons remain bound in nuclei in this process.

Like charges repel and unlike charges attract. A charged object can also attract a neutral object by redistributing its charges slightly. A spark occurs when a large enough potential difference causes charge to move through the air. Static effects do not require a continuous battery circuit.

topics.tip: An earth wire is a fault-protection route; it should not normally carry the appliance current.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Investigating current-voltage characteristics

sections.heading: Build the measurement circuit
sections.body: Use an ammeter in series with the component and a voltmeter across it. A suitable variable supply or resistance controls the operating point. Take paired voltage and current readings and record the direction of each quantity consistently. Reverse polarity where the approved circuit and component permit it to investigate the other branch. Protect the component from excessive current and follow the school’s circuit instructions.

sections.heading: Recognise the shapes
sections.body: An ohmic resistor at constant temperature gives a straight current-voltage graph through the origin. A filament lamp’s curve becomes less steep as it heats and resistance increases, when current is plotted vertically against voltage. A diode shows strong directional behaviour, with relatively little current in reverse under the normal intended operating conditions. Axis choice matters when interpreting steepness.

sections.heading: Separate component behaviour from experimental effects
sections.body: Heating is the intended reason for the lamp’s changing resistance, but can be an unwanted confound in a resistor investigation. Allow suitable cooling or limit current where needed. Calculate V/I at a point to obtain that operating resistance; do not automatically call the tangent gradient resistance on every graph. Check instrument ranges, connections and zero readings before attributing an unexpected curve to new physics.

sections.heading: Connect the meters to the quantities measured
sections.body:
Place an ammeter in series with the component so it measures its current. Connect a voltmeter across the component so it measures the potential difference between its ends.

Change the supply or suitable control resistance to obtain a range of readings using the approved circuit. For an ohmic conductor at constant temperature, current is proportional to potential difference. The straight line passes through the origin. A curved graph does not automatically mean the equipment is faulty; the component’s resistance may be changing.

sections.heading: Explain a lamp curve using temperature
sections.body:
As current heats a filament, its resistance increases. On a graph of current against potential difference, the curve becomes less steep as voltage magnitude grows. A larger voltage increase is needed for each further current increase.

A diode behaves differently: it allows substantial current mainly in one direction after a suitable forward voltage is reached. State which quantity is on each axis before describing a gradient. A graph drawn with reversed axes has a different numerical gradient.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Wave behaviour, sound and the electromagnetic spectrum

sections.heading: Track the oscillation and the energy separately
sections.body: Waves transfer energy without net transport of the medium. In transverse waves the oscillation is perpendicular to travel; in longitudinal waves it is parallel. Amplitude measures maximum displacement, wavelength measures repeat distance, frequency counts cycles per second and period is time per cycle. Wave speed = frequency × wavelength.

sections.heading: At boundaries, follow what changes
sections.body: Reflection returns a wave from a boundary; refraction occurs when wave speed changes between media. Frequency remains fixed by the source during refraction, while wavelength changes. Diffraction spreads waves around obstacles or through openings and is greatest when wavelength and opening width are comparable. Sound needs a medium; pitch relates to frequency and loudness to amplitude.

sections.heading: One spectrum, different interactions
sections.body: Electromagnetic waves are transverse and have the same speed in vacuum. Increasing frequency runs from radio through microwaves, infrared, visible, ultraviolet and X-rays to gamma radiation. Use depends on penetration, absorption and energy transfer. Ionising radiation can damage cells; exposure decisions weigh dose, shielding, distance and benefits. Infrared is associated with thermal emission and absorption, not with a special category of heat particles.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: At a boundary, a wave’s frequency remains controlled by its source, so a speed change produces a corresponding wavelength change. Echo measurements use a return journey: divide the product of speed and time by two to find the reflecting distance. Increasing sound amplitude generally increases loudness; increasing frequency raises pitch. Different electromagnetic bands interact differently with matter, which explains uses such as radio communication, thermal imaging and medical imaging. The label ionising concerns sufficient energy to remove bound electrons in relevant interactions, not simply whether a wave travels through a solid.

sections.heading: Distinguish a particle’s vibration from wave travel
sections.body:
In a transverse wave, oscillation is perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer. In a longitudinal wave, oscillation is parallel to it. Sound in air has compressions and rarefactions as particles vibrate back and forth.

Frequency is the number of complete oscillations per second; period is the time for one. They are related by T = 1/f. A 50 Hz vibration has period 0.020 s. Amplitude measures the size of the oscillation, not the spacing between successive wave crests.

sections.heading: Use the electromagnetic spectrum as one family
sections.body:
Radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray and gamma radiation are all electromagnetic waves. In a vacuum they have the same speed. Higher frequency means shorter wavelength because c = fλ.

Their interactions with matter differ, which explains different uses and hazards. Infrared is useful for thermal imaging; X-rays can reveal differences in transmission through body tissues and other materials. Explain a use through the relevant property rather than saying a wave is useful simply because it is powerful.

topics.tip: Frequency does not change just because a wave enters a different medium.
topics.formula: v = fλ; T = 1/f

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Refraction, total internal reflection and lenses

sections.heading: Draw from the normal
sections.body: Angles of incidence and refraction are measured from the normal, not the surface. A ray entering a slower medium generally bends towards the normal; entering a faster medium generally bends away. The refractive index compares speeds and, for air-to-material geometry, relates sin i to sin r. Keep calculator angles in degrees for school ray calculations.

sections.heading: A critical angle sets a boundary
sections.body: Total internal reflection requires travel from a higher-index medium toward a lower-index medium and an incidence angle greater than the critical angle. At the critical angle the refracted ray travels along the boundary. Optical fibres use repeated internal reflection, although real systems also have attenuation and manufacturing constraints. Reflection below the critical angle is not total internal reflection.

sections.heading: Lenses produce images by ray geometry
sections.body: A converging lens brings parallel rays towards a focal point. Draw a ray parallel to the principal axis that passes through the far focus and a ray through the optical centre that continues essentially undeviated in the thin-lens model. Where real rays meet, a real image forms; where their backward extensions meet, the image is virtual. Magnification is image size divided by object size.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A real image can be formed on a screen because light rays actually converge there. A virtual image is located where backward extensions of rays meet, and cannot be projected directly onto a screen in the same way. A converging lens can form either type depending on object position. Ray diagrams must use a clear principal axis and accurately placed focal points. At total internal reflection, the critical-angle condition concerns a higher-index to lower-index boundary; simply making any incidence angle large does not guarantee it.

sections.heading: Measure angles from the normal
sections.body:
The normal is perpendicular to the surface at the point where the ray meets it. In a standard air-to-glass example, light slows and bends towards this normal. Frequency stays the same while wavelength decreases.

For the stated air-to-material model, refractive index n = sin i/sin r. If i = 40° and r = 25°, n is about 1.52. Angles measured from the surface would give the wrong substitution. Draw a new normal at each differently oriented boundary.

sections.heading: Distinguish a real image from a virtual image
sections.body:
A real image forms where light rays actually meet and can be projected onto a screen. A virtual image forms where rays appear to come from when traced backwards; it cannot be caught on a screen at that apparent position.

For a thin converging lens, draw one ray parallel to the axis and then through the far focus, and another through the optical centre. Their meeting point or backward extensions show the image. Label the focal points so the construction has a clear scale.

topics.tip: Total internal reflection cannot occur when the ray first enters a higher-index medium from air.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Ray diagrams, total internal reflection and optical fibres

sections.heading: Draw a normal at each boundary
sections.body:
The normal is perpendicular to the boundary. Light bends when its speed changes and it enters at an angle.

In the usual air-to-glass case it bends towards the normal. Frequency stays the same while wavelength changes. A second boundary needs its own normal.

sections.heading: Check both conditions for total internal reflection
sections.body:
Light must travel from higher towards lower refractive index, and the incidence angle must exceed the critical angle.

At the critical angle, the refracted ray runs along the surface. For a material-to-air boundary, sin c = 1/n in the simplified model. Angle size alone is not enough.

sections.heading: Construct a converging-lens image
sections.body:
Draw a parallel ray that refracts through the far focus, and a ray through the optical centre. Their intersection gives a real image.

For an object inside the focal length, extend the emerging rays backwards. The virtual image is upright and magnified; the light does not actually meet there.

sections.heading: Explain how a fibre guides light
sections.body:
A suitable core–cladding boundary allows repeated total internal reflection for rays meeting the angle condition. A sharp bend can change the angle and let some light escape.

Real fibres also lose energy through other effects. They are useful guides, not perfectly lossless paths for every ray.

sections.heading: Separate refraction from reflection in a single diagram
sections.body:
Below the critical angle at a glass-to-air boundary, some light can reflect while some leaves by refraction. At the critical angle, the refracted ray lies along the surface. Above it, the ideal ray model gives total internal reflection.

Draw the reflected angle equal to the incident angle, both measured from the normal. The refracted angle follows a different rule because the light speed changes across the boundary. Do not force both rays to have the same angle.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Energy transfers, work, power and resources

sections.heading: Energy accounting must balance
sections.body: Energy can be stored kinetically, gravitationally, elastically, thermally, chemically and in other ways. It transfers through mechanical work, electrical work, heating and radiation. The total is conserved, even when useful energy spreads into less useful thermal stores. Work done by a constant force parallel to displacement is W = Fd. Power measures energy transfer per second.

sections.heading: Calculate the change, not an unrelated total
sections.body: Kinetic energy is ½mv² and gravitational potential energy change is mgΔh near Earth’s surface. Efficiency is useful output divided by total input, expressed as a fraction or percentage. A machine can have high power and low efficiency; these quantities answer different questions. Reduce unwanted transfers through insulation, lubrication or appropriate material choices.

sections.heading: Evaluate resources in context
sections.body: Fossil fuels are energy-dense but finite and produce emissions. Nuclear generation has low operational carbon emissions but creates radioactive waste and needs substantial infrastructure. Wind and solar are renewable but variable; hydroelectric and other storage schemes can help balance demand. Compare reliability, output, environmental impacts and cost over the system’s lifetime rather than using renewable as a synonym for impact-free.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: Work requires displacement with a component along the force direction. A force can be present without doing mechanical work on a stationary object through that force’s application point. An energy-flow diagram should account for the entire input and define the useful output for the task. In transmission systems, raising voltage reduces current for a given power, lowering I²R losses; this does not mean voltage itself is energy. For resource comparisons, define the intended demand pattern and compare lifecycle impacts, reliability and storage needs rather than only fuel availability.

sections.heading: Use power to connect energy and time
sections.body:
Power is energy transferred per second. A 500 W heater transfers 500 J each second, so it transfers 60 000 J in two minutes if its power stays constant. Convert minutes to seconds before using E = Pt.

Work done by a constant force along the direction of movement is W = Fd. A 20 N force acting through 3 m transfers 60 J. If the force is not along the movement, do not multiply its full magnitude by the distance without considering direction.

sections.heading: Read an efficiency calculation as a fraction
sections.body:
Efficiency = useful energy output/total energy input, or the equivalent power ratio. If a motor receives 800 J and gives 600 J of useful mechanical output, its efficiency is 0.75 or 75%.

The remaining 200 J has not vanished. It has been transferred in other ways, often warming components and surroundings. What counts as useful depends on the device’s purpose. A transfer useful in a heater may be unwanted in a motor.

topics.tip: Efficiency cannot exceed 100% for the stated energy input-output boundary.
topics.formula: Eₖ = ½mv²; ΔEₚ = mgΔh; P = E/t

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Specific heat capacity, latent heat and insulation evidence

sections.heading: Choose between mcΔT and mL
sections.body:
For a temperature rise without a state change, use E = mcΔT. For a state change at the relevant constant temperature, use E = mL.

A flat section on a heating curve can show melting or boiling while energy is still being transferred. Temperature staying constant does not mean heating has stopped.

sections.heading: Use the correct heater energy
sections.body:
For steady power, electrical input is E = Pt. Use time in seconds when power is in watts.

Some energy warms the container or escapes to the surroundings. The full heater input is not automatically the energy gained only by the sample. State the approximation if you equate them.

sections.heading: Keep the three transfer routes separate
sections.body:
Conduction transfers energy through a material. Convection involves moving fluid. Infrared radiation can transfer energy through a vacuum.

Trapped gas can reduce conduction and convection. A reflective surface can reduce radiation. A vacuum cannot block every possible energy-transfer route.

sections.heading: Make a cooling comparison fair
sections.body:
Use matched water masses, starting temperatures, containers, lids and surroundings. Measure temperature at the same time intervals.

A smaller temperature fall supports lower energy loss under those conditions. Repeats help judge consistency, and evaporation or different surface areas can affect the result.

sections.heading: Explain a heating-curve plateau using particles
sections.body:
During melting, particles gain freedom to move as the solid structure breaks down. Energy changes their arrangement and interactions rather than simply increasing the average kinetic energy in the way it does during a temperature rise.

Once melting is complete, further heating can raise the liquid’s temperature. If a problem begins with cold ice and ends with warmer water, divide it into stages: warming ice, melting ice and warming water. Use the correct relation for each stage, then add the energies.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Density, pressure and thermal changes

sections.heading: Density relates material amount to volume
sections.body: Density is mass divided by volume. Use a balance and appropriate volume measurement: regular dimensions for a block, displacement for a suitable irregular solid. Keep units consistent; 1 g/cm³ equals 1000 kg/m³. Pressure is force per area, so the same force produces greater pressure on a smaller area.

sections.heading: Particles explain liquid and gas pressure
sections.body: Pressure in a liquid increases with depth and density: Δp = ρgΔh. Gas pressure arises from particle collisions with surfaces. At constant temperature for a fixed mass, pressure times volume remains constant in the ideal-gas approximation used here. Kelvin temperature begins at absolute zero; convert Celsius by adding about 273. State which quantities remain fixed in any gas-law problem.

sections.heading: Heating can raise temperature or change state
sections.body: Specific heat capacity relates energy to mass and temperature rise. Specific latent heat relates energy to mass changed between phases without a temperature rise during the idealised phase change. During melting or boiling, supplied energy changes particle arrangement rather than increasing mean kinetic energy. Conduction, convection and radiation are different transfer mechanisms, each favoured by different materials and conditions.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: Pressure in a liquid depends on depth below the surface, liquid density and gravitational field strength, not on the total amount of liquid in a particular vessel. For a gas-law comparison, keep the gas mass fixed and identify whether temperature or volume is constant. Heating a solid or liquid may cause expansion, while a phase change absorbs or releases latent energy without the same temperature response. In a heating experiment, insulation reduces losses, but measurements may also need to account for the container, heater and thermometer response.

sections.heading: Choose the correct area or volume unit
sections.body:
Density = mass/volume. A 300 g block with volume 100 cm³ has density 3 g/cm³. In SI units this is 3000 kg/m³. Both mass and volume units must change consistently.

Pressure = force/area. The same force produces greater pressure on a smaller area. A 100 N force on 0.020 m² produces 5000 Pa. Using an area in cm² while labelling the result pascals would be wrong unless you first convert the area to m².

sections.heading: Explain why liquid pressure increases with depth
sections.body:
A deeper point supports the weight of more liquid above it. For a liquid of roughly constant density, the pressure difference from its surface is Δp = ρgh.

For water with density 1000 kg/m³ at depth 2 m, using g = 10 N/kg gives a pressure increase of 20 000 Pa. Atmospheric pressure must be added if the question asks for absolute pressure. Pressure at a given depth does not depend simply on the container’s overall width.

topics.tip: A temperature change of 20°C is a change of 20 K; an absolute temperature of 20°C is about 293 K.

topics.title: Thermal measurements and gas-law calculations

sections.heading: Choose the correct thermal model
sections.body: A temperature rise uses E = mcΔT. A change of state uses E = mL for the stated latent heat. If both occur, calculate separate stages and add their energy transfers rather than applying one equation to the entire process. Real experiments may also warm the container or lose energy to the surroundings. State assumptions before interpreting a result as a material constant.

sections.heading: Keep gas conditions explicit
sections.body: For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, pV is constant in the simple model. If volume is fixed, pressure is proportional to absolute temperature. Convert Celsius to kelvin when using temperature ratios. A change from 20°C to 40°C is not a doubling of absolute temperature. The measured pressure should be the appropriate absolute pressure when the relationship requires it.

sections.heading: Explain behaviour using particles
sections.body: Compressing a gas at constant temperature increases collision frequency with the container walls, raising pressure. Heating at constant volume increases mean particle kinetic energy and collision effects. A particle explanation should connect motion, collision and force per area rather than say particles become bigger. During a phase change, energy changes separation or arrangement instead of the same increase in mean kinetic energy as a temperature rise.

sections.heading: Convert to kelvin before using temperature ratios
sections.body:
Temperature in kelvin is approximately temperature in °C plus 273. A gas going from 27°C to 127°C goes from 300 K to 400 K, not to more than four times its original absolute temperature.

At constant volume, pressure is proportional to kelvin temperature in the ideal-gas model. The pressure ratio is therefore 400/300 = 4/3. Using 127/27 would greatly overestimate it. State that the gas amount and volume remain fixed.

sections.heading: Explain compression at constant temperature
sections.body:
For a fixed gas amount at constant temperature, pV stays constant. Halving the volume doubles pressure in the model. Particles have the same average kinetic energy because temperature is unchanged, but they hit the walls more often in the smaller space.

Do not explain this isothermal change by saying that particles must move faster. A different process in which temperature also changes needs a different set of conditions. Real measurements should allow temperature to settle before comparing the pressure–volume readings.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Magnetic fields, motors and induction

sections.heading: Fields represent force patterns
sections.body: Magnetic field lines outside a magnet run from north to south. Their direction is the direction a north test pole would move, and closer spacing indicates a stronger field. A current in a wire produces a magnetic field; a coil concentrates it, and a suitable iron core strengthens an electromagnet. Field direction depends on current direction.

sections.heading: A current can produce motion
sections.body: A current-carrying conductor in an external magnetic field can experience a force. The force is greatest when current and field are perpendicular and becomes zero when they are parallel. Fleming’s left-hand rule relates field, conventional current and force. Motors use forces on a coil to create a turning effect, with appropriate switching to maintain rotation.

sections.heading: Changing flux can produce a voltage
sections.body: Moving a magnet relative to a coil or changing the field through it can induce an emf. Faster change, stronger fields and more turns can increase the effect. The induced current opposes the change that produces it. Transformers use changing magnetic flux to transfer energy between coils; their simple operating model requires alternating input. A higher transmission voltage lowers current for the same power and reduces resistive losses.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: Induction depends on changing magnetic flux linkage, not on the simple presence of a magnetic field. Reversing the motion or magnetic orientation reverses the induced voltage direction in the usual arrangement. A motor transfers electrical energy into mechanical work; a generator transfers mechanical work into electrical energy. For an ideal transformer, voltage follows turns ratio and input power equals output power, so increasing voltage decreases current. Real transformers have losses, so an efficiency statement must use the actual input and output powers.

sections.heading: Connect a current with its magnetic field
sections.body:
A current in a straight wire produces a field around the wire. Reversing the current reverses the field direction. A coil combines the effects of many turns, and a suitable iron core can strengthen the field.

A solenoid behaves like a bar magnet with north and south poles. Field lines outside a magnet run from north to south by convention. The field is strongest where lines are closest together; a drawn line is not a physical thread of material.

sections.heading: Separate motor force from induced voltage
sections.body:
A current-carrying wire in a magnetic field can experience a force. This motor effect needs current and a suitably oriented field. Reversing the current or field reverses the force; reversing both keeps the original force direction.

Induction instead produces a voltage through a changing magnetic field linked with a conductor. A generator uses mechanical input to cause that change. A stationary coil and magnet can have a field between them without producing a continuous induced voltage.

topics.tip: A stationary magnet beside a stationary coil does not continuously induce an emf.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Induction, transformers and efficient power transmission

sections.heading: Identify what is changing
sections.body:
Moving a magnet relative to a coil, or changing current in a nearby coil, can induce a voltage. Faster change or more turns can increase it in suitable comparisons.

A steady field alone is not enough for continuous induction. A closed circuit is needed for a continuous induced current, but an open circuit can still have a voltage.

sections.heading: Distinguish a generator from a motor
sections.body:
A generator turns mechanical input into electrical output through induction. A motor uses the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field to produce movement.

In a simple AC generator, rotation makes the induced voltage change direction periodically. Use the energy-transfer direction to identify the device.

sections.heading: Apply the ideal transformer rules
sections.body:
Alternating current in the primary creates a changing field that induces voltage in the secondary. In the ideal model, Vs/Vp = Ns/Np.

More secondary turns gives a step-up transformer. Ideal input and output powers are equal, so increasing voltage reduces current at the same power. Real transformers have losses.

sections.heading: Explain high-voltage transmission
sections.body:
For fixed transmitted power, a higher voltage means a lower current because P = VI. Cable heating loss is I²R, so the lower current reduces it.

Resistance has not disappeared. Step-down transformers are still needed to provide suitable voltages nearer users.

sections.heading: Follow the energy rather than assuming extra voltage creates energy
sections.body:
An ideal transformer taking 100 W cannot give 200 W simply by doubling the voltage. If its output voltage doubles, its output current must halve so that VI remains 100 W.

The transformer changes voltage and current together. In a real device the output power is slightly smaller than the input because some energy warms components. This is why a voltage ratio can be used directly in the ideal model, while a power calculation must state whether losses are ignored.

a device using a changing magnetic field to transfer energy between coils and change alternating voltage
a lossless model with equal input and output powers

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Radioactivity, half-life and nuclear reactions

sections.heading: Unstable nuclei change spontaneously
sections.body: Alpha radiation is a helium nucleus; beta-minus radiation is an electron emitted when a neutron changes to a proton; gamma radiation is electromagnetic radiation from nuclear de-excitation. Their penetration and ionising powers differ. Nuclear equations conserve charge number and nucleon number. Radioactive decay is random for an individual nucleus but predictable statistically for a large population.

sections.heading: Use background-corrected measurements
sections.body: Activity measures decays per second in becquerels. A detector records a count rate that also depends on geometry and efficiency. Subtract background before analysing decay. A half-life is the time for activity, or number of undecayed nuclei, to halve. After n half-lives the remaining fraction is (1/2)ⁿ. A graph may need repeated halving rather than a single chosen interval.

sections.heading: Applications involve a risk-benefit choice
sections.body: Contamination introduces radioactive material into or onto something; irradiation exposes it to radiation without necessarily leaving radioactive material behind. Shielding, distance and short handling times reduce exposure. Fission splits heavy nuclei and can sustain a chain reaction; fusion combines light nuclei and requires extreme conditions. Nuclear energy releases involve a small decrease in total rest mass, not a failure of mass-energy conservation.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: The range of emitted radiation is different from the half-life of its source. Range describes travel through a material, whereas half-life describes the statistical decrease in undecayed nuclei over time. In beta-minus decay, nucleon number remains unchanged while proton number rises by one. In alpha decay, nucleon number falls by four and proton number by two. Gamma emission changes nuclear energy without changing either number. Repeated background-corrected measurements and suitable counting times reduce the relative influence of random fluctuations, but they do not make individual decays predictable.

sections.heading: Track nuclear numbers in decay
sections.body:
Alpha emission removes two protons and two neutrons, so mass number falls by 4 and atomic number by 2. In beta-minus decay, a neutron changes into a proton and a beta particle is emitted; mass number stays the same and atomic number rises by 1.

Gamma emission transfers energy without changing either number. The emitted beta electron is not an ordinary outer-shell electron being shaken loose. Check atomic and mass numbers separately when completing a nuclear equation.

sections.heading: Link penetration to a suitable use
sections.body:
Alpha radiation is strongly ionising but has a short range and low penetration. Beta is more penetrating, and gamma is highly penetrating compared with the other two in the usual school comparison.

The best source for a thickness gauge must partly pass through the material so changes can be detected. A source stopped completely gives little useful transmission information. A very penetrating source may show too little change for a thin sheet. Match the radiation to the task and explain that link.

steps: The initial corrected source count rate is 820 − 20 = 800 counts/min.

Add background again: expected measured rate = 120 counts/min.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Background radiation and decay calculations

sections.heading: A detector does not measure only the source
sections.body: Count rates include background radiation from the surroundings and detector conditions. Measure background for a suitable interval and use a corresponding rate. Subtract it from source-plus-background readings before analysing the source’s change. Keep detector geometry and measurement procedure consistent. Random variation means successive short measurements will not usually match exactly even when source activity is effectively constant.

sections.heading: Apply half-life to the corrected quantity
sections.body: After each half-life, activity or undecayed-nucleus count is halved. Work through repeated halvings or use a power of one half. A measured total count rate eventually approaches background rather than zero. If the question asks for the final detector reading, add background back after calculating the remaining source contribution. A half-life is not the time for every nucleus to decay.

sections.heading: Interpret graphs and uncertainty
sections.body: Read several suitable half-life intervals rather than selecting a single noisy pair where possible. Longer counting intervals collect more events and can reduce relative statistical variation, but the source may itself change appreciably during the interval. Distinguish activity in becquerels from a detector’s counts per second; detection efficiency and geometry mean they are not automatically equal.

sections.heading: Subtract rates, not unmatched counts
sections.body:
If a source gives 420 counts in two minutes and background gives 60 counts in three minutes, their rates are 210 and 20 counts/min respectively. The corrected source rate is 190 counts/min.

Subtracting 60 directly from 420 would compare different time intervals. Take sufficiently long measurements and repeat where suitable because counts fluctuate. The detector’s count rate is evidence about detected events, not necessarily the total activity of the source without accounting for the measurement arrangement.

sections.heading: Apply half-life repeatedly to the remaining amount
sections.body:
After each half-life, half of the remaining undecayed nuclei are left. A corrected count rate of 160 counts/min becomes 80, then 40, then 20 after three half-lives under comparable detection conditions.

If three half-lives take 18 hours, one half-life is 6 hours. The process is not subtraction of a fixed number every hour. Individual decay times are unpredictable, while the overall half-life pattern is useful for large populations of nuclei.
