topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Orbits, stars and the expanding universe

sections.heading: Gravity continually changes orbital direction
sections.body: A planet or satellite in a circular orbit accelerates because its velocity direction changes. Gravity supplies the centripetal resultant force. The period is the time for one orbit; speed in a circular orbit is circumference divided by period. Use consistent radius and time units. Natural and artificial satellites can have different orbital purposes, altitudes and periods.

sections.heading: Stars evolve according to mass
sections.body: A star forms when gravity compresses gas and dust until fusion becomes established. During the main sequence, inward gravity balances outward pressure supported by energy release. Lower-mass and higher-mass stars follow different later stages. A Sun-like star can become a red giant and then leave a white dwarf; much more massive stars can undergo supernovae and leave neutron stars or black holes.

sections.heading: Evidence supports a developing cosmological model
sections.body: Spectral redshift from distant galaxies is interpreted as evidence of recession in the expanding-universe model. More distant galaxies generally show larger recession velocities on large scales. The cosmic microwave background is another major piece of evidence for an early hot dense universe. Models depend on observations and can be refined; expansion does not imply that every gravitationally bound object is itself expanding.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A circular orbit can have constant speed while its velocity changes continuously because direction changes. A star’s luminosity is its total emitted power, whereas apparent brightness also depends on distance. A spectrum contains lines associated with particular atomic transitions; shifting the pattern towards longer wavelengths supports a recession interpretation in the relevant astronomical model. Stellar mass strongly influences the later stages of evolution. A scientific explanation of the universe should connect observations to a model and recognise the distinction between directly measured spectra and quantities inferred using assumptions.

sections.heading: Explain why an orbit still has acceleration
sections.body:
In a circular orbit, speed can stay constant while direction changes. Velocity therefore changes, so there is acceleration towards the centre. Gravity supplies the resultant force needed for that motion.

There is no need for a separate outward force balancing gravity in the usual inertial-frame explanation. Without the inward force, the object would move along a tangent rather than continuing around the circle. Weightlessness inside an orbiting spacecraft does not mean gravity has disappeared there.

sections.heading: Find orbital speed from a complete journey
sections.body:
For an approximately circular orbit, one revolution covers distance 2πr. Divide by the period T to get average orbital speed v = 2πr/T. Use the distance from the centre of the attracting body, not just the height above its surface.

For r = 7.0 × 10⁶ m and T = 6000 s, speed is about 7.3 × 10³ m/s. Keep radius and time units consistent, and distinguish the orbital period from the object’s own rotation period.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Stellar evolution, redshift and evidence for an expanding universe

sections.heading: Explain a main-sequence star
sections.body:
Gravity pulls material together to form a protostar. Under suitable conditions, nuclear fusion begins. In the main-sequence stage, inward gravitational effects balance outward pressure.

Fusion is a nuclear process, not chemical burning in oxygen. A more massive star has more fuel but uses it much faster, so its main-sequence life is shorter.

sections.heading: Choose the correct final-stage branch
sections.body:
A Sun-like star can become a red giant and later leave a white dwarf after losing outer material.

A much more massive star can become a red supergiant and undergo a supernova. Its remnant may be a neutron star or black hole. Not every star becomes a black hole.

sections.heading: Read redshift from a spectral pattern
sections.body:
Elements produce recognisable spectral lines. If matching lines in a galaxy spectrum have longer wavelengths than their reference positions, they are redshifted.

In the relevant galaxy context this supports recession. It is the line shift that matters, not simply a galaxy looking red in a photograph.

sections.heading: Connect evidence to the model
sections.body:
The large-scale link between galaxy distance and recession supports an expanding universe. Cosmic microwave background radiation is another important piece of evidence for the Big Bang model.

Nearby galaxies can also have local motions. One approaching nearby galaxy does not erase the wider pattern.

sections.heading: Distinguish an observation from its explanation
sections.body:
An observation could be that several identified spectral lines are shifted to longer wavelengths. Recession is an interpretation of that pattern in the stated context. An expanding-universe model explains the broader pattern across many galaxies.

These are linked stages, but they are not the same statement. In a longer answer, move from the measured evidence to what it supports. Avoid saying that a single red-looking image proves the whole history of the universe, or that expansion requires one special centre visible in space.

topics.subject: Computer Science
topics.title: CPU architecture and embedded systems

sections.heading: A stored program is fetched and executed
sections.body: The CPU repeatedly fetches an instruction, decodes it and executes its operation. The control unit coordinates these activities; the ALU performs arithmetic and logical operations. Registers hold small amounts of immediately needed data or addresses. In the von Neumann model, instructions and data share memory. The program counter identifies the next instruction, while other registers support memory access and intermediate results.

sections.heading: Performance has several bottlenecks
sections.body: A higher clock frequency can increase cycles per second, but does not guarantee an equal increase in overall program speed. Cache keeps frequently used information close to the processor. Additional cores can execute suitable tasks concurrently, but software must support effective parallel work. Compare CPUs using the task, memory behaviour, power and architecture rather than one headline figure.

sections.heading: Embedded systems have a focused job
sections.body: An embedded system is a computer integrated into another device for a particular function. Examples include a washing-machine controller, engine management system and thermostat. They often have constrained memory, input/output and power requirements, and may need dependable real-time responses. A general-purpose computer instead runs a wider range of applications chosen by the user.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: The program counter stores the address of the next instruction rather than the instruction itself. The memory address register identifies a memory location, while the memory data register holds data being transferred. The accumulator can hold intermediate ALU results. These roles explain the difference between an address and its contents without requiring a hardware-level account of every signal transfer. An embedded controller is chosen for its specified response, inputs and outputs. A suitable answer explains why a constrained, dependable purpose-built system fits the device rather than merely naming a household appliance.

sections.heading: Distinguish an address from its stored value
sections.body:
Think of memory as numbered locations. An address tells the CPU which location to use; the content is the instruction or data stored there. The two numbers need not be the same.

The address bus carries location information, the data bus carries content and the control bus carries control signals. A register holding an address is not automatically holding the value at that address. This distinction helps explain the different jobs of the program counter, MAR and MDR.

sections.heading: Explain an embedded system using its purpose
sections.body:
A washing-machine controller receives inputs, follows a program and controls outputs such as the motor or valves. Its main purpose is a limited set of appliance tasks rather than running many unrelated user applications.

Embedded does not mean the system must have no screen or network connection. Those features depend on the product. Compare requirements such as low power, reliability, cost, response time and the available inputs and outputs rather than assuming every embedded device has identical hardware.

sections.heading: Give registers distinct roles
sections.body:
The program counter holds the next instruction address. The memory address register holds an address used in a memory transfer. The memory data register holds the content transferred.

An accumulator holds intermediate results in suitable CPU models. These are different jobs, so do not swap their names in a trace.

sections.heading: Follow a fetch in order
sections.body:
The program counter’s address is copied to the MAR. Memory at that address is read into the MDR in the simplified model.

The next-instruction address is updated, then the control unit decodes the instruction. Use any additional registers and exact sequence specified by the question.

sections.heading: Explain what execution can change
sections.body:
Execution can calculate a value, compare data, transfer data or change the next instruction address. A branch updates control flow rather than continuing to the next sequential instruction.

The ALU handles arithmetic and logic. The control unit coordinates the steps and signals.

sections.heading: Judge performance using the task
sections.body:
Clock speed is cycles per second. Cache can reduce some memory delays, and more cores can help work that can be split.

None gives a universal speed guarantee on its own. A task with sequential steps may gain little from extra cores, even when another task benefits greatly.

sections.heading: Follow one instruction address without confusing it with the instruction
sections.body:
If the PC contains 120, that is an address. The CPU uses it to fetch whatever instruction is stored at location 120. The instruction itself might encode an addition, a load or a branch; it is not automatically the number 120.

The MAR helps identify the location and the MDR carries the retrieved content in the simplified account. After decoding and execution, the PC determines where the next fetch begins. Keeping location and content separate makes the cycle much easier to trace.

topics.title: Memory, secondary storage and file sizes

sections.heading: Primary memory and persistent storage serve different roles
sections.body: RAM stores programs and data currently in use and is volatile. ROM is non-volatile and stores instructions needed for tasks such as starting a device. Cache is small, fast memory used to reduce CPU waiting. Virtual memory uses secondary storage to support memory management when RAM is insufficient, but access is slower and excessive swapping reduces performance.

sections.heading: Choose storage for its context
sections.body: Magnetic, optical and solid-state storage differ in access speed, capacity, portability, durability and cost. Solid-state devices have no moving read mechanism and are useful in portable equipment; magnetic storage can offer high capacity at a competitive cost. A justification should connect a property to the actual user need. Non-volatile does not mean immune to corruption, damage or accidental deletion.

sections.heading: Translate representations into storage requirements
sections.body: A bit has two values, a nibble is four bits and a byte is eight bits. Follow the conversion convention specified in the question. Uncompressed image size depends on pixel dimensions and colour depth; sound size depends on sample rate, bit depth, duration and channels. Include metadata or compression only if supplied. More samples or greater depth can improve fidelity but increase storage demand.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: Virtual memory does not physically expand RAM. The operating system moves data between main memory and secondary storage to manage available memory, with slower access when needed data is not in RAM. For sound-file calculations, include channel count only when the question specifies it; a stereo recording normally stores two sampled channels. State any metadata or unit convention assumed. A storage recommendation should link a required characteristic, such as portability or durability, to a user scenario. A list of device names without those links does not justify a choice.

sections.heading: Separate RAM, ROM and secondary storage
sections.body:
RAM holds programs and data currently in use. It is volatile, so its contents are normally lost when power is removed. ROM is non-volatile and holds data or instructions that must remain available, including suitable startup information.

Secondary storage keeps files even when the device is off. Increasing storage capacity does not directly give a running program more RAM. When RAM is limited, using slower storage to support memory management can affect performance. The different stores have different speed, capacity and persistence requirements.

sections.heading: Compare storage devices for a stated use
sections.body:
An SSD has no moving mechanical read head, so it can offer fast access and resist some movement-related problems. A magnetic hard disk often provides large capacity at a lower cost per unit of storage. Optical media have other uses and capacity limits.

A suitable comparison considers capacity, speed, durability, portability and cost. For a device carried while operating, movement matters. For an archive, capacity and how data will remain readable may matter more. Do not declare one technology best for every purpose.

topics.subject: Computer Science
topics.title: Binary, hexadecimal and digital representation

sections.heading: Represent whole numbers using place value
sections.body: An unsigned eight-bit value uses places 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1, giving a range from 0 to 255. Binary addition follows carry rules; a carry beyond the available width causes overflow in the unsigned model. Hexadecimal uses digits 0–9 and A–F; each hex digit corresponds to four bits, making binary values easier to read.

sections.heading: Text and images need agreed encodings
sections.body: A character set maps characters to numerical codes. ASCII covers a relatively small set, while Unicode supports many writing systems and symbols. The number of available codes depends on the encoding’s allocated bits, but real Unicode encodings can use differing byte lengths. Bitmap images store pixel colours; greater resolution or colour depth generally increases file size and may improve detail.

sections.heading: Sampling and compression make trade-offs
sections.body: Sound sampling measures amplitude at regular intervals. A higher sampling frequency captures more temporal detail, and greater bit depth provides more amplitude levels. Lossless compression allows exact reconstruction, useful for text and program code. Lossy compression discards selected information to reduce size further, useful when a controlled quality loss is acceptable. Compression does not always reduce every input file.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: An unsigned eight-bit system cannot represent every result of adding two eight-bit values. For example, 200 + 100 is 300, beyond its maximum 255, so a fixed-width representation overflows. A left shift can multiply by two only while the intended value remains within range; bits shifted out are lost. Character encoding, image pixels and sampled sound all map information into binary, but their interpretations differ. Lossless compression is required when reconstructing every original program instruction or text character matters. A smaller lossy media file is not an exact copy of its original data.

sections.heading: Convert binary by using place values
sections.body:
For an eight-bit unsigned value, the place values from left to right are 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1. In 10110100, the set positions give 128 + 32 + 16 + 4 = 180.

Hexadecimal groups binary into four-bit sections. 1011 is B and 0100 is 4, so the same eight-bit pattern is B4. Hexadecimal makes long bit patterns shorter to read; it does not change the stored information.

sections.heading: Explain overflow and left shifts carefully
sections.body:
Eight unsigned bits can represent values from 0 to 255. If an addition needs a ninth bit, the result cannot fit in that eight-bit range: overflow has occurred.

A logical left shift moves bits left and inserts zeros on the right. It can multiply an unsigned value by a power of two only if significant bits are not lost. For example, 00000101 shifted left once becomes 00001010, changing 5 to 10. State the bit width when judging whether a shift preserves the expected value.

topics.tip: A binary shift can lose bits at the fixed-width boundary; it is not always a safe multiplication.

topics.title: Image and sound file sizes, units and compression choices

sections.heading: Calculate bitmap data
sections.body:
A bitmap has width × height pixels. Multiply that count by bits per pixel to find raw bits, then divide by 8 for bytes.

A colour depth of b bits can represent up to 2ᵇ values. More pixels add spatial detail; more bits per pixel increase available colour values.

sections.heading: Calculate sampled sound
sections.body:
Raw sound bits = sample rate × bit depth × duration × channels. Sample rate counts samples per second; bit depth counts bits per sample.

Stereo has two channels. Use seconds for duration. Increasing sample rate and increasing bit depth change different parts of the recording.

sections.heading: Use the stated units
sections.body:
There are 8 bits in one byte. Follow the question’s convention for kilo and mega rather than silently mixing 1000 with 1024.

Under decimal conventions, 1 kB = 1000 bytes and 1 MB = 1 000 000 bytes. Label the final answer correctly and remember that metadata may add to the raw estimate.

sections.heading: Choose a suitable compression method
sections.body:
Lossless compression allows exact recovery of the original data. Lossy compression discards selected information and may reduce perceptual quality.

Exact source code and documents need lossless recovery. A photo or recording may accept some quality loss for a smaller file, depending on its purpose.

sections.heading: Spot which change has the biggest size effect
sections.body:
Doubling both image dimensions gives four times as many pixels: a 200 × 100 image has 20 000 pixels, while a 400 × 200 image has 80 000. At unchanged colour depth, raw image data is four times larger.

Doubling only the colour depth makes it twice as large. For sound, doubling duration or channel count each doubles raw size. Separate the factors before multiplying so that “double the quality” does not become an undefined calculation.

cards.question: How many distinct values can a 12-bit sample represent?
cards.answer: Each bit doubles the possible combinations. The count is 2¹². There are 4096 distinct values.

cards.question: A 1000 × 500 bitmap uses 24-bit colour. Find its raw size in decimal MB.
cards.answer: Bits = 1000 × 500 × 24 = 12 000 000. Bytes = 12 000 000/8 = 1 500 000. The size is 1.5 MB before metadata.

cards.question: Why should a program’s source code be stored using a lossless method rather than a lossy image-style method?
cards.answer: The exact characters are required to reconstruct the source. Discarding or changing characters can alter syntax or program behaviour. Lossless compression preserves the original data exactly while reducing size where possible.

cards.question: Define colour depth.
cards.answer: the number of bits used to represent the colour value of one pixel

cards.question: Define sample rate.
cards.answer: the number of sound samples recorded per second

cards.question: Define lossless compression.
cards.answer: compression permitting exact reconstruction of the original data

topics.subject: Computer Science
topics.title: Networks, addressing, protocols and layers

sections.heading: Networks share resources and communication
sections.body: A LAN covers a limited organisational or geographical area; a WAN connects networks over wider distances. A switch directs traffic within a network and a router forwards traffic between networks. Wireless access points connect wireless devices. Network performance depends on available bandwidth, connected devices, transmission conditions and the service being used, not just whether the connection is wired.

sections.heading: Addresses and protocols support delivery
sections.body: A MAC address identifies a network interface at the local-link level; an IP address supports routing between networks. DNS resolves human-readable domain names into address information. Protocols are agreed communication rules: HTTP/HTTPS support web communication, and email protocols perform sending and retrieval roles. Encryption in HTTPS protects data in transit; it does not prove a website’s content is truthful.

sections.heading: Layers reduce dependence between tasks
sections.body: A layered model separates concerns such as application communication and transmission. Each layer provides services to the layer above and follows agreed interfaces. Standardisation helps equipment and software from different organisations interoperate and makes faults easier to isolate. Client-server networks centralise services and management; peer-to-peer arrangements distribute sharing without the same dedicated-server structure.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A router’s role is to forward traffic between networks; a switch directs local network traffic using information appropriate to its layer. DNS makes addressing easier for people by resolving names, but it does not store the entire content of the requested website. Protocol layering allows one implementation to change while compatible interfaces remain stable. Distinguish bandwidth from measured performance: a high-bandwidth link can still be slow because of congestion, latency, interference, a busy server or another bottleneck. Client-server management can simplify accounts and backups but also creates dependencies requiring availability planning.

sections.heading: Compare client–server and peer-to-peer arrangements
sections.body:
In a client–server arrangement, servers provide services or centrally managed resources to clients. This can simplify shared accounts, backups and access control, but the server and its management add costs and can become points of failure.

In a peer-to-peer arrangement, devices can share resources directly without the same dedicated central server. It can suit a small setup, but consistent security and backups become harder to manage as it grows. The best choice depends on scale and the services required.

sections.heading: Explain a star topology through its connections
sections.body:
In a star topology, each device connects to a central switch or similar central point. A failed cable to one device need not disconnect the others. Failure of the central device can affect the whole connected group.

The central point needs enough connections and capacity. A star does not mean all computers connect directly to one another. Distinguish physical topology from whether the network uses client–server services: these describe different aspects of the same network.

topics.subject: Computer Science
topics.title: From a web address to a page: DNS, packets and protocols

sections.heading: Separate a name from an address
sections.body:
DNS resolves a domain name to suitable IP-address information. IP addresses support communication and routing between networks. MAC addresses have a relevant local-network role.

A DNS server does not normally send the entire web page itself. Name lookup and fetching page content are different stages.

sections.heading: Follow data through network devices
sections.body:
A switch forwards data within a LAN. A router forwards packets between networks. Wireless access supplies a radio link into a network.

Packets contain payload and control information. On a packet-switched network, packets need not all take the same route to the destination.

sections.heading: Give protocols their own jobs
sections.body:
IP supports addressing and routing. TCP supports reliable ordered delivery in the common model. HTTP defines web request–response communication; HTTPS adds security protection.

FTP concerns file transfer. SMTP concerns sending email, while POP and IMAP concern email access. Explain the job rather than listing abbreviations.

sections.heading: Separate capacity, delay and trust
sections.body:
Bandwidth is how much data a connection can carry per unit time. Latency is delay. More bandwidth does not remove every server or network delay.

HTTPS protects communication, but an encrypted connection can still lead to dishonest or misleading content. Transport security is not a guarantee of truthful information.

sections.heading: Compare a large download with a short request
sections.body:
A long video download can benefit greatly from higher bandwidth because much data must be transferred. A tiny request to a slow remote service may still spend most of its time waiting for a response.

That waiting can include network latency and server processing. Increasing connection capacity does not automatically remove either. When a scenario says “the internet is slow”, identify the measured problem before choosing a solution. Slow transfer and slow first response are not always caused by the same bottleneck.

topics.subject: Computer Science
topics.title: Threats, prevention and layered defence

sections.heading: Identify the mechanism of the threat
sections.body: Malware includes programs designed for harmful or unauthorised activity. Phishing and other social engineering manipulate people into revealing information or taking unsafe actions. Brute-force attacks try many credentials. A denial-of-service attack exhausts resources so legitimate users cannot obtain service. SQL injection exploits unsafe handling of data in database queries; it is not prevented simply by making a password longer.

sections.heading: Match each control to a threat
sections.body: Access controls restrict what authenticated users can do. Strong unique passwords and suitable account protections reduce credential risks. Anti-malware tools detect known or suspicious software, while updates close discovered vulnerabilities. Firewalls filter network traffic according to rules. Encryption protects confidentiality when keys are managed correctly; it does not itself prevent deletion or validate the accuracy of stored data.

sections.heading: Plan for failure as well as prevention
sections.body: Backups support recovery after loss or corruption. Keep appropriate separate copies, test restoration and control who can alter them. Staff training and clear procedures complement technical controls. Penetration testing explores weaknesses with authorisation and an agreed scope. A sound answer links the proposed measure to the scenario rather than claiming any single tool makes a system completely secure.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: Defence should cover prevention, detection and recovery. A firewall can block specified traffic but does not replace patching a vulnerable application. Password hashing is not the same as encrypting passwords for later recovery: a suitable password-verification design avoids needing to retrieve the original password. Backups must be protected from the same event that damages the main copy, and restoration should be tested. In scenario questions, name the specific threat, explain how the control interrupts it and identify a realistic limitation rather than claiming that one control eliminates every risk.

sections.heading: Match a control to the route of attack
sections.body:
Phishing tries to persuade someone to reveal information or take a harmful action. Training, careful checking and suitable authentication controls can reduce the risk; antivirus alone does not stop someone willingly giving away a password.

Malware may be limited by appropriate software protection, updates and controlled permissions. A firewall filters traffic according to rules, but does not make all content trustworthy. Layering controls helps because one control rarely covers every way a system can fail.

sections.heading: Explain why backups and access rights matter
sections.body:
A backup provides a separate recoverable copy of data. It can help after accidental deletion, equipment failure or some attacks. Recovery needs a usable copy and a tested restore process, not just a message saying that a backup ran.

Access rights limit what a user or process can read or change. Giving everyone administrator privileges makes mistakes and compromised accounts more damaging. Permissions reduce potential harm, while backups support recovery; they do not perform the same job.

topics.subject: Computer Science
topics.title: Operating systems, utilities and translators

sections.heading: The operating system manages shared resources
sections.body: An operating system provides a user interface and coordinates memory, processes, peripherals, files and users. Memory management allocates available memory and prevents inappropriate interference between processes. Device drivers let the system communicate with hardware through suitable interfaces. File management organises names, locations and access permissions; user management establishes accounts and privileges.

sections.heading: Utilities support maintenance
sections.body: Encryption utilities protect data confidentiality, compression utilities reduce representations where possible, and backup utilities support recovery. Defragmentation can improve access patterns on some magnetic disks by reorganising fragmented files; it is not a general performance remedy for solid-state storage. A utility should be chosen for the actual storage and maintenance problem.

sections.heading: Translate source into executable operations
sections.body: A compiler translates a program into another form before execution, commonly producing object or executable code. An interpreter executes through a runtime by translating or processing instructions during execution. An assembler translates assembly language. An IDE supports writing, running and debugging with tools such as syntax highlighting, error diagnostics and breakpoints. No translator proves that the program meets its user requirements.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A process can be ready to run yet waiting because the operating system shares limited processor time between tasks. Memory management allocates resources and helps isolate programs. Device drivers translate the operating system’s requests into the appropriate device interface. Compilation and interpretation are implementation strategies rather than measures of program quality; either can execute a logically incorrect program. A compiler may report syntax errors before execution, but it cannot generally establish that every user requirement is met. Choose utility software based on the actual maintenance task and storage technology.

sections.heading: Explain multitasking without claiming everything happens at once
sections.body:
An operating system shares processor time between tasks, manages memory and controls access to files and peripherals. Rapid switching can make several applications appear to run together on a single processing core.

Interrupts tell the processor that an event needs attention, such as input being ready. The system can pause or schedule work appropriately. Multiple cores can execute some work in parallel, but multitasking and parallel execution are not identical ideas.

sections.heading: Distinguish a translator’s job from a program’s logic
sections.body:
A compiler translates source code into another form before the resulting program runs. An interpreter carries out code through an interpretation process during execution. An assembler translates assembly language.

Translation can identify certain errors, but it does not prove the program solves the intended problem. A syntactically valid calculation can still use the wrong formula. Testing and reasoning about expected outputs remain necessary after code translates successfully.

topics.tip: A syntax error concerns language rules; a logic error can remain in a runnable program.

topics.subject: Computer Science
topics.title: Ethics, legislation and environmental decisions

sections.heading: A legal action can still raise an ethical problem
sections.body: Evaluate stakeholders, benefits, harms and alternatives in a computing decision. Privacy, surveillance, accessibility, inclusion and algorithmic bias may affect different groups unequally. A reasoned judgement connects evidence to the scenario and acknowledges a genuine trade-off, rather than listing disconnected advantages and disadvantages.

sections.heading: Understand the purpose of relevant legislation
sections.body: In UK computing contexts, data protection law controls handling of personal data; computer misuse law concerns unauthorised access and related misuse; copyright law protects qualifying works; software licences define permitted uses. Name the relevant law or licence where the course requires it and relate it to the conduct in the question. Consent is not the only possible lawful basis for every personal-data use.

sections.heading: Consider the whole life cycle
sections.body: Equipment manufacture requires energy and materials, use consumes power and disposal creates waste. Repair, reuse, longer product lifetimes and responsible recycling can reduce some impacts. Cloud services still rely on physical infrastructure. Open-source and proprietary licensing provide different permissions and responsibilities; free of charge is not the same as open source, and either model may include commercial services.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A balanced evaluation should identify stakeholders who gain convenience, cost savings or access, and stakeholders who may face exclusion, surveillance or error. An automated decision can reproduce bias in its training data or design. Accessibility includes suitable interaction for users with differing needs, not just whether a device is inexpensive. Software licensing distinguishes permissions to inspect, modify and redistribute from the question of price. Environmental claims should consider manufacturing, running energy, repair and disposal; moving a service to a remote data centre changes where impacts occur rather than eliminating them.

sections.heading: Connect each named law to the issue
sections.body:
The Computer Misuse Act concerns offences including unauthorised access and unauthorised acts affecting computer systems. The Data Protection Act forms part of the UK framework governing personal-data use. Copyright law protects relevant original works, including software.

In an exam scenario, identify what happened and explain the connection. Access being technically possible does not itself make it authorised. Data being useful to an organisation does not mean it can be used without considering the relevant rules and people’s rights.

sections.heading: Build a balanced ethical argument
sections.body:
A school monitoring system might help protect equipment or detect misuse, but it can also affect privacy, trust and how much data is collected. Explain benefits and drawbacks for different people, using the scenario rather than a memorised opinion.

An action being legal does not automatically settle whether it is ethical. Environmental evaluation also needs the whole lifecycle: manufacturing, electricity use, repair and disposal. Replacing a working device with a slightly more efficient one has an upfront manufacturing cost as well as possible use-phase savings.

topics.subject: Computer Science
topics.title: Decomposition, searches, sorts and trace tables

sections.heading: Make a problem small enough to reason about
sections.body: Decomposition divides a problem into manageable subproblems. Abstraction retains relevant details and removes irrelevant ones. An algorithm is a finite, ordered description of how to solve a defined problem. Inputs, outputs and preconditions should be clear. A trace table records values as instructions execute; update a value only when the corresponding instruction runs.

sections.heading: Search depends on the data arrangement
sections.body: Linear search checks items in sequence and works without sorting. Binary search compares with a middle value and discards one half repeatedly, requiring sorted data. Be explicit about first and last positions and how the middle is rounded. A search must handle the item-not-found case and terminate even on an empty or one-item range.

sections.heading: Sorting algorithms do different work
sections.body: Bubble sort compares neighbouring values and swaps those out of order over repeated passes. Insertion sort inserts each new value into a growing sorted region. Merge sort splits the data, sorts smaller parts and merges them in order. Show the state after the precise pass or merge requested; a correct final ordering alone may not demonstrate the specified method.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: For binary search, write down the current search boundaries and update them so the already-tested middle value is excluded when appropriate. This guarantees progress towards termination. A trace table should reflect the algorithm as written, including loop conditions and update order. For insertion sort, the sorted region grows as the next value is inserted in its correct position; for bubble sort, repeated adjacent swaps move values through a pass. A final sorted list does not show which algorithm produced it, so intermediate states matter when a method is specified.

sections.heading: Make a trace show the order of changes
sections.body:
A trace table records variable values as an algorithm runs. Work through the instructions in order and update a value only when its assignment is executed.

For total ← total + value, first use the old total on the right, calculate the sum, then store the new total. Keep loop counters and conditions visible. A trace that shows only the final output may hide the exact step where an error occurred, such as an extra loop iteration or a reset in the wrong place.

sections.heading: Explain the work done by a sorting method
sections.body:
In bubble sort, neighbouring items are compared and swapped if they are in the wrong order. After one full pass in ascending order, a largest item has moved to the end of the unsorted portion.

Merge sort divides a list into smaller parts, sorts those parts and combines sorted lists in order. When tracing a sort, show the list after the stage requested. A fully sorted final list does not show that the specified algorithm or number of passes was followed.

topics.tip: An algorithm description should include what happens when no matching item exists.

topics.subject: Computer Science
topics.title: Worked search and sort traces

sections.heading: Keep state and comparison separate
sections.body: A trace records what changes as each instruction executes. For a search, keep the current position or lower and upper bounds visible. A comparison does not automatically update every variable; apply only the update specified by the algorithm. An empty search range should produce a not-found outcome rather than attempt an invalid index.

sections.heading: Compare adjacent passes and insertion steps
sections.body: Bubble sort repeatedly compares adjacent items and swaps an out-of-order pair. A left-to-right ascending pass moves a large value towards the right. Insertion sort instead maintains a sorted prefix and inserts the next value into its correct place. Record the precise state after the requested pass or insertion, because two methods can produce the same final sorted list by different intermediate steps.

sections.heading: Merge ordered parts carefully
sections.body: Merge sort divides the sequence into smaller parts and combines sorted parts by repeatedly selecting the next smallest available element. All values must be retained, including duplicates. A trace should not silently discard equal items or treat them as a single value unless the algorithm explicitly removes duplicates. Algorithm names matter less than accurately following the operations and termination conditions.

sections.heading: Show why binary search needs sorted data
sections.body:
Binary search compares the target with a middle value and discards the half that cannot contain it. This only works because the values are ordered.

For [2, 5, 8, 11, 14, 17, 20], target 17 is above the middle value 11, so the lower half is excluded. The next search uses only the remaining range. Record lower, upper and middle indices according to the question’s convention so updates do not repeatedly include the same middle item.

sections.heading: Distinguish comparison from a successful swap
sections.body:
In bubble sort, a pair is compared even if it is already in order and no swap occurs. A count of swaps is therefore not the same as a count of comparisons.

For [1, 3, 2], comparing 1 with 3 needs no swap, but comparing 3 with 2 does. One pass ends at [1, 2, 3]. Use the exact counting definition requested rather than assuming every examined pair causes a movement.

topics.subject: Computer Science
topics.title: Programming constructs, data types and subprograms

sections.heading: Control execution deliberately
sections.body: Sequence performs instructions in order. Selection chooses a path using a condition. Iteration repeats work through count-controlled or condition-controlled loops. Variables store values that may change; constants represent fixed named values. Choose integer, real, Boolean, character or string types to fit the meaning and required operations. Input normally needs conversion and validation before numerical use.

sections.heading: Use collections and files appropriately
sections.body: Arrays store indexed elements, and two-dimensional arrays organise a grid of values. Check index boundaries and whether the language starts at zero or one. String operations include length, slicing and searching, with language-specific details. File handling needs opening, reading or writing and closing using appropriate modes; a program should handle missing files and invalid input where required.

sections.heading: Subprograms make interfaces explicit
sections.body: A function returns a value; a procedure performs a task without a required returned value in the exam model. Parameters pass data through the interface. Local variables reduce unintended interference, while global state can create hidden dependencies. Testing a subprogram separately helps isolate faults. Meaningful identifiers and clear modular structure support maintainability better than comments that merely repeat each line.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A count-controlled loop is convenient when the number of repetitions is known; a condition-controlled loop suits input validation or work with an unknown number of items. Initialisation must occur at the correct scope: reset a total before processing a new dataset, not inside the loop that accumulates it. Parameters make a subprogram’s required inputs explicit. A returned value must be stored or used by the caller if later computation needs it. For arrays and strings, check both valid index limits and the behaviour on empty input rather than assuming every collection contains an item.

sections.heading: Distinguish a returned value from displayed output
sections.body:
A function can calculate a result and return it to the calling code. That code can store it, use it in another calculation or display it. Printing a result on screen is not the same as returning it.

A parameter supplies information to a subprogram. A local variable belongs to that subprogram’s scope, while a global variable can be accessed more widely under the language’s rules. Limiting unnecessary shared state can make the code’s effects easier to follow.

sections.heading: Use an accumulator and counter for different jobs
sections.body:
An accumulator combines values, such as a running sum. A counter tracks how many items or events have been processed. To calculate a mean, both can be useful: total/count.

Initialise them before the loop, add each valid value to total and increase count once per included item. Do not divide by zero if there are no items. Choosing descriptive names helps prevent counting every input when the requirement says to count only valid or matching ones.

topics.subject: Computer Science
topics.title: Arrays, files and defensive input handling

sections.heading: Validate before converting and using
sections.body: Input arrives in a form defined by the interface, commonly a string. Check permitted form and conversion behaviour before treating it as a numerical quantity. Then check its range or other domain constraints. A valid-looking number may still be inappropriate for the task. Keep an error response distinct from successful processing, and preserve useful user input when an operation fails.

sections.heading: Handle empty and boundary cases
sections.body: An array of n items indexed from zero has valid indices 0 through n − 1. Iterating to n inclusive causes an out-of-range access. A total can be zero for valid data, so do not confuse that value with an empty collection. A mean needs a non-zero count. File handling should consider a missing file, an empty file and malformed records separately where required by the program specification.

sections.heading: Use a clear subprogram interface
sections.body: Pass needed data through parameters and return a defined result or failure representation. Avoid relying on hidden global variables when a local value is sufficient. A caller must check the success result before announcing completion. Testing should include a normal record, the smallest valid input, a missing record and a representative invalid record rather than only repeating a successful example.

sections.heading: Use the array length to set safe loop bounds
sections.body:
A zero-based array of length 6 has valid indices 0 to 5. A loop ending at 6 inclusive tries to read a seventh element.

For a grand total, set total to zero before the loop, then add each element once. For a filtered total, perform the condition check before the addition. An array can contain zero or negative values, so do not assume that every useful value must be positive unless the requirement says so.

sections.heading: Treat end-of-file as a condition, not a data value
sections.body:
A file-reading loop needs to know when there are no more records. Use the end-of-file mechanism or iteration method supplied by the language rather than inventing a final data value that might also occur legitimately.

Check that the file opened, process each record in the intended format and close resources appropriately. Empty files and missing files are different cases. A successful open does not guarantee that every later record is valid or that a later write will succeed.

FUNCTION meanOf(values)
    IF LENGTH(values) = 0 THEN

topics.subject: Computer Science
topics.title: SQL selection, filtering and sorting a single table

sections.heading: Read rows and columns correctly
sections.body:
A row is a record; a column is a field. A primary key uniquely identifies each record. Names may repeat, so they are not automatically good keys.

Use the table and field names supplied. SQL queries refer to fields, not spreadsheet cell addresses.

sections.heading: Use SELECT, FROM and WHERE
sections.body:
SELECT chooses output fields. FROM names the table. WHERE gives the condition records must satisfy. SELECT * returns every field.

Text values need suitable quotes. Score >= 60 includes 60. AND requires both conditions; OR allows either. Choose the operator from the wording.

sections.heading: Sort the returned records
sections.body:
ORDER BY Score DESC gives highest scores first. ASC gives ascending order. A second sort field can resolve ties when required.

Sorting a query’s result does not rewrite the stored records or change their primary keys. Include the requested order even when the selected records are otherwise correct.

sections.heading: Trace a query record by record
sections.body:
Apply the WHERE test to every record. Keep the requested fields from the passing records, then sort them.

For “Biology students scoring at least 60”, both conditions must hold. A student passing a different subject should not be included merely because the score is high.

sections.heading: Check both indices in a grid
sections.body:
A zero-based array with 3 rows and 4 columns uses row indices 0–2 and column indices 0–3.

An index is a position, not the element’s value. Check which index represents rows in the question. The largest index is one less than the size in each dimension.

sections.heading: Trace nested loops carefully
sections.body:
An outer loop can select each row while an inner loop visits its columns. Record the current row and column to check every element is processed once.

For a grand total, initialise the accumulator before both loops. For separate row totals, reset it at the start of each row.

sections.heading: Distinguish text from numbers
sections.body:
Joining the strings "12" and "3" gives "123". Adding the numbers 12 and 3 gives 15. Convert valid numeric text when arithmetic is intended.

String operations also depend on the language’s position and substring rules. Check whether a parameter means length or ending index.

sections.heading: Use cases that reveal indexing mistakes
sections.body:
Test the first and last valid positions and a non-square array. A square array can hide a loop using row count for both dimensions.

For strings, consider empty and one-character inputs where allowed. State the expected content or output, not only that the code should avoid crashing.

sections.heading: See how a reset changes a total
sections.body:
For rows [2, 4] and [3, 5], a grand total should be 14. Set total to zero once, then add all four values.

If you reset at the start of each row, the final stored total is only 8, the last row’s sum. If you reset before every element, it becomes 5, the last element. Each program may run without an index error, but only one initialisation position matches the grand-total requirement.

topics.subject: Computer Science
topics.title: Validation, defensive design and testing

sections.heading: Reject invalid input for a specific reason
sections.body: Validation checks whether input satisfies rules such as range, length, type, presence or format. It does not establish truth: a plausible but incorrect birth date can pass a range check. Verification checks a copy against an original, for example through double entry or visual comparison. Authentication establishes who a user is; access rules then govern what they may do.

sections.heading: Plan tests around meaningful boundaries
sections.body: Normal test data represents acceptable typical input. Boundary data probes edges of allowed ranges, including values just outside them where appropriate. Invalid data should be rejected safely. State the expected result before testing; otherwise an observed output has no standard of comparison. Include zero, empty inputs, duplicates and missing records when they are relevant to the program’s contract.

sections.heading: Separate finding an error from explaining it
sections.body: A syntax error violates language rules; a logic error produces incorrect behaviour despite valid syntax. Runtime problems arise during execution. Use trace tables, breakpoints and focused tests to locate the first incorrect state. Correct one cause and rerun affected tests. Defensive design should keep user data intact when an operation fails rather than falsely reporting that it succeeded.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A boundary test should state an input and its expected output or rejection. For an inclusive range 1–10, 0, 1, 10 and 11 check both permitted edges and their immediate outside neighbours. Verification compares copied data with an original; validation checks conformity to rules. Neither necessarily proves that a claimed real-world fact is true. A test plan should include normal operation as well as relevant failure cases such as an unavailable file or empty collection. When saving fails, retain the user’s unsaved work and explain the failure instead of falsely confirming completion.

sections.heading: Turn a requirement into a Boolean condition
sections.body:
If a whole-number age must be between 11 and 18 inclusive, validity requires an integer and both age ≥ 11 and age ≤ 18. Checking only one boundary accepts unwanted values.

Using OR between those two range comparisons is also wrong: almost every number satisfies at least one of them. Write down the acceptable interval first, then translate it into code. Handle a failed numeric conversion before trying to compare text as though it were a number.

sections.heading: Test the behaviour after a failure
sections.body:
An invalid input should lead to the specified error message and retry or exit behaviour. Test that the program does not continue using an old value or accidentally save incomplete data.

For a file-save failure, useful behaviour may include retaining unsaved work and offering a retry. Catching an error is not enough if the next line still displays “saved successfully”. A good test checks the user-visible result as well as whether the program avoids crashing.

topics.tip: “The program runs” is not an expected result; state the required output or rejection.

sections.heading: Keep the three checks separate
sections.body:
An age can pass a range check and still be untrue. Two matching entries can also both be wrong. A password check concerns identity rather than the accuracy of every later input.

Name the check that fits the problem, then explain what it can and cannot establish.

sections.heading: Write the input rule first
sections.body:
For integer marks from 0 to 100 inclusive, check both type and range. Handle invalid numeric text before comparing it as a number.

After failure, give the specified message and retry or exit. The program should not continue with invalid data or an old value by accident.

sections.heading: Choose purposeful test data
sections.body:
Normal data is valid and typical. Boundary tests check the edges; just-outside values test rejection. Invalid data breaks a rule.

For 0–100 inclusive, test 0 and 100 as accepted, and −1 and 101 as rejected. State the expected behaviour, not simply “works”.

sections.heading: Identify the type of error
sections.body:
A syntax error breaks language rules. A logic error produces wrong behaviour even when code can run. A runtime error occurs during execution.

Retest the original failing input after a fix, then check relevant neighbouring cases. One corrected output does not prove the whole program is correct.

sections.heading: Use a boundary to reveal a hidden mistake
sections.body:
Suppose a program checks mark > 0 AND mark < 100. Ordinary inputs such as 45 pass, so a normal test alone might look successful.

But 0 and 100 should also pass under an inclusive requirement. Testing those boundaries reveals the wrong comparison operators. Change the condition to use ≥ and ≤, then test −1 and 101 as well to confirm that rejection still works. Choose tests from the requirement rather than from values that are convenient to type.

topics.subject: Computer Science
topics.title: Boolean expressions and truth tables

sections.heading: Logic operates on true and false
sections.body: AND is true only when both inputs are true. OR is true when at least one input is true. NOT reverses its input. Use brackets to show the intended grouping of a compound expression. A condition such as age ≥ 11 AND age ≤ 18 expresses an inclusive range; replacing AND with OR would accept many invalid values.

sections.heading: Enumerate the whole input space
sections.body: A truth table for n independent Boolean inputs has 2ⁿ rows. List combinations systematically to avoid omission, calculate intermediate columns, then evaluate the final expression. Logic diagrams and expressions must represent the same connection structure. A negation over a complete expression applies after evaluating that expression, not separately to whichever symbol is visually nearby.

sections.heading: Use logic to explain program behaviour
sections.body: Comparisons produce Boolean results and can be combined in selections and loops. A loop condition describes when to continue or stop according to the construct being used. Test both outcomes and important combinations. Redundant checks can sometimes be simplified, but clarity and correctness take priority over making the expression short.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A condition that checks an inclusive interval normally combines two comparisons with AND. Using OR for x ≥ 1 or x ≤ 10 accepts every real x, because each value satisfies at least one comparison. Construct truth tables in a fixed order, then add intermediate columns for compound expressions. De Morgan’s relationships explain why NOT(A AND B) is equivalent to NOT A OR NOT B, while NOT(A OR B) is equivalent to NOT A AND NOT B. A loop condition must be interpreted with the construct: repeating until a condition is true differs from continuing while it is true.

sections.heading: Build a truth table one operation at a time
sections.body:
For (A AND B) OR C, first calculate a column for A AND B, then combine that result with C. With A false, B true and C true, the AND result is false but the final OR result is true.

Three independent Boolean inputs have 2³ = 8 possible combinations. Include each once. A missing row can hide a case where the circuit or condition behaves differently from the requirement.

sections.heading: Use brackets to make a rule clear
sections.body:
NOT A AND B means the negation applies to A before the AND in the usual precedence rules. NOT(A AND B) negates the combined result and is different.

For A false and B false, the first expression is false while the second is true. Brackets show which operation is intended. When translating a sentence, decide whether “not” refers to one condition or the whole combined statement before writing the expression.

topics.subject: Design & Technology
topics.title: Research, user needs and specifications

sections.heading: Start with an evidenced need
sections.body: A design problem describes the context and difficulty; a design brief states the intended task. Identify the user and the environment before proposing a solution. First-hand observation, interviews and product analysis reveal practical constraints. Secondary research adds material, technical and contextual knowledge. Record why each finding matters to a later design decision, rather than filling pages with unrelated images.

sections.heading: Turn findings into testable requirements
sections.body: A specification states what the product must achieve. Make criteria measurable where possible: dimensions, load, safe operation, cost, environmental exposure and maintenance. Distinguish essential constraints from preferences. Ergonomics concerns the relationship between people and products; anthropometric data supplies body measurements. Select relevant data ranges for the actual users and task, not simply an average person.

sections.heading: Generate and evaluate alternatives
sections.body: Produce genuinely different ideas before developing one. Use sketches, annotations and models to investigate mechanisms, construction and user interaction. Compare proposals against weighted or justified criteria; a decorative scoring table is weak without evidence. Show how feedback leads to changes. Good development explains why a decision improves function or manufacturability, not just that the new drawing looks better.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: Research quality depends on relevance and interpretation. A photograph of an existing product becomes useful analysis when it identifies a feature, explains its effect and connects that finding to the design brief. Use more than one user or observation where practical to reduce dependence on one preference. A specification should distinguish a target from a testing method. A maximum dimension can be measured directly; comfort may require an appropriate user trial and a clearly described judgement. Keep the brief open enough to investigate alternatives before committing to a material, joint or mechanism.

sections.heading: Choose research that answers a design question
sections.body:
Primary research collects information directly, such as observing a user carrying an existing product. Secondary research uses existing material, such as product dimensions or relevant published data. Both can be useful.

Choose the method from the question you need to answer. A short interview may reveal a difficulty, while a measurement may show how much clearance is needed. Asking only friends who already like your idea can give a biased picture. Record who was studied and the limits of the evidence.

sections.heading: Turn a finding into a justified requirement
sections.body:
“The product should be easy to use” is too broad to test on its own. Identify the intended user, task and condition, then decide what evidence would show successful use.

For a storage unit, a requirement might concern fitting the actual objects, access while seated or carrying the expected load. The chosen dimension or test load needs a reason from research. Do not add precise numbers only to make a specification look technical. Every important requirement should guide a design decision or a later test.

topics.tip: A specification describes performance and constraints; it should not prematurely fix every construction detail.

topics.subject: Design & Technology
topics.title: Ergonomics, prototypes and product testing

sections.heading: Test a defined user task
sections.body: Ergonomics concerns effective and comfortable interaction, while anthropometrics supplies relevant body measurements. Identify who will use the product, in what posture, for what task and under which constraints. A handle can fail through poor clearance or reach even if its material is strong. Select dimensions for an appropriate user range rather than assuming the average measurement suits everyone.

sections.heading: Build a prototype to answer a question
sections.body: A low-cost model can investigate grip, access, arrangement or proportion. A structural sample can investigate a joint or material choice. Decide the question before building, choose a method capable of answering it, and record observations clearly. A visual model alone cannot validate a loaded structure; a destructive test is not automatically appropriate for an assessed school product. Plan safe tests with the teacher.

sections.heading: Turn results into development
sections.body: Compare evidence with measurable specification criteria and relevant user feedback. Explain the cause of a weakness before proposing a change. A wider base may improve stability but use more space; a larger handle may improve clearance but interfere with storage. Retest an appropriate modified model or sample. Evaluation should document both strengths and limitations without fabricating a perfect outcome.

sections.heading: Use reach and clearance in different ways
sections.body:
A reach distance should suit users who cannot reach as far, while a clearance should usually allow for users who need more space. One average measurement may fail at both ends of a user range.

Consider posture, clothing, gloves and the actual task. Adjustable designs can accommodate variation, but adjustment adds cost and possible complexity. Explain why a selected measurement is appropriate rather than adding a percentile number without linking it to the product.

sections.heading: Test the task, not only a user’s first opinion
sections.body:
Ask a representative user to perform a defined task with a suitable prototype. Observe access, grip, visibility, force and errors as relevant. A statement that it “looks comfortable” is weaker than evidence of completing the task under the intended conditions.

Record limitations: a light card model may reveal layout problems but not the weight or stiffness of a final product. Use the findings to change a specific feature, then repeat the relevant test so improvement can be judged fairly.

topics.subject: Design & Technology
topics.title: Product analysis, lifecycle decisions and evidence-led evaluation

sections.heading: Start with a real user task
sections.body:
Identify who uses, carries, cleans or repairs the product and under which conditions. Examine the materials, construction, usability and appearance in that context.

Useful measurements and observations explain performance better than a list of likes and dislikes. Different users may need different features.

sections.heading: Make requirements testable
sections.body:
Turn a broad aim into a user, task, condition and a way to judge success. Use research to justify dimensions or loads.

Distinguish essential constraints from preferences. Anthropometric choices depend on whether you need reach, clearance or adjustment; one average size will not suit every user.

sections.heading: Consider the whole lifecycle
sections.body:
Material sourcing, manufacture, transport, use, maintenance and end-of-life all matter. Less material per item may not help if the product fails much sooner.

Compare alternatives providing the same function over a useful service period. Recycled content or local production is one consideration, not proof of the lowest total impact.

sections.heading: Use test results to make a specific change
sections.body:
Record the method, conditions, result and judgement against a requirement. User feedback can support measurements but should not replace all evidence.

Explain the cause of a weakness before changing the design. Assessed project records must come from genuine work, not invented research or tests.

sections.heading: Make an evaluation more useful than “it worked well”
sections.body:
For a portable storage product, describe whether it held the intended objects, whether the handle could be used under the stated conditions and whether any deformation appeared. Compare those results with the original criteria.

If one test fails, propose a change aimed at its cause and explain how you would retest it. Also record a strength you would retain. Evaluation should guide the next version, rather than acting as a decorative final page that declares every requirement met.

topics.subject: Design & Technology
topics.title: Drawing, modelling, CAD and CAM

sections.heading: Communicate enough for someone else to understand
sections.body: Freehand sketches explore ideas quickly; annotations explain operation, materials and construction. Orthographic views communicate shape and dimensions, while pictorial views help a user visualise the object. Keep projection conventions consistent and include dimensions in suitable units. An exploded view can clarify assembly, and a sectional view can reveal hidden construction.

sections.heading: Models should answer a design question
sections.body: A card model can test proportion or access; a mechanism model can test movement. Full-size ergonomic mock-ups reveal reach and comfort problems that a small visual model may miss. Record the question, method, observation and design change. A polished model that tests nothing is less informative than a rough model with a clear purpose.

sections.heading: Digital tools change the workflow
sections.body: CAD can support accurate geometry, rapid revision and visualisation. CAM can improve repeatability when the toolpath, material, fixtures and machine settings are appropriate. Digital manufacture still needs process planning, tolerances, tool access and safety supervision. Account for cutter diameter, stock thickness or kerf rather than assuming the screen model is identical to the final part.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A manufacturing drawing should provide dimensions that remove ambiguity without unnecessary duplication. Orthographic views must align and use consistent projection conventions; hidden detail should not be confused with a visible edge. A prototype can be a test of function, scale, fit or user interaction, and need not reproduce every final material. When using CAM, a nominal digital dimension can produce a different physical fit because of kerf, tool diameter, stock variation and machine calibration. Test critical joints or slots on a small sample before committing all the final parts.

sections.heading: Use each drawing to communicate a particular job
sections.body:
A pictorial drawing helps someone understand overall form. Orthographic views show dimensions and features needed for manufacture. Section views reveal details that would otherwise be hidden.

Keep related views aligned and avoid giving conflicting dimensions. State units and scale, and use the projection method required by the task. A drawing can look attractive yet still lack the hole position or material thickness needed to make the part. Check it from the maker’s point of view, not only the viewer’s.

sections.heading: Explain what a model actually proves
sections.body:
A card model may test size, layout or access, but it does not necessarily prove the strength of the final material. A joint sample can test a connection without showing the whole product’s appearance.

Choose the model to answer a specific uncertainty. CAD can help test fit and revise dimensions; CAM can reproduce a tool path. Incorrect dimensions, offsets or material settings can still produce incorrect parts consistently. Verify a trial component before relying on the digital process for a full batch.

topics.tip: A rendered CAD image does not by itself prove that parts fit or can be manufactured.

steps: Measure the actual stock thickness rather than assuming it equals the nominal value.
Check kerf and machine calibration because the cutting path removes material around the design line.

topics.subject: Design & Technology
topics.title: Life cycles, production and responsible design

sections.heading: Look beyond the finished object
sections.body: A product life cycle includes extraction, processing, manufacture, transport, use and end of life. A lightweight product may still have high production impacts; a durable product may use more material but last longer. Design decisions need an explicit boundary and context. Repairability, replaceable components and accessible fastenings can extend useful life.

sections.heading: Choose a production scale that fits demand
sections.body: One-off production suits individual requirements but has high unit labour costs. Batch production makes groups with shared setup; mass production uses high volumes and specialised systems. Standard components reduce design effort and can simplify repair. Tolerances specify acceptable variation and should match functional need and process capability, rather than assuming all parts can be made perfectly exact.

sections.heading: Sustainability includes practical trade-offs
sections.body: Reduce unnecessary material, consider reuse and select realistic recycling routes. A recyclable material is not guaranteed to be recycled if collection or separation is impractical. Laminates, permanent adhesives and mixed materials can complicate end of life. Responsible evaluation also considers workers, users, accessibility, cost and cultural context. Justify a choice with product-specific evidence rather than calling a material universally eco-friendly.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A tolerance communicates an acceptable interval, not a demand for absolute precision. Use tighter tolerances where fit or safety requires them, while considering the capability and cost of the chosen process. Quality-control checks inspect whether outputs meet requirements; quality-assurance arrangements establish processes intended to make consistent quality more likely. Batch planning should consider setup, material flow and standard components. Sustainable choices require a lifecycle comparison: a product that uses more material initially may have lower total impact if it lasts longer, is maintained and replaces repeated disposable alternatives.

sections.heading: Match production scale to quantity
sections.body:
One-off production makes a single item or individual design. Batch production makes a set number before the equipment or setup may change. Mass production makes large numbers of standardised products.

Special tooling can cost a lot initially but reduce the time or cost per part when many identical parts are made. For a one-off prototype, the same tooling may not be worthwhile. Compare setup cost, labour, repeatability, material waste and the actual quantity rather than choosing automation simply because it sounds advanced.

sections.heading: Compare products over an equal service period
sections.body:
A lightweight product may use less material per unit but need replacement more often. A heavier, repairable product might last longer. Compare the same function over a useful time period before judging the overall impact.

Maintenance, transport, electricity use and realistic recovery options all matter. A recycling symbol does not show that the material will actually be collected and processed locally. Explain the trade-off and identify missing evidence rather than claiming one environmental feature automatically makes the whole product sustainable.

topics.tip: Evaluate the product life cycle; changing one material does not automatically reduce every environmental impact.

worked.question: Give two design changes that improve the repairability of a small wooden storage product.
steps: Use accessible mechanical fasteners where repeated disassembly is needed.
Use replaceable standard parts rather than permanently bonding every component.
Explain how these choices permit a damaged part to be replaced without destroying the whole product.

topics.subject: Design & Technology
topics.title: Structures, mechanisms and safe control

sections.heading: Forces affect shape and stability
sections.body: Products experience tension, compression, bending, torsion and shear. Triangulation can make a frame more rigid because a triangle resists shape change without altering side lengths. A wide support base and suitable centre of gravity improve stability. Reinforcement should address the actual load path; adding material indiscriminately may add weight without solving the weakness.

sections.heading: Mechanisms transform movement
sections.body: Levers trade force and displacement about a pivot. Gears transfer rotary motion and change speed, torque or direction; meshing gears rotate oppositely. Cams convert rotary input into a chosen follower motion, while linkages can change direction or coordinate movement. Consider guarding, wear, lubrication and the user’s access to moving parts when developing a mechanism.

sections.heading: Control needs inputs, processing and outputs
sections.body: A control system receives an input, processes a decision and operates an output. Feedback compares the actual state with a target and adjusts behaviour. When using electrical or mechanical systems in a school project, select components with suitable ratings and seek teacher approval for equipment, loads and power supplies. Risk controls belong in the plan and working practice, not only in a final written list.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A design’s load path follows how forces pass through parts and joints into the supports. Reinforcing a surface far from the critical joint may not prevent the actual failure. Gears trade speed and torque according to their tooth ratio, while friction and other losses mean a real output does not receive all the input power. For feedback control, identify the measured variable, target, comparison and corrective output. A sensor alone is not a complete control system. Guarding should account for foreseeable user contact with pinch points and moving parts, alongside workshop operating instructions.

sections.heading: Explain bracing through the shape
sections.body:
A rectangular frame can change shape by racking if its corners can move. A diagonal brace makes triangles, which hold their shape more effectively without changing side lengths.

The brace must connect properly to the frame and carry the relevant tension or compression. A long thin compression member can buckle even when its material is strong. Position, section shape and unsupported length therefore matter alongside the material name. A decorative diagonal that is not joined securely may add little useful support.

sections.heading: Trace input, process and output
sections.body:
An input could be a switch or a sensor. The processing stage applies the control rule. An output device, such as a motor, light or buzzer, carries out the response.

For a temperature-controlled fan, the temperature sensor provides information, the controller compares it with a setting and the motor drives the fan. A suitable power interface may be needed because a small sensor signal cannot directly provide a motor’s current. Identify each role before discussing the circuit.

topics.tip: Mechanical advantage is not free energy: reducing effort force usually increases the distance moved.
