topics.subject: Design & Technology
topics.title: Project portfolio, manufacture and evaluation

sections.heading: The project records a developing argument
sections.body: For the 2027 course, the project contributes half of the qualification alongside two written components. A strong portfolio connects the identified need, research, specification, alternative ideas, development, production planning and evaluation. Keep evidence selective and legible. Your centre’s instructions, assessment criteria and authenticated work requirements govern the actual submission; revision notes do not replace teacher guidance.

sections.heading: Plan manufacturing before irreversible steps
sections.body: An ordered production plan identifies material preparation, marking, shaping, joining, assembly, finishing and checks. Include dimensions, tolerances, tools, fixtures and suitable safety controls. Record changes honestly when the process differs from the plan and explain the reason. Test critical interfaces early; discovering a fit problem before finishing is easier to correct than after final assembly.

sections.heading: Evaluate against the original requirements
sections.body: Test the product using methods appropriate to its intended use and safe school practice. Combine measured performance with relevant user feedback. Explain what met the specification, what did not and why. Propose specific realistic improvements and consider their consequences. A neat product with no meaningful testing is not fully evaluated; a thoughtful evaluation can identify limitations without pretending the design has none.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: An effective project record forms a chain of justified decisions. A finding from research should influence a specification point, idea or test; a failed model should lead to an explained development; a manufacturing change should be recorded with its reason. Separate evidence collected during the process from a reflection written afterwards. Evaluation should return to the original measurable criteria and include relevant user evidence, not only personal satisfaction. Proposed improvements should be sufficiently specific to test and should consider consequences for cost, construction and appearance. Follow the centre’s current authenticated-work requirements throughout.

sections.heading: Make development show a reasoned change
sections.body:
An initial sketch becomes useful development when it is tested or compared with requirements. If a handle is awkward, show what was observed, which feature caused the problem and how the next model changed it.

Annotations should explain materials, dimensions, operation or trade-offs, not just label obvious parts. Several nearly identical drawings do not automatically demonstrate development. Keep actual test findings, mistakes and limitations: they give a stronger basis for decisions than an invented perfect process.

sections.heading: Plan manufacture in a workable order
sections.body:
A production plan needs a sensible sequence. Marking and drilling may need to happen before a bend or assembly makes access difficult. Some surfaces may need finishing before they become enclosed.

Include the tools, holding arrangements, checks and relevant safety measures for each important stage under your centre’s guidance. Compare the finished result with the specification using evidence. The notes teach a method; the assessed research, manufacture and project record must reflect the student’s own genuine work.

topics.tip: Keep project work your own. Use Rian AI for explanations and feedback, not fabricated research or evidence.

topics.subject: Design & Technology
topics.title: Timbers and manufactured boards

sections.heading: Material families are starting points, not quality grades
sections.body: Hardwoods come from broad-leaved trees and softwoods from conifers; the names do not guarantee physical hardness. Timber is anisotropic: properties depend on grain direction. Knots, splits and moisture content influence strength and working behaviour. Seasoning reduces moisture to improve stability, but timber can still absorb or lose moisture in use.

sections.heading: Boards offer different compromises
sections.body: Plywood uses bonded veneers with alternating grain directions, giving useful dimensional stability. MDF has a uniform fibre structure and machines well but creates fine dust and needs suitable extraction. Chipboard is economical but edge strength and moisture resistance depend on grade. Veneers can improve appearance while using a different core material. Specify an appropriate board grade for wet or demanding environments.

sections.heading: Match property, process and product
sections.body: Choose timber for load, appearance, exposure, availability, cost and workability. Orient grain and position joints to support the expected forces. Plan how movement might affect panels and fastenings. Use finishes to protect or enhance surfaces, but do not treat a coating as a substitute for suitable material selection. Responsible sourcing matters alongside efficient cutting layouts and reduced waste.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: Solid wood movement is greatest across rather than along the grain, so wide panels may require construction that accommodates moisture-related dimensional change. Manufactured boards can reduce some variability but do not all behave alike. Plywood’s alternating veneers distribute grain directions; MDF offers a uniform machining surface but needs suitable dust control; chipboard performance depends on particle bonding and grade. Identify visible faces, exposed edges, fixing positions and expected moisture exposure before choosing a board. A decorative veneer changes the surface appearance but does not automatically change the core’s structural or moisture behaviour.

sections.heading: Allow for natural grain and movement
sections.body:
Wood is not equally strong in every direction. Grain affects splitting, surface quality and how a component carries a load. Knots and other defects can weaken or complicate a particular part.

Timber also changes dimensions as moisture content changes. A wide panel fixed rigidly across its movement can split or distort. Consider grain direction, joint design and the final environment together. A dry indoor project and an exposed outdoor component may need different material and construction choices.

sections.heading: Match a board’s core and surface to the task
sections.body:
Plywood uses bonded layers, usually with neighbouring grain directions arranged differently. MDF uses bonded wood fibres and gives a relatively uniform surface. Particleboard uses bonded particles and often needs suitable facing and edge treatment.

A veneer supplies a thin real-wood surface; it does not make the whole board solid timber. Compare thickness, grade, moisture suitability, edge quality and fixing behaviour. The best-looking surface does not guarantee the core will carry the required load.

topics.tip: Hardwood does not always mean physically harder than every softwood.

It can provide useful strength with relatively thin sections and good panel dimensions.
The actual choice must still account for plywood grade, edges, moisture exposure and joining.

topics.subject: Design & Technology
topics.title: Metals, polymers and material properties

sections.heading: Properties should be linked to the failure you want to avoid
sections.body: Strength concerns resistance to failure under load; stiffness concerns resistance to elastic deformation. Toughness concerns energy absorbed before fracture, and hardness concerns resistance to indentation or scratching. Ductility allows drawing into wire and malleability allows forming into sheet. A material can be hard yet brittle, so do not use strong, tough and hard as synonyms.

sections.heading: Metals and alloys provide specialised combinations
sections.body: Ferrous metals contain iron; corrosion behaviour depends on composition and treatment. Low-carbon steel can be readily formed and welded, stainless steels offer useful corrosion resistance, and aluminium alloys can provide low density. Copper is valued for electrical and thermal conductivity. Selection must balance required properties, manufacturing processes, cost, section form and environmental exposure.

sections.heading: Polymers respond differently to heat
sections.body: Thermoplastics can soften and be reshaped on heating within suitable processing limits. Thermosetting polymers form networks that do not remelt in the same way; overheating can degrade them. Additives and reinforcement modify properties. Acrylic may provide clarity but can crack under poor machining or stress; polypropylene is useful for some repeated-flexure applications. Identify the precise grade and process rather than relying only on the material family.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: Choose a property by considering the failure mode. A cover may need impact toughness rather than just scratch hardness; a shelf may need stiffness as well as strength. Section shape and thickness influence performance alongside material. Thermoplastic and thermosetting describe response to heat and molecular structure, not whether a product is generally strong. A polymer grade can contain fillers or reinforcement that changes behaviour. For metal selection, corrosion resistance, finish, forming, joining and cost must be considered together, because a suitable base material can still fail through an unsuitable joint or surface treatment.

sections.heading: Keep strength, hardness and toughness separate
sections.body:
Strength concerns resisting failure under load. Hardness concerns resisting indentation or scratching. Toughness concerns absorbing energy without fracture. These are not three names for the same property.

A cutting edge needs suitable hardness, while a component receiving impacts also needs toughness. Stiffness concerns how much something bends elastically under a load. A part can be strong enough not to break yet bend too much to work well. Explain the property needed in the particular product.

sections.heading: Use polymer type to explain heating behaviour
sections.body:
Thermoplastics can soften and be reshaped under suitable heating conditions. Thermosets do not remelt in the same way after their structure has cured. A thermoplastic is therefore needed for many heat-forming operations.

The exact grade still matters: not every thermoplastic has the same safe working temperature, impact strength or chemical resistance. A flexible sheet and a rigid moulding may both be polymers but suit different tasks. Avoid choosing a process from the general word “plastic” alone.

topics.tip: Stiffness and strength answer different questions: bending less is not the same as resisting fracture.

topics.subject: Design & Technology
topics.title: Choosing materials with evidence

sections.heading: Start with the failure mode
sections.body: A material decision should specify the product requirement before naming a material. A shelf needs adequate stiffness and load capacity; a transparent guard may need toughness, clarity and suitable heat resistance; an outdoor fitting may need corrosion resistance. Geometry, thickness, grain direction and support spacing influence the performance as well as the material name.

sections.heading: Compare realistic candidates
sections.body: Timber can offer appearance and workability but changes with moisture. Plywood can provide useful panel stability; MDF provides uniform machining behaviour but needs suitable dust control and a grade suited to exposure. Aluminium alloys offer low density, while steels can provide high stiffness for common structural uses. Polymers differ greatly in impact response, surface hardness, heat behaviour and processing. Select a grade, not an imagined universal material family.

sections.heading: Use evidence to justify the trade-off
sections.body: A comparison table should connect properties to the actual design. Explain why a disadvantage is acceptable or how it is addressed by construction. Consider available stock, processes, tools, finishes, cost, repair and end of life. A score without a stated basis can create false precision. Support the choice with prototype evidence or relevant material information, and revisit it if a test reveals an important failure.

sections.heading: Turn a property into a useful comparison
sections.body:
For a shelf, “strong” is less useful than a stated load, span and acceptable deflection. Two boards made from the same material can behave differently if their thickness or support changes.

A useful comparison keeps the test arrangement the same and changes the candidate material or section deliberately. Record mass, deflection, damage and other relevant results. A property table can narrow the choice, while a representative test helps judge the actual construction.

sections.heading: Explain why the final choice is a compromise
sections.body:
A lighter material may be easier to carry but need a thicker section. A corrosion-resistant alloy may cost more or require a different joining method. A beautiful surface may be difficult to repair.

Choose the option that best meets the important requirements, then explain the disadvantages you accept and how the design deals with them. Naming one advantage does not show that a choice beats all alternatives. Identify which evidence would change your decision if the conditions changed.

topics.subject: Design & Technology
topics.title: Timber conversion, seasoning and choosing a manufactured board

sections.heading: Link timber properties to the product
sections.body:
Species, grain, defects and moisture affect strength, appearance and working behaviour. Hardwood and softwood are botanical groups, not guaranteed rankings of hardness.

Name the stock and the job it must do. A shelf, handle and decorative panel can need different combinations of properties.

sections.heading: Explain seasoning as moisture control
sections.body:
Conversion cuts a log into usable sections. Seasoning reduces moisture to a suitable level for use.

Timber that dries after manufacture can shrink, warp or split. Air and kiln seasoning differ in time and control. The goal is suitable moisture content, not removing every trace of water.

sections.heading: Compare boards by their construction
sections.body:
Plywood uses bonded layers. MDF uses wood fibres. Particleboard uses particles. Each has grades and thicknesses with different suitable uses.

A veneer supplies a thin wood surface; it does not turn the core into solid wood. Check edges, fixing behaviour, moisture suitability and load needs.

sections.heading: Design around the stock you will actually use
sections.body:
Measure actual thickness before finalising fits. Choose joints and fixings suited to the material, especially near board edges.

A finish can help protect a surface but cannot make every board suitable outdoors. Use approved dust control and workshop methods when making samples or parts.

sections.heading: Explain why a large panel may need room to move
sections.body:
Natural timber can change width as its moisture content changes. If a wide panel is locked tightly across that movement, stresses can cause splitting, distortion or damaged joints.

A suitable design allows for the expected movement without losing the panel’s function. Manufactured boards can offer greater stability, but their grade and exposure limits still matter. Material choice and joint design should be considered together: replacing the timber name alone may not solve a construction problem.

topics.title: Alloys, heat treatment and protecting a metal product

sections.heading: Compare the properties the product needs
sections.body:
Strength, hardness, stiffness, toughness and density describe different behaviours. A hard edge and a tough frame do not have identical requirements.

An alloy combines a metal with other elements to obtain useful properties. The grade, stock shape, joining process and cost are part of the choice.

sections.heading: Match heat treatment to the material
sections.body:
Annealing can soften suitable material or relieve stresses. Hardening suitable steel can increase hardness but leave it brittle; tempering adjusts the balance with toughness.

The effect depends on composition and the full process. A treatment name used for one alloy cannot simply be transferred to every other metal.

sections.heading: Distinguish barrier and sacrificial protection
sections.body:
Paint can keep the environment away from steel where coverage remains sound. A scratch can expose it.

Zinc on galvanised steel can also corrode preferentially, protecting nearby iron under suitable conditions. A decorative coating does not necessarily have this extra mechanism.

sections.heading: Plan protection through manufacture and use
sections.body:
Joining or cutting can damage an existing coating. Enclosed areas and cut edges may be hard to protect later.

Choose the finish order and maintenance plan accordingly. Evaluate adhesion, wear or corrosion using relevant evidence. A shiny appearance alone does not prove long-term protection.

sections.heading: Explain why hardness is not the only useful property
sections.body:
A very hard component may resist surface damage but still fracture under an impact if it is too brittle. A part expected to bend slightly or absorb knocks needs a suitable balance of properties.

For a tool, the edge may need to stay hard while the whole item must resist breaking in normal service. Explain the expected load and failure mode before choosing an alloy or treatment. The highest value in one property column is not automatically the best material.

topics.subject: Design & Technology
topics.title: Measuring, marking, cutting and shaping

sections.heading: Accuracy begins with a datum
sections.body: A datum is a reference surface, edge or line from which other measurements are made. Establish square, flat references before marking. Use an appropriate rule, square, marking gauge or measuring instrument for the required tolerance. Mark waste and identify paired parts. Repeatedly measuring from previously cut edges can accumulate error; reference critical dimensions consistently.

sections.heading: Select a process for the material and shape
sections.body: Sawing removes stock along a planned cut, drilling makes holes, filing refines edges and suitable machining produces controlled forms. Account for the saw kerf and finish to the line where needed. For a hole, centre marking and secure workholding improve positioning. Tool choice, speed and feed depend on the material, tool and school equipment guidance.

sections.heading: Make quality control part of the sequence
sections.body: Check dimensions, squareness, fit and surface condition at stages where correction is still possible. Use jigs for repeatable positioning and fixtures for secure support, distinguishing their roles where required. Keep guards, extraction and appropriate protective equipment in use. Never hold a workpiece by hand for a machine operation that requires clamping, and follow trained supervision rather than improvising a technique from notes.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A process plan needs a datum strategy as well as nominal dimensions. Mark critical features from a consistent reference and check the reference remains square and undamaged. Tool geometry affects the final shape: an internal milled corner cannot be sharper than the cutter permits without another operation. A jig can guide repeatable tool positioning, while a fixture securely locates or holds the work. Measure at points where an error can still be corrected. Workshop safety depends on trained supervision, correct guarding and secure workholding, not merely a list of protective clothing in the portfolio.

sections.heading: Measure from a common datum
sections.body:
A datum is a reference face, edge or line. Measuring several hole positions from the same datum avoids adding one small spacing error to the next.

For holes at 20, 40 and 60 mm from an end, measure those positions from that end rather than stepping along with separate 20 mm measurements. Check the stock’s actual size and squareness before marking. A precise scale reading is not useful if the reference edge itself is wrong.

sections.heading: Allow for material removed by the process
sections.body:
A cut has width, called the kerf. Mark the waste side and allow the appropriate finishing material rather than cutting through the required final line indiscriminately.

Filing, sanding and other finishing operations can change dimensions further. A fitting surface may need closer control than a hidden decorative edge. Check key sizes during manufacture while they can still be corrected. Use suitable clamping, tools and the workshop’s approved procedures for each operation.

topics.title: Joints, adhesives, fasteners and assembly

sections.heading: A joint must suit its forces and construction
sections.body: Butt joints are simple but may need reinforcement; housings locate shelves; mortise-and-tenon arrangements provide useful frame connections. Dowel and finger joints offer other positioning or glue-area advantages. The best joint depends on section size, grain, load direction, access, equipment and whether disassembly is needed. A named joint without a contextual reason is only a partial justification.

sections.heading: Permanent and removable connections differ
sections.body: Screws, bolts and suitable fittings permit some disassembly; adhesives can produce continuous bonded areas but may complicate repair. Choose adhesive for both materials, service conditions, surface preparation and cure requirements. Clamp correctly without forcing parts out of alignment. Metal joining includes mechanical fastening, soldering, brazing and welding, each with different operating temperatures, joint properties and safety requirements.

sections.heading: Assembly order can determine whether a design is possible
sections.body: Trial-fit critical parts before final bonding or finishing. Check squareness, clearances and fastener access. Consider which surfaces will become inaccessible and whether a component must be inserted before closing an assembly. Allow for material movement and use appropriate pilot or clearance holes. A production drawing should communicate the joint detail and required fit, not leave the manufacturer to guess.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A joint may carry tension, shear, bending or a combination, and its shape and fastenings should address those loads. Adhesive joints require compatible materials, suitable surface preparation, the correct bond-line conditions and adequate cure. A large bonded area can help, but poor fit or contamination can still make it fail. Removable fasteners need access for assembly and later maintenance. Plan the assembly sequence so a tool can reach each fixing and a captured component is inserted before its enclosure is closed. A successful trial fit should be checked before applying a finish that changes clearances.

sections.heading: Follow the load through the joint
sections.body:
Consider where a force enters one component and how it reaches the next. A shelf may transfer load through bearing surfaces, screws, adhesive or a combination. A small end-grain butt joint is different from a well-supported housing.

Identify whether a joint is likely to pull apart, slide, rotate or rack. Reinforcement should address that failure mode. Adding more fixings randomly can split a thin edge or make repair harder without solving the main load-path problem.

sections.heading: Plan access and assembly order
sections.body:
A screw or nut must be reachable with the intended tool. A permanent bond may prevent later replacement of a worn part. Design access, clearances and component order before making the final assembly.

Check adhesive compatibility, surface preparation, fit and curing instructions. A joint that seems firm immediately after assembly may not have developed its intended strength. A representative sample can test the connection before it becomes difficult to alter inside the finished product.

topics.tip: Adhesive performance depends strongly on preparation and curing; more adhesive is not automatically a stronger joint.

topics.subject: Design & Technology
topics.title: Forming, casting, heat treatment and finishes

sections.heading: Shape can be added, removed or transformed
sections.body: Subtractive processes remove material; forming changes shape; casting introduces material into a mould. Thermoplastic sheet can be heated and formed within a safe controlled process. Metal sheet may be bent around suitable tooling. Casting needs allowance for material flow, shrinkage and removal. The appropriate process depends on quantity, shape complexity, material and available equipment.

sections.heading: Treatment changes the working behaviour
sections.body: Annealing can soften suitable metals and reduce effects of prior working; hardening and tempering can modify suitable steels. The process and outcome depend on composition, heating, cooling and supervision. Do not assume every metal responds identically. A school revision explanation describes the principle; it is not a safe procedure for unsupervised furnaces, molten material or chemical treatment.

sections.heading: A finish protects as well as communicates quality
sections.body: Paint, varnish, oil, wax, plating and other treatments have different appearance, wear and maintenance properties. Prepare the substrate, remove defects and ensure compatibility between layers. Some finishes protect against corrosion or moisture while others mainly enhance appearance. Plan masking and inaccessible surfaces. Specify ventilation, drying and disposal according to the product instructions and workshop rules.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: Casting design must permit the pattern or finished part to be removed from its mould, allowing for geometry, shrinkage and the chosen mould system. A forming process changes shape without the same material removal as machining, but can introduce springback or thinning. Heat-treatment effects depend on composition and the complete heating-and-cooling process; applying a term such as annealing without naming the material and intended property is incomplete. Surface finishing can improve protection and appearance but needs preparation, compatible layers and appropriate drying or curing. Follow product instructions and school procedures for ventilation, heat and chemical handling.

sections.heading: Explain why a casting pattern needs careful geometry
sections.body:
A casting takes shape in a mould. The pattern or finished part must be removable in the chosen process, so draft, parting arrangements and undercuts matter. Material can also shrink as it cools or sets.

A shape that looks correct in a drawing may need allowances or a different mould construction before it can be made. A trial should check useful details such as fill, release and finishing, not only whether some material entered the mould.

sections.heading: Treat a finish as a functional layer
sections.body:
A finish can improve appearance, protect against exposure or change how a surface feels. Its success depends on a sound substrate, preparation and compatibility.

Paint cannot repair a weak joint, and a decorative coat does not automatically make a material waterproof or suitable for food contact. Coating thickness may also affect a close fit. Plan access and drying or curing before assembly where needed, using the product instructions and school handling procedures.

topics.tip: A finish cannot reliably repair a poorly fitting joint or an unsuitable base material.

topics.title: Designing reliable joints, fixings and adhesive bonds

sections.heading: Start with the force and service needs
sections.body:
Identify whether the joint mainly pulls apart, slides, bends or twists. Think about repeated loading and the product’s environment.

A permanent bond may suit one product while an accessible fixing suits another. The strongest permanent joint is not automatically the best choice for a replaceable part.

sections.heading: Make geometry and preparation support the adhesive
sections.body:
Adhesive needs suitable materials, clean surfaces, a good fit and the right curing conditions. Useful contact area and joint shape matter.

A housing or suitable frame joint can locate parts and improve the connection. More adhesive alone does not guarantee strength. Follow the chosen adhesive’s instructions.

sections.heading: Choose holes and fixings for their jobs
sections.body:
A pilot hole prepares or guides suitable screw engagement. A clearance hole lets a shank pass without gripping that component. Countersinking seats a suitable head flush.

Check edge distance, thickness and repeated removal. A fixing that works in solid timber may not work equally well in a thin board edge.

sections.heading: Test a representative sample
sections.body:
Use the intended material, thickness, geometry and loading direction where practical. Record movement, damage and the conditions used.

One static test does not prove unlimited fatigue or weather resistance. Also check tool access and assembly order: the joint must be possible to make and maintain in the final product.

sections.heading: Compare a removable joint with a permanent bond
sections.body:
If a seat pad will wear out, screws into suitable reusable fixings may allow replacement while keeping the main frame. A permanent adhesive could make that repair destructive.

The removable option still needs enough strength and a way to prevent unwanted loosening. Explain both the benefit and the design work it creates. “Use screws because they are removable” is a starting point; a complete choice also checks material engagement, access and expected service loads.

topics.title: Thermoforming, injection moulding and designing for release

sections.heading: Choose a suitable polymer type
sections.body:
Thermoplastics soften under suitable heating and can be reshaped. Thermosets do not remelt in the same way after curing.

Name the exact material or grade where needed. Temperature, thickness, toughness and finish affect the process choice. Use approved heating and ventilation arrangements.

sections.heading: Follow vacuum forming
sections.body:
A suitable thermoplastic sheet is heated, drawn against a mould by a pressure difference, cooled, released and trimmed.

Draft and venting help the form release and develop detail. Deep draws and sharp corners can cause thinning. An undercut may trap the shell on a simple mould.

sections.heading: Explain injection moulding for repeated parts
sections.body:
Softened polymer enters a closed mould and cools enough for the part to be ejected. Dedicated tooling costs more initially but can produce consistent parts repeatedly.

Wall thickness, gates, split lines and release affect the design. For a one-off model, expensive tooling may not be justified.

sections.heading: Use a prototype to test a manufacturing question
sections.body:
A shape model can check form or fit, while a manufacturing trial checks whether the chosen process can produce it.

Inspect release direction, thin areas, fixing features and finishing access. Compare quantity, setup cost, cycle time and waste rather than selecting a process from appearance alone.

sections.heading: See why an undercut changes the tooling problem
sections.body:
Imagine a formed shell wrapping behind a projecting hook on a one-piece mould. Pulling the shell straight off would make it hit the hook, so the simple release path is blocked.

A designer might change the hook, change the release direction or investigate a more complex tool. The right solution depends on material flexibility, shape and production needs. A draft angle helps release along a direction, but it does not automatically remove every trapping feature.

topics.subject: Design & Technology
topics.title: Tolerances, jigs, quality control and repeatable batches

sections.heading: Turn a tolerance into limits
sections.body:
A dimension of 20.0 ± 0.2 mm allows values from 19.8 to 20.2 mm. Choose the tolerance from function, such as the fit needed.

Tighter limits can need more careful processes and inspection. Applying the tightest possible tolerance everywhere can add cost without improving the product.

sections.heading: Give templates, jigs and fixtures their roles
sections.body:
A template helps transfer a shape or position. A jig helps guide an operation or tool. A fixture locates and holds the work.

A device may combine roles. Check its references, holding and clearances before using it repeatedly: a wrong setup can reproduce the same error across a batch.

sections.heading: Check at useful stages
sections.body:
Incoming material, partly finished parts and completed products can need different checks. An early hole-position check may prevent expensive later rework.

Use a clear datum and a suitable measuring tool. A go/no-go gauge checks an acceptance condition quickly but may not give the exact dimension.

sections.heading: Start with a trial part
sections.body:
Verify the setup, process sequence and result before making the whole batch. Watch for tool wear, loose stops or material changes.

Repeatability means consistency, not correctness. A batch of identically wrong parts still fails the specification. Record results and investigate trends rather than checking only appearance.

sections.heading: Distinguish a fixed offset from random variation
sections.body:
If every hole is 2 mm too far left, the setup or datum may be wrong. Making the operation more repeatable will not remove that offset. Correct the reference or jig, then verify a new trial part.

If hole positions vary unpredictably, check holding, wear, measurement or process control. The pattern of the results helps choose the remedy. Collect actual measurements where practical instead of reducing every observation to a simple pass/fail tick.

topics.subject: Design & Technology
topics.title: Structures, motion and electronic control

sections.heading: Choose the option deliberately
sections.body: Systems & Control is an alternative 2027 specialist route, not an additional compulsory paper for the Resistant Materials route. Structures carry loads through frames and members, while mechanisms transmit motion. Identify compression and tension in members and explain how triangulation, section shape or reinforcement influences stiffness and load capacity.

sections.heading: Mechanisms trade speed, direction and force
sections.body: A gear train’s tooth counts determine its speed ratio. Belts, pulleys, chains and sprockets offer different alignment and slip properties. Cams and linkages convert motion patterns. Bearings reduce friction and support moving shafts. Explain a mechanism using its input, output and intermediate interactions; saying it makes the product work does not establish its suitability.

sections.heading: Electronic systems connect sensing to response
sections.body: An input such as a light or temperature sensor changes an electrical signal. A processing stage compares, switches or amplifies, and an output such as a lamp, motor or buzzer responds. Use component ratings, suitable power supplies and protection. Feedback can maintain a controlled condition. Circuit and mechanical tests should use approved school equipment and teacher-guided methods.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A gear train’s ratio depends on the driver and driven tooth counts, while an idler changes direction or spacing without changing the overall simple ratio between the first and last gears. A belt drive may slip under load, which can be either a limitation or a protective effect in a suitable design. A feedback diagram should separate sensor, comparison and output stages. Real electronic outputs may need a driver stage because a sensor or logic output cannot directly supply a motor’s current. Select safe low-voltage components and ratings using approved school guidance.

sections.heading: Use gear teeth to calculate a speed change
sections.body:
For a simple gear pair, output speed/input speed equals driver teeth/driven teeth. A 12-tooth driver turning a 36-tooth driven gear reduces output speed to one-third. Adjacent external gears rotate in opposite directions.

An idler changes the arrangement or overall direction without changing the simple ratio between the first and last gears. A reduction can increase available torque in an ideal model, but real systems have losses. Do not claim speed and torque both increase without an extra energy source.

sections.heading: Explain feedback as a comparison
sections.body:
A closed-loop control system measures the output or a related condition and compares it with the desired setting. The controller changes the output in response to the difference.

A thermostat-controlled heater uses temperature information to regulate heating. A timed heater running for a fixed duration without checking temperature is a different arrangement. Name the sensor, the comparison and the actuator. The controller must also use a suitable interface and power supply for the output device.

topics.subject: Design & Technology
topics.title: Projection, developments and graphic manufacture

sections.heading: Draw the information the reader needs
sections.body: Graphic Products is another 2027 specialist route. Orthographic drawings communicate separate aligned views, while isometric and perspective views help visualise form. Add dimensions, line conventions and annotations appropriately. Construction accuracy and clarity matter more than decorative shading when the question asks for a technical view.

sections.heading: Flat developments need working allowances
sections.body: A development unfolds a three-dimensional surface into a two-dimensional pattern. Packaging nets need tabs, closures, folds and allowances for actual material thickness. Grain direction, scoring and bending influence performance. Test a model to check that faces meet and that a user can open, close and carry the package without damaging it.

sections.heading: Presentation and manufacture use material constraints
sections.body: Typography, contrast, hierarchy and layout make information readable. Paper, card, boards and suitable polymers have differing stiffness, surface and forming properties. Printing, cutting, folding, joining and finishing must fit the quantity and use. CAD and CAM can improve repeatability, but the designer still needs to account for registration, tool geometry, tolerances and disposal or recycling routes.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A packaging development should show fold and cut lines distinctly and include tabs or other closures that can actually be assembled. Material thickness changes how adjacent faces meet, while grain direction and scoring influence fold quality. For a technical drawing, choose line conventions and views for construction information; for communication graphics, use contrast and hierarchy so the intended message remains legible at the final size. A physical prototype checks more than the flat outline: test fitting, opening, closing, carrying and protection using the intended objects or a safe representative load.

sections.heading: Keep orthographic views aligned
sections.body:
An orthographic drawing shows separate views, such as front, plan and end. Their alignment lets the maker connect a feature across views. Use the projection arrangement required and keep dimensions consistent.

Hidden detail should use the appropriate line conventions. A pictorial view can help explain form, but does not replace the exact sizes and positions needed for manufacture. State scale and units, and check that a hole or fold is located unambiguously rather than only looking approximately right.

sections.heading: Test a development as a folded object
sections.body:
A development is the flat pattern that forms a three-dimensional surface. Packaging also needs practical fold lines, cut lines, tabs and closures. Material thickness and fold behaviour affect how the faces meet.

Make a suitable full-size prototype to check fit with the intended contents, opening, carrying and assembly. A correct outline alone does not prove that the closure stays shut or the package protects its contents. Graphic information must remain legible after folding, trimming and printing.

topics.tip: A net that looks correct flat may still fail when folded in a real material.

worked.question: Why should a packaging net be tested using a physical model before production?
steps: It checks whether faces, folds and tabs assemble into the intended form.
It reveals closure, fit and handling problems affected by material thickness.
The pattern can be corrected before committing to a production batch.
